FIRST PART I HISTORY OF DONATISM I. BIRTH 1. Causes

The origins of that complex religious phenomenon and mother of all divisions that was the D. * respond to multiple, close and remote causes. On the one hand, the geopolitical context of a history that is at once ethnographic, social, economic, cultural and political, whose key term is Romanization. This movement provokes in North Africa, in the face of clear adhesions from the upper classes of society, feelings of protest and rebellion on the part of the humble and proletarian people, indigenous or rural Berbers, for the most part determined to shake off the controlling yoke of Rome. Inclined towards the theological, the great specialist P. Monceaux did not highlight this nuance of anti-Roman resentment with the intensity later reached by F. Martroye, G. Willis and Ch. Courtois?, whom he surpasses in his controversial thesis P. Brisson?.

It is necessary to add, on the other hand, and, given its importance, of course also put first, the religious factor, especially in its theological and ecclesiastical dimensions. The D. is a Western schism whose first circumstances must be studied without disregarding Carthage and the African writers Tertullian and Cyprian, nor Rome and the prominence exercised there by Cornelius, Novatian and Stephen 1. In addition, as is logical, the respective influences and environments. The crime of traditor, for example, a fundamental Donatist pretext to justify the schism, has connotations very similar to those of the lapsi of 250. 2. Events and prominences
between the years 303 and 312

The opinion of scholars when dating the Donatist origins ranges between the years 306-307 and 311-312. O. Seeck, Duchesne, Monceaux and Barnes, among others, point to 307, while W. H. C. Frend and K. Clancy *, after discussing the dates of the former, have recently leaned towards 311-312. Everything will depend on the criteria that prevail when analyzing this chronological parenthesis.

On February 23, 303, Diocletian decrees a persecution of Christians, the last systematic and concrete persecution of imperial history. Thus he comes to renew the anti-religious policy of Emperor Decius and the anti-church policy of Galerius*. Preceded by a repressive anti-Manichean action, four successive edicts will trigger this great persecution of the years 303-305. On May 19, 303, he arrived in Numidia who urgently needed to deliver (=tradere, hence traditores) the books of the Holy Scriptures. It also orders the confiscation of ecclesiastical property and, if necessary, the destruction of churches. In February 304, a second edict provides for obligatory incense to the gods of the Empire (=*hurificatio, from which comes thurificatores). As in ancient persecutions, in this one too there are some—the few—who stand out for their heroism, often fanatical, in the face of the cowardly attitude of the majority. Many circumstances of when the lapses are repeated now with the traditores and turificadores $.

Many clerics, bishops among them, obey the imperial order by delivering the Holy Books, whose destiny is already known to be fire. This brief, although violent, persecution costs the Church of Africa its martyrs 7. Among those who manage to resist, once the storm is over, in the spring of 305, there will be no shortage of those who see in the weak traditors true apostates and traitors to Christianity *.

It turns out that on March 5, 305 - 307 according to Lancel - the first Donatist council met in Cirta for some, a simple assembly or council for the majority, certainly the oldest episcopal meeting of the future schismatics. Prepared to consecrate Silvanus, they are suddenly struck by a scruple that will not take long to add to the Donatist theses: "the sacrament can only be conferred by irreproachable clergy." Segundo de Tigisi, therefore, first tries to make sure whether those present are worthy of laying on hands. There are those who do not come out well, but they all end up turning a blind eye, With which a precedent is set for the left-handed Donatist maneuvers. IT. CONSOLIDATION AND DEVELOPMENT 1. Before Emperor Constantine

We will see how the D. faced this legislative cornering in this same introduction, but later. At first glance it gives the impression of finding ourselves before a martyr Church, persecuted within its meekness. Reality, however, requires clarifying that the D. was never characterized by nurturing pacifist sentiments, and that precisely this legal chapter belongs to one of the moments of most ruthless anti-Catholic persecution, ultimately extending to those, whether inside or outside, who did not agree with the ideas of the party. The name of Optato of Tamugadi would be enough to realize what some leaders were capable of, given the worst.

Upon the death of Parmenian (391/2) the great internal schism of Maximianism occurred, causing considerable deterioration in the cohesion and stability of the "Church of the Martyrs." The succession of Parmenianus falls on Primianus, a rude man, little less than coarse and ignorant, a notorious exponent of the Numidian circles, which were the most intransigent and radical. On the contrary, together with the relative of the great Donatus and his adversary Maximian, the moderate sectors were grouped, with to a certain extent flexible ideas and disposition, typical of proconsular Africa and Byzacena *.

Initially, the advantage went to the Maximianists. No less than one hundred bishops, mostly from the Byzacena *, agreed on June 24, 393, at the council of Cabarsusa, to condemn Primianus as a consequence of some disciplinary infractions. But the force majeure was on the radical side. So it took little effort for Primianus to gather on April 24, 394, and in Bagai, a city in Southern Numidia, another council of three hundred and ten bishops, who responded by excommunicating the Maximianists of Cabarsusa, with which the schism within the Schism was consummated *. Such had been the solidity achieved under Parmeniano, that at the beginning of this internal division, it can even be said that in some successive years, the open wound in the party produced less havoc than normally foreseeable. Saint Augustine and Optatus of Milevi continue to be sources of the first order, not only because they have, especially the first, entire works dedicated to the controversy, but because they have incorporated into the text, for a more effective reply, literature specific to the movement, from its most illustrious leaders, now lost or which at least has come to us in a fragmentary form in the original, and which in this way we can to a certain extent recompose. II. The CIRCUMCELIONS

The critical phenomenon of the previous section is repeated in this one. The circumceliones reflect, after all, the economic-social aspect of the D. and, in a certain way, the religious one. Here too, Saint Augustine and Optatus of Milevi provide precious references when descending into a theological analysis of the suffering caused to the Catholic Church with the circumcelionic persecutions. But the abundant descriptive material about places, events and actions, as well as the study of their historical, political and psychological facets, so enriched recently thanks to certain finds of epigraphic and funerary tenor, force, once again, the corresponding rereading of the traditional sources.

What the circumceliones represented within the D. is something yet to be seen in its exact limits. The same thing happens with his true condition. Vagrant monks? Uncontrolled bandits? Hired thugs? 1. Definition and actions

Saint Augustine explains that circumceliones comes from circum cellas vagantur, that is, those who wandered through the cells or caves in search of food *, mainly in partibus Numidiae et Mauretaniae *. Apparently, the Donatists themselves rejected the term circumceliones as insulting; an insult %. Their custom preferred, rather, agonists, that is, combatants of God; or milites Christi, that is, soldiers of Christ.

In the short space of these lines we already find disparate interpretations: some (Frend), of cellae, tombs of the martyrs; others (Calderone), from cotopitae, a Latin word transliteralized from the Coptic cutzupitae, or cutzupitani, according to a text from the Commentary on the Apocalypse, by Tyconius, in which hypothesis the circumceliones would be a class of wandering monks *,

The origins remain uncertain. In the commotion that arose when the episcopal election of Silvanus of Cirta, in 307, as narrated thirteen years later *, a group outside the town (= Campenses) stood out for its violent emergence, which, according to Lancel, offers marked similarities with the future Circumcelion movement. What happens is that the philological basis of this hypothesis is weak?

2. Interpretation of specialists

Naturally, modern historians have not forgotten the Augustinian indications, nor, of course, the law of Honorius issued on January 30, 412, nor the social climate prevailing at the end of the 15th century and the first half of the 5th when addressing the issue of the circumcelions. It happens, however, that some have done so by applying to those circumstances social criteria that are more typical of our days, and the result could not have been other than seeing true revolutionaries in the circumcelions, according to the scheme of the class struggle.

Furthermore, there is a Russian literature determined to want to discover in this movement precedents of the class struggle typical of Marx and the socialist countries *, without a lack of authors who openly censure Saint Augustine for his "partiality" in the matter, regretting, furthermore, that the sources we have come precisely from adversaries to the cause like him %. In the relationship that follows, two lines stand out: the political-social and the religious.

In 1948, Dmitrev denied that the agonists had anything to do with the circumcelions or wandering monks described by the Bishop of Hippo, who would have united some and others to compromise them before the Roman authorities. Frend's conclusion in 1983 was that the Donatist leaders initially rejected the Circumcelions, as Optatus allows us to deduce (111 4)", although later they welcomed them and even acted as a leader, so that today we can affirm that the schismatic Church ended up associated, whether admitted or not, with a movement radicalized in its demands for social reform.

It is difficult, even so, to fully admit what Frend says, and even that "fluke relationship" proposed by Congar. The incident of the schismatic Donatus of Bagai calling the circumcelions to his aid seems to me to go beyond the limits of a simple coincidence. And what is not acceptable is to judge these African terrorists exclusively by their social face. TIT. DONATIST OPPOSITION TO THE ROMAN EMPIRE

Catholics and Donatists adopt different attitudes towards the Roman Empire: the former loyal, the latter avowedly hostile. Since both parties adduced reasons, it will be important to know them at least as much as to record the phenomenon itself. As far as D. is concerned, it is urgent to distinguish well between the determining factors of its birth and those that later contributed to its expansion. Religious and theological causes predominated in the origins, to which others of a social and cultural nature were soon added. But neither one nor the other are exclusive, because if the D. finds expansion also due to religious reasons, it is equally necessary to recognize that perhaps he would not have been able to prosper if he had not found, from the beginning, a rebellious and rebellious environment due to the social climate, already established by the dates of his birth *.

Recovering the psychology of the martyrs and the apocalyptic tradition of North African Christianity greatly attracted Christians from rural communities, for whom the administrative and fiscal reform of Diocletian and Constantine meant the imposition of heavy taxes. This double dimension—political and religious—explains that the Schism intended from the first moment to remain within a religious conservatism while being open to a social avant-garde eager to break the oppressive and controlling siege *,

It was left behind, regarding the Donatist origins, that rivalries of religious scope reigned between the Proconsular and Numidia. The most active Donatist centers were located in inland Numidia. TII THE THEOLOGY OF THE DONATIST CHURCH IL. SCHISM OR HERESY? *

The answer is easy for modern authors: schism and heresy. The question in the 15th century was, on the contrary, complicated, because the Catholic-Donatist differences, explainable due to the sectarian and conservative spirit of the party, were of a schismatic order, just as the Latins had been understanding the term schism since the 111th century?, but not to be simply inscribed in the catalog of heresies. At most, perhaps heratic hints could be discovered with these data: 1) that the Donatists seem to have moved somewhat closer to Arianism at the council of Serdica in 343 *; 2) that the work on the Trinity, by Donatus the Great, shows dangerous concessions in this sense *; 3) that when the Arian Goths invaded Italy, at the beginning of the 5th century, the Donatists attempted to reach an agreement with them, but in order to prevent possible reprisals *. As the reader will understand, all this is not enough to advance the thesis of an Arian D..

When the official split occurred in 312, the spacious territory of the African Church included six administrative provinces, of which only one, Numidia, was clearly constituted. Since 305, in fact, Segundo de Tigisi had been acting as primate of the Numidian Churches. The ecclesial communities of the other regions, Mauretania, Tripolitania, Byzacena, etc., did not yet integrate distinct groups, but, as in the time of Saint Cyprian, depended directly on the bishop of Carthage, supreme head of the Church of Africa. TII. HOLY SCRIPTURE IN DONATISM

The foundation of Donatist theology was Holy Scripture. Same as in Catholics. Although schismatic, the Church of Donatus, mostly of course its hierarchs and theologians, boasted of its constant recourse to the sacred text, for the entire ecclesial life in general, but with special interest in what was related to theological truths, and whenever circumstances demanded it for exposition or defense of the theses during the dispute with the Catholics. The crux of the matter is none other than the famous Donatist Bible.
Quite conservative, the Donatists adhered diligently, one might even say obstinately, to the African Bible. The Catholics, on the other hand, made use of the Vulgate.

There is good reason for those who think this way, since during the first centuries of our era it turns out that in proconsular Africa only Latin was spoken, while the most known and spoken language in Rome until the 111th century was that of Homer. It is, therefore, logical to assume that a Latin version of the Bible was then judged less necessary in the metropolis than in the Proconsular. The same could be said of Spain, Gaul and northern Italy, where the predominant linguistic current at that time was, as in the Proconsular, Latin, and where the corresponding Latin version must have arrived very soon, although there are those who, despite what has been said, prefer to attribute the first to Rome, or at least to Italy.

Three great controversies occupied and worried Saint Augustine: Manichaeism, Donatism and Pelagianism. The second is, chronologically, before and after his biography'. When he comes into the world (354), many things will have already happened between Catholics and Donatists. Recently converted, upon his return from Rome (388), he found a strong and well-organized Schism spread throughout Africa, of which there is copious historical material in ecclesiastical and civil archives. Important Catholic figures until then, the truth is, there has only been one: Optato de Milevi?.

The favorable policy of Julian the Apostate, on the one hand, and the effective government of Parmenian, on the other, gave the party that push that, from the first moment of his intervention, the young presbyter of Hippo must face. Very soon his entry into the controversy will be noticed. It must also be said that the terrible management of the intransigent Primiano, without the excellent skills of his predecessor Parmeniano, will also contribute to this. At that time, the D. Hiponense was a hostile majority, with well-organized propaganda and aggressiveness at the ready through the fanatical bands of circumceliones? Perhaps this is one of the main reasons for the survey that the Bishop of Hippo opened during the summer of 404 in the Proconsular. It appears that the survey mostly covered geographical areas of Asuras and Musti, as well as Membresa and Abitina, the latter localities in which feuding Donatists fought frequent battles. The idea of ​​opening surveys and verbal processes regarding disputes between primianists and maximianists came from the council held in Carthage on September 13, 401. Was it those mutual violence that awakened in the Bishop of Hippo the need to learn more about this resource filed by the primianists before the civil authority for the repression of their dissidents, the Maximianists? The data, as an argument to be used by the Catholic Church against the Donatists, was priceless.

II. METHODOLOGY IN THE ANTIDONATIST CONTROVERSY

In principle it is possible to say that very similar procedures and characteristics predominate in the Bishop of Hippo when confronting Manichaeism, Donatism and Pelagianism. But it is evident that later, specifically, things change depending on circumstances, type of controversy, arguments and even adversary within the same dispute. With the Donatists in general, he contributes and works with numerous arguments, which can be channeled, in my opinion, through these four vectors: Sacred Scripture, Ecclesiastical Tradition, History and Dialectic.
1. Holy Scripture

Like all the Holy Fathers, with Saint Augustine we must begin by saying that Sacred Scripture was the foundation, the hinge and the soul of his theology, both preached and written, so that it was, consequently, the vertex, it was the center, it was the point of reference and the north of any theological dispute undertaken. Since the Sacred Scripture has as its center of revelation the mystery of Christ and the Church, it is understandable that for Saint Augustine it is only this, the Church, who can offer, and guarantee or support, the true meaning of Scripture. It is not surprising that he was concerned about always reflecting the Sensus Ecclesiae. Being faithful to Scripture and Tradition is equivalent, according to him, to being faithful to Christ.

The sum "saints plus sinners" seemed inadmissible to Tyconius. Rather, he advocated the dilemma "saints or sinners" (bipartite Church), differentiating a Corpus of Christ from a corpus of the devil, and ministers according to Peter from ministers according to Judas. In his renowned Commentary on the Apocalypse he had gone so far as to oppose Jerusalem to Babylon. All the apocalyptic verses served to prove that the holy, universal and bipartite Church walks throughout history among hypocrisy, persecutions and so many other manifestations of the antichrist,

Such a Ticonian approach did not fully convince Saint Augustine, no matter how much the brilliant exegete, along with him, departed somewhat from his party. In the end, opening a dichotomy in the Body of Christ seeing one part of God and another of the devil, which he called the bipartite Church or corpus bipertitum, was no longer a simple Donatist scheme. Dissatisfied, in the end, with this explanation, the Hipponense preferred to focus on the "good-bad" antagonism in the Church no longer as the opposition of two visible corporeal societies, but of two men or two spiritual groups of men. To put it briefly and simply, it was not about ecclesiological integrity or purity, which those of the Sect maintained, but about theological sanctity or purity *.

The purity to which Saint Augustine referred went beyond the scope of the Church as an earthly ecclesial institution, to enter another interior, spiritual and personal, pure work of God, which was equivalent to considering the ecclesial reality from an angle of spiritual anthropology. P.2.* I11. Ecclesiology and sacraments 147 cienda est And, in summary, the sacraments are from God, from Christ and from the Church, in the sense that the Church has received them from Christ as a divine gift.

As a result of the Augustinian distinction communio sacramentorum, it follows from what precedes that the sacraments are common to good and bad, and the Donatist claim to separate them so that the bad do not contaminate the good is absurd. That is nothing more than a clumsy pretext to legitimize a schismatic split that already exists de facto. The objective sanctity of the sacraments does not depend on either the good or the bad, and neither one nor the other can condition or influence it in any way. The thesis of rebaptism, therefore, does not stand; that if the sacraments are common to heretics and schismatics, it is because they are divine: "We are not enemies of their sacraments," Saint Augustine alludes to the Schism, "since we have them in common with them; The sacraments are not human, but divine. We must banish the error, which they so disastrously absorbed, but we must not banish those sacraments; as we received them, they carry and retain them. The more unworthily they carry them, the more the sacraments harm them, but they carry them anyway.

According to their schismatic ecclesiological vision, the Donatists presented sacramental theology incorrectly, relating it to the priesthood and the episcopacy to the point of affirming that the minister, when conferring the sacrament, also transmits whatever he himself is at that moment. This, for Saint Augustine, was inadmissible: God, Christ, his Holy Spirit is the first subject of ecclesial infallibility and of any sanctifying operation of the Church. Agree that the Donatists have true baptism, but let them not have any illusions or deduce from it any Catholic justification for their ecclesiology and sacraments. Recognizing their baptism is not affirming that their doctrine is all right, and even less so that they are the Church of Christ. On the contrary, a rigorous logical discourse reveals, rather, that not only is the schismatic Church not a true subject of the sacraments, but that it is not even the Church of Christ, because subject as subject, the source, the foundation, is none other than Christ *,

P.2.* III. Ecclesiology and sacraments 155

Saint Augustine also adds that to obtain grace conversion is not enough, the sacrament is necessary. That is to say, sacrament and sacramental virtue, although different, are of necessary complementarity. And as to what kind of element grace depends on, whether on the objective (=sacrament) or the subjective (=conversion of the heart), it is necessary to respond by specifying that Saint Augustine adopts a different dialectical strategy depending on whether he faces Donatists or Pelagians. At the beginning of the anti-Donatist controversy the Saint confesses himself indebted to both elements. Later he will lean more and more towards the objective (=sacrament) Y. But in De baptismo contra donatistas he has no other choice than to insist with special insistence on the subjective as he is forced to demonstrate to the Schism that, despite the existence of sacraments in him, they are of no use to him, lacking as he does in Caritas. Against the Pelagians, however, the emphasis falls more on the objective *,

During the anti-Donatist controversy, in short, it was barely proposed to deal with the causality of grace. The dispute rather affected the person of the minister and the influence that he could exert on sacramental sanctification. Saint Augustine of Hippo clarified what concerns the objective value of the sacraments, their effectiveness inside and outside the Church, their relative belonging to it and their direct dependence on Christ, who is the one who acts in them through the Holy Spirit. The notions of causality of grace will come later, already in scholasticism.'" Splendid and grandiose ecclesiological and sacramental picture, this one of the anti-Donatist Augustinian literature! It seems fair to me to recognize it like this. And although the two factors intervene, I believe that the theological Augustinianism is still more important for its correct evaluation than the political one.

II. CONTENT OF THE POEM

The Psalm is all an exhortation to the unity of the two churches, based on forgetting past errors, which are not exclusively those of the Donatists - he admits this several times - and whose most representative verse would be 142: Let us now embrace peace. What difference does it make to us about what happened before? This is the consequence that is constantly dropped through the historical thread of the origins and consequences of Donato's party.::
However, several parts are distinguished in the composition: 1.* part or introduction
a) Proem or presentation of the central theme (w.1-6).

b) The Church and the evangelical network, str. A-B. It begins by relying on the evangelical allegory of the fisherman's net that collects good and bad fish (Mt 13:47-50). This same comparison of the Church with the network will be present throughout the poem. His strong argument is that the Church has within it good and evil, while the Donatists considered themselves only good, without admitting evil; They are not, therefore, of the true Church.

It is not strictly a summary of the facts, but rather highlighting those most vaunted by his adversaries, as a support point for the accusations against the Catholics: ordination of Caecilian as bishop of Carthage, origin of the division by the ambitious of the primal see and historical starting point of the unfounded accusations; judicial process in the time of Constantine, entirely adverse to Donatus; attitude of Macarius, the emperor's Catholic emissary, who treated them harshly in view of their obstinacy and rejection, and whose severity Saint Augustine admits as possible and condemnable.
As Monceaux and others point out, correctly *, Augustine follows in the footsteps of Optatus of Milevi, whom he himself cites as a historical source *.

b) Controversy, str. N-V. In this part of the poem, Saint Augustine tries to pulverize the arguments of his adversaries. It uses, above all, ad hominem argument, making them see that they have, in fact, admitted, and continue to admit, sinners into their ranks. Both this part and the previous one are peppered with exhortations to unity, full of charity and pastoral sensitivity.

From an aesthetic point of view, these stanzas, which are a large part of the poem, are the most prosaic. We must recognize that, in the difficult game between dialectics and poetry, the one who loses is poetry.

A) External structure

The Psalmus contra partem Donati is a poem of 297 verses of 16 syllables, divided into two well-differentiated hemistichs of 8 syllables each. It consists of a proem of 6 verses, 20 stanzas of 12 verses each, and an epilogue of 30. Between stanza and stanza a chorus (ypopsalma) or responsorial verse is repeated.

If we do not take into account from the beginning that this psalm is composed exclusively to be sung, we will be missing something essential when judging it. These are the lyrics of a song, and we must value them without losing sight of this. We know that a lyric is good—musically—when it fits well with a certain melody, the tonic parts of the literary phrase coinciding with the strong or arsis parts of the musical phrase.

After an analysis of the text, and taking this into account, we affirm that the "letter" of the psalmus lends itself well to a music of trochaic rhythm, a rhythm that is moreover deeply rooted in popular meaning, as proven by the choruses of the first Greek tragicists, many centuries ago, and as we can see today in popular folklore. It is a spontaneous rhythm in our intimate musical being. Introduction 171 V. MUSICAL PERFORMANCE

At the end of the 4th century there were three ways of reciting or singing hymns in religious services: 4) the cantus directmeus, or complete execution of the psalm by the entire people. It was practiced by Saint Ambrose; b) the cantus antiphonus, or division of the assembly into two choirs that sing alternately. The antiphons are sung by all the people at the same time. And, finally, c) the cantus responsorims: the body of the psalm was performed by a soloist (praecentor) or perhaps by a small select choir, while the antiphon was repeated by the assembly from time to time. Saint Augustine alludes to this way of singing when, wanting to repress his delight in music, even sacred, it occurred to him to remove from the church the melodies with which David's psalter was sung, "it seemed to me more certain," he says, "what I remember having heard said by the bishop of Alexandria, Athanasius, who made the reader sing the psalms with such a weak inflection of voice that it seemed more like reciting them than singing them."

This mode has resurfaced in the post-conciliar liturgy of Vatican IT, especially in the responsorial songs of the Liturgy of the Word. It is this—the cantus responsorims—that was chosen by Saint Augustine for his Psalmus, according to his own testimony”: Some more expert faithful or faithful performed the stanzas that the people heard (qui eis—£ieles— cantoretur), and the refrain was repeated by all (ypopsalma quod respondertur).

Although Saint Augustine calls it a psalm, we do not believe that it can be fully equated with the performance of the biblical psalms. The reason is that the Latin text of the psalms does not retain rhythm. Its hemistichs are unequal, with a central recited part and a final inflection, identical in all verses. On the other hand, the Augustinian Psalimus maintains, as we have seen, an accentual rhythm and a fixed number of syllables. All this suggests an execution that is more hymnic than psalmic, with a marked flavor of popular rhythm. The trochaic rhythm of his verses lends itself perfectly to this, an animated air as Saint Augustine intended, who complains about the passivity of his Christians when singing. We have seen the graphic expression before. This rhythm lends itself to any type of easy, popular accompaniment. We could even think, given its length, of an execution in the style of rhapsodes or minstrels, with an almost monotonous recitation highlighting the rhythmic supports, and stopping at the assonant ending. The chorus, on the other hand, would be more melodic and slower.
VI. LITERARY ASSESSMENT

If we want to judge the Psalmus literaryally, we cannot lose sight of the declaration of its own author: to reach the understanding of less privileged and less cultivated minds, to reach them in the explanation of some dark facts. Let us recognize that the material chosen for the narrow framework of a versified composition is arduous and very unpoetic. Narrating some facts, insisting on some arguments, repeating some exhortations, entering, in short, into a controversy, is

Introduction 173 inevitably exceed poetic possibility. Furthermore, in the didactic and pastoral nature of the poem, the author chooses to sacrifice the poetry itself before the fruits that are pursued. Let us openly say that the Psalmus contra partem Donati is an example of intended popular art: frequent repetitions, vulgar and spontaneous phrases, both in construction (each verse is normally a phrase) and in the vocabulary and obvious rubbish. Augustine appears to be much more literate in most of his writings than in these popular verses.

However, the literary merit of this work, openly didactic, must be sought in the achievement of its objectives: clarity, happy and eloquent comparisons (the world is the sea; the Church is a fisherman's net, an era, a mother, which has within it good and bad: fish, straw, ungrateful children, but forming a single unit); strong antitheses; marked unity maintained throughout the poem, and great ease in the language, supposedly vulgar. Sometimes, however, the qualities of grandeur and eloquence, so typical of her rhetoric, emerge, as, for example, in the final epilogue, which reminds us of a tragic scene of the strongest classicism, where the mother - the Catholic Church - complains about her children who have abandoned her, and whom she continues to love tenderly.

! XI. OUR "TRANSLATION We wanted to reflect something fundamental in this work of
Augustine: the rhythmic structure. The structure is also preserved
syllable structure: 16 syllables in two hemistiches of 8 syllables, well

differentiated. We have preserved the alphabetical order of the stanzas. And since the style of the psalm is deliberately popular, with a characteristic "rhyme", we have chosen the assonant romance, which is the structure par excellence of popular Spanish romance. In each stanza we change rhyme to avoid monotony and also due to the demands of the translation.
In reality, the only rhyme in the Augustinian poem would be less
monotonous because it is less significant, in terms of accent, than
our rhymes, precisely always supported by some accent.
We have deliberately avoided chosen terms or phrases,
just as its author intends. Rather we have sought a

direct, popular language, at the level of the masses who should sing it. Fidelity to the translation has prevented us from keeping the exact number of 12 verses in each stanza. If every translation is difficult, the difficulty increases when the channels of the version are narrowed into counted syllables and requiring a rhyme. But fidelity to the content is essential. 1. I composed a psalm with the intention that the trial of the Donatists would come to the knowledge of even the most humble and totally ignorant and rude people, and in this way, as far as it depended on us, it would remain recorded in their memory, being sung before them. I did it following the order of the Latin letters, called the alphabet, but only up to U. I omitted the last three, adding in their place a final part, as an epilogue, as if the Church spoke to them as a mother. The chorus that is repeated, and the proem of the process, which we wanted to be sung, do not follow the order of the letters. This begins after the proem. I did not want to do it in any kind of metric verses, so that the laws of measurement would not force me to use terms little used by the common people.
2. This psalm begins like this: Omnes qui gaudetis de pace, moda uerum iudicate, which is its refrain.

1 The theme of this simulation of trial is raised in this stanza-prologue: let's see who is to blame for the tearing of unity and peace. But first it is necessary that there be impartiality, that we put aside respect for persons and prejudices, the eternal cause of the prolongation of the schism. 2 Peace is here as in a musical composition the theme, which is constantly repeated. There are many meanings of the word peace in Saint Augustine. That of Psalmus is, above all, ecclesiastical, alien to any political idea. Peace in a religious and ecclesial sense, of reconciliation of the sinner, of reconciliation with the Church, of absolution of sinners. In the metonymic sense here, peace=the Catholic Church. There are three nuances of this rich religious meaning: 1.0 Peace as something to be loved (Ep. 76,2: Euigilate ad salutem, amate pacem, redite ad unitatem). Peace and unity, which makes charity possible, which translates into inclination to custody unitatis (=guardian of unity), to love for unitatis compago (=unity as a compact cohesion of a single body, the ecclesial; cf. ThLL III 2001-2003). Peace as unitatis caritas. The beginning of this peace of unity and charity is Christ. 2.2 Peace = communion or unity of the Church. Very frequent meaning in funerary inscriptions and in Donatist epigraphy (WILLIS: 41 n.3; FREND, The Donatist Church 238, although Congar prefers to distance himself somewhat from Frend, cf. BA 28,713). 3.2 Peace in the sense of good disposition, of the fraternal love of Christians. Love that is consummated in the reality of peace and unity as a fruit of the living presence of the Spirit. By reproaching Catholics for being sinners, the Donatists place themselves, precisely, outside this unity and this peace in which sins are forgiven: Karitatem Christi qui habet, pacem non potest odisse (Psalmus c.P.Donati 125); Nos amemus pacem Christi, gaudeamus in unitate (ib., 167); cf. Of baptism WI 18, passim. Cf. E. HOFMANN, Kirchenbegriff 268s; 3735; CONGAR, «Pax» chez saint Augustin: BA 28,711-713; A. BLAISE, Dictionnaire latin-frangais des auteurs chrétiens (Ed. $Tradiderunt books. The word betrayal and traitor have their etymological origin in this Latin word (to surrender to the enemy, to surrender). Although the Donatists used it in this pejorative sense, however, its meaning in the entire Donatist controversy is limited to those who handed over sacred books or objects to the fire or to the pagans, as a consequence of Diocletian's edict of 303. But the accusation of traditors does not arise until after the persecution, in the year 305, in Cirta. The accusation of traditors against the Catholics of Africa was always one of the key points in the origin and continuation of the schism. See General introduction, 1.3 part, 1, 1, 2, p.6.

25 This is Augustine's definitive solution to the problem of non-contamination or complicity by living in communion with sinners. In C. Parm. TU 2,13: CSEL 51,115, develops this topic extensively. The parable of the tares (v.186) grounds the Augustinian position, which is that of the Catholic Church: the incorrigible should be excluded if there is no room for schisms (salva pace, v.169). What was essential in him was always the inner life?

REPLAY TO PARMENIANO'S LETTER (In three books) BOOK I REASON FOR THE WORK AND ITS PURPOSE

I 1. On several occasions I have already discussed a multitude of issues against the Donatists, either orally or in writing, according to the possibilities that the Lord offers me. And now a letter from a certain Parmeniano, your bishop in times past, has come into my hands. He writes it to Tyconius, a sharp and ingenious man of abundant eloquence, but a Donatist *. He believes that Tyconius is in error on a point that Parmenianus is forced to confess as true. My brothers in the faith asked me, and even begged me, to write a reply to Parmeniano's letter, especially because it does not interpret certain passages of Holy Scripture as it should. And it seemed good to me to do it in this work.
In fact, Tyconius, besieged by the testimonies of the sacred pages, which shouted at him everywhere, woke up and realized that the Church of God is spread throughout everything.

In light of these facts he proposed to demonstrate and maintain, against his own coreligionists, that no human sin, no matter how cruel and shameful it may be, can put a stop to the promises of God; that no impiety among the members of the Church can be an obstacle to God's fidelity regarding the spread of the Church throughout all the confines of the world, contained in the promises of the Fathers and which has now been made clear.

Tyconius treats all of this with great force and abundance of arguments, covering the mouths of his adversaries with an enormous amount of deep and clear testimonies, taken from Holy Scripture. But he fails to see what, logically, he should have seen: that the Christians of Africa belong to that Church, spread throughout the world, who are united not precisely with them, the Donatists, separated from the universal communion, but with those who enter into communion with the entire world.

But Parmenian and the remaining Donatists realized that this was the logical consequence, and preferred to remain in their hardened stance against the clearer-than-daylight truth asserted by Tyconius, rather than accept the triumph of the African Churches enjoying the common unity, sponsored by Tyconius, and from which they had separated. PARMENIANO BETRAYS THE MEANING OF THE HOLY SCRIPTURES

II 2. Now, in view of these facts, whoever believes himself to be impartial, who will decide to attest to both sides? To the judges who handed down the sentence, or to the litigants against whom it has fallen and who are never willing to end the litigation? What is beyond doubt is that the entire world has given credit to the judges. Now, those who give their consent and defend the Donatists are confessing that they lend faith to individuals who have not been able to win their cause, whatever it may be, in the overseas trial, despite so many disputes, and, furthermore, that they accept with naive levity all the protests and accusations against their judges. If at this point they consider themselves innocent and refuse to believe lightly that the defeated are so due to the weight of the truth, how much more innocent will those who refuse to lightly believe something against the judges themselves will be! VIII 15. «In the Gospel – says Parmeniano – it is written: God does not listen to sinners. What does this quote tell you, or how is it possible that you take it as in your favor, when the good, trusting in these words, can be safe among the bad? There is no need for physical separation. With reference to the “oil of the sinner,” the same psalm tells us how we should understand it. It goes like this: May the righteous punish me with mercy and rebuke me; but the sinner's ointment will not perfume my head. It is clear that the oil of the sinner means the flattery of adulation. He detests them, repudiates them, and chooses to be punished and corrected by the just, because the just acts not with the false softness of flattery, but with the sincere harshness of rebuke, and his action is much more merciful. Of this same sentiment is that of the Apocalypse: I, whom I love, rebuke and punish him; and that sentence of Solomon: Preferable are the wounds caused by the friend, rather than the spontaneous kisses of the enemy. And many other texts are similar.

The "ointment of softness", that is, the pleasant perfume given off by the good reputation of Christians, is "spoiled" by all those who, with the intention of remaining in their bad life, and of returning to the state of death of their previous injustices, rush en masse to ruin: through baptism they intend to have their sins forgiven, to commit them again. The same could be said with all truth of the prayer of Saint Daniel, which, of course sincerely, says: When I was praying and confessing my sins and those of my people.

Who, then, is the sinner in whose mouth praise loses its beauty, but the false and the hypocrite, whom the Holy Spirit who educates us rejects? When the hypocrite tells the truth, his mouth loses its beauty, because we are not capable of referring that truth to him with whom the hypocrite has no part. This is how prophecy lost its beauty in the mouth of Caiaphas, the high priest who did not know what he said, but because he was the high priest he prophesied. However, divine praise in itself is beautiful in the ears of those who hear and in the hearts of those who believe.

28. Some of them, convicted by the truth, have begun to say: "By separating from the Church, baptism is not lost, but the right to administer it is lost." Clearly unfounded and meaningless statement in any way you examine it. In the first place, there is no reason why an individual who cannot lose baptism should lose the right to transmit it. Both things are sacraments, and both are conferred upon man by virtue of a consecration: one upon receiving baptism and the other upon receiving sacramental order. Even in the case that a layman, moved by extreme necessity, administers the baptism that he himself, upon receiving it, learned to transmit, I do not know who will dare to maintain, if he is a pious man, that this baptism should be repeated. If this is done when no need is urgent, there is usurpation of a foreign function; But if there is an urgent need, there is no crime, or at most it is minor. XIV 32. What is the point of what Parmeniano allows himself to say with ridiculous boasting? "Never," he says, "the rigor of the divine law will allow a dead person to be given life, a wounded person to be healed, a blind person to be given sight, a naked person to be clothed, or a stained person to be cleansed." It is the Lord who raises the dead, the Lord who heals the wounded; It is the Lord who gives light to the blind, the Lord who clothes the naked; It is the Lord, yes, who purifies the impure. How does he have the arrogance to appropriate what does not belong to man? Are the Donatists who do not sin so alive that it can even be said of them that they make life arise, when they cannot even give growth? "I planted," says Paul, "Apollo watered, but God is the one who gave the growth." Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but he who gives the growth is God. How is he going to give life to a dead person who is incapable of making a living person grow? As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wishes.

Are there among the Donatists individuals so healthy that they can even give health to the sick? What do they intend with this but to supplant the Lord in order to receive praise instead? But they cannot in any way seduce those who put their hope not in man, but in God, when they sing: Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all his benefits. He forgives all your sins, He is the one who heals all.

In this way Parmenianus, with the testimonies adduced by himself, condemns his own cause as evil. It is true that the Son claims to have received from the Father, and that the Holy Spirit, in turn, has received from Him. 2. For now let us see if the Apostle was right in not saying: "Separate the evil from your company," but in saying: separate evil from your midst. Because, although we are prohibited from separating the wicked from the ecclesial unity, in order to remove evil from oneself, there is no room for interior complicity with them, and in this way there is not only a spiritual union of the good, but there is also a spiritual separation of the bad. Paul, in the passage cited above, addressed to Timothy, says: Do not become an accomplice in the sins of others, as if he were telling him that it could be the case that it was impossible for him to separate some wicked people from ecclesial society, and, therefore, he saw the need to tolerate them; and as if advising him on how not to be involved in other people's sins, he tells him: you4 keep yourself whole. The truth is that complicity with bad people can only be had by those who are bad: by no means the good, even when they have to live in the same society as them. In this same regard he says to those in Corinth: Is it my business to judge those outside? Is it not those within who you judge? And perhaps not to feel worried about the excessive number of bad people mixed in such a way with the wheat that it was not (1 Cor 5,13 sec. Parm.). 9. Are these crimes perhaps small, are they despicable? Because the Donatists often even affirm this, weighing them not in the faithful balance of the divine Scriptures, but in the deceitful balance of their customs. Any crime, any injustice that intoxicates the crowds, loses the objectivity of its qualification. On the other hand, the oracles of the divine pages have been proposed to men as a most faithful mirror, so that each one can see in them the just measure of any sin, which is perhaps serious, and yet the blindness of corrupt behavior despises it.

Is there a more serious accusation of greed than that made by the divine Scriptures when it is equated with idolatry, calling it by this name in the mouth of the Apostle: and greed, which is idolatry? Could it have been judged worthy of a greater punishment than being placed along with those crimes that prevent those who are dominated by them from possessing the Kingdom of God? Open the eyes of your heart - perhaps it is not enough for you to have those of your body open - and read what that sincere herald of truth wrote in that same first letter to the Corinthians: Do not be deceived: neither the immoral, nor the idolaters, nor the adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor the sodomites, nor the thieves, covetous, drunkards, slanderers, nor those who give themselves to fraudibus raprent, usuris multiplicantibus faenus augerent, panem domini manducabant et calicem domini bibebant.

He says, in fact, of the one whom he had wanted to heal with an intervention like this: The punishment imposed on him by the majority is enough for him. And the corrective imposed by many cannot take effect except when the guilty party does not have a complicit crowd to support him.

Now, in the event that the evil has infected a large majority, all that remains for the good is pain and regret. Thus, by the well-known sign revealed to Saint Ezekiel, they will escape unscathed from the devastation that threatens the wicked. In fact, to him who cannot make a mistake they shout: Do not let my soul perish with the wicked, nor my life with bloodthirsty men. Thus they will not run the risk of also uprooting the wheat, in trying to eliminate the tares, nor of failing in their attempt to carefully purge the Lord's harvest, making themselves worthy, by their recklessness, to be counted among the filth.

That is why the Apostle himself, having discovered a considerable number of those mired in lust and immorality, in his second letter to those of Corinth does not order them in the same terms not to take food in his company: there were already many, and it could not be said of them: "If anyone calls himself a brother, and is immoral, or miserly, or something similar, with such a one, do not even eat with him," but he says: (I fear) that uoluit, parum esse ut sit quisque talis, nisi etiam nominetur id est famosus appareat, ut possit omnibus dignissima uideri quae in eum fuerit anathematis prolata sententia. 16. How many good Christians actually practice this precept of the Apostle: With this type of individuals do not even eat together! Parmeniano has chosen the quote well. But he does not realize that these words must be interpreted avoiding all sacrilege of harmful division. Indeed, the beauty of the house and the abode of the glory of the Lord resides in its vessels, but not in all those that - as I have already said - are found in the only great house, but in those that are consecrated for noble uses, useful to their owner, always available for every good work. Any one of them who loves the beauty of the house of God and the place where his glory resides, tolerates those who are destined for low uses, and does not abandon the house for them, lest he himself become no longer a vessel of vile uses - which, despite everything, is tolerated within the house - but rather the dung that is thrown outside the house. And precisely because of this temporary coexistence with the wicked in the same house, he prays saying: Do not take away my breath with sinners, nor my life with bloodthirsty men, whose hands are stained with crimes, and their right hand is loaded with bribes. Pray, without a doubt, in these terms to avoid perishing together with those with whom charity forces you to live together. And it is charity that offers the sacrifice that was mentioned above: Lord, I love the beauty of your house and the place where your glory resides. Because I love yours. VI 29. Despite everything, these sacrilegious schisms and impious heresies, if the case arises of being admonished to be corrected by means of some punishment, have the audacity to grant the punishments suffered for their follies the names of martyrdom? What Salvio suffered was of little importance, some will say. Well, I ask you: in the event that a Donatist bishop was threatened with wild beasts and the stake, would he not prefer to be tortured like this rather than go through that humiliation? Would the Donatists not recite his name in the canon of martyrs, once his passion was consummated? Salvio's passion was more painful, making him dance with them, than if they had burned him alive.

If one of them, in fact, were proposed one of two things: to choose between dancing not alone, but having a dance chorused by others or being burned alive, there is no doubt about his response to this choice. He may reply that the primianists only obtained from the proconsul permission for those of Abitina to expel Salvius from his basilica, and that all the cruelties and indecencies that they later committed against him were done by them on their own. INTRODUCTION LI. OCCASION, DATE AND PURPOSE OF THE WORK!

a) Occasion.—The precious work DB, on the validity of the baptism of heretics, is closely related to the circumstances surrounding the appearance of the reply to Parmeniano. The author comes precisely to this with his first words: "In the books that I wrote against Parmenian's letter to Tyconius I promised to deal more closely with the question of baptism" (DB, I 1,1)? Furthermore: "even if I had not promised it then, I keep in mind and recognize the debt owed to the brothers who are asking me for it" (=debitum tamen a nobis flagitantibus fratribus meminimus et agnoscimus: DB, 11.1). And he further adds: to overcome "the objections that the Donatists present to us in this matter" (ibid.). The motivating occasion, therefore, is threefold: 1) to study more closely (=diligentius) the baptismal question; 2) to satisfy the debt contracted with the brothers who ask for it (=authentic pastoral reason); 3) to reject the Schism's objections on this matter (polemic).

The occasion, furthermore, is clarified from the content of the work, to which the third of the reasons just stated points. In fact, all three flow towards the baptismal theme (=quaestionem baptismi tractaturos). But it turns out that Saint Augustine points out for the moment, in the chapter on purposes, with a double purpose, namely: "not only... to reject the objections that the Donatists present to us in this matter (=baptism), but also to explain what the Lord suggests to me about the authority of the blessed martyr Cyprian" (ibid.). Later we will see how, and curiously, the material extension of the writing is not proportional to the order of both arguments, since the authority of Saint Cyprian appears here in an explanatory, auxiliary function of the baptismal question.

b) Date.—The DB, like the bulk of anti-Donatist literature, is a desk work and, consequently, we must imagine it written in Hippo *, and on a date that is around 400, months up months down, composed with little certainty.

But far from insisting on the internal contradiction that such a Cyprianist postulate entails, Saint Augustine prefers to emphasize, rather, the doctrinal point where the Catholic Church and Saint Cyprian coincide, namely: in considering valid the baptism administered by sinful bishops. Because Saint Cyprian regrets the unevangelical behavior of some colleagues, although, of course, he will never deny or question the value of their sacramental functions. That is to say, even at the doctrinal level the Church can claim, even if only in part, the authority of Saint Cyprian. It is true that he rejects, like the Donatists, the baptism of heretics. 2. Has it already been said in the aforementioned books? that, outside the Catholic communion, baptism can occur, as it is undoubtedly possible that it exists outside of it. In fact, no one among them dares to deny that even apostates have baptism, since when they return repentant, the Donatists do not administer it to them again, precisely because they think that they have not been able to lose it. In the same way, those who, through the sacrilege of schism, distance themselves from the communion of the Church, certainly retain the baptism they received before separating, since, if they return, it is not given to them again. This shows that what they had received while they were in the truth, they could not lose in the separation.

Now, if it can exist outside, why can't it be administered? > Perhaps it is said that outside does not exist legitimately. To which I have to answer: As it is not legitimately preserved, and yet it is preserved, in the same way it is not legitimately administered, although it is really conferred. Just as through reconciliation in unity cout intellegant omnes, qui non studio partium caecati iudicant, non solum eos non adiuuari auctoritate Cypriani, sed per ipsam maxime conuinci adque subuerti.

1,2 LI Baptism and its value 407 what was used unnecessarily outside of it begins to be taken advantageously; what was given without any fruit outside of it also begins to be beneficial through reconciliation. But it is not licit to affirm that what was granted was not granted, nor should anyone be slandered for not having given something, when he himself confesses that he gave what he had received. The sacrament of baptism is, in effect, what the baptized person has; and the sacrament that empowers to confer baptism is what the one who has been ordained has. So that just as the baptized person, if he separates himself from the unity, does not lose the sacrament of baptism, in the same way he who has been ordained, if he separates himself from the unity, does not lose the sacrament of administering baptism *.

There should be no difference between the sacraments: if one withdraws from the bad ones, both sacraments must be withdrawn; If one remains in evil, both must remain. And just as the baptism that could not be lost by someone who separated from unity is accepted, the baptism that was given by someone who, upon separating, did not lose the sacrament that gives the power to confer it, must also be accepted. In fact, those who were already baptized before separating are not rebaptized again when they return; In the same way, those who convert, if they had been ordained before their separation, are not ordained again: on the contrary, if the usefulness of the Church demands it, they continue to administer what they previously administered, or if they do not administer it, they always preserve the sacrament of their ordination; and for this reason hands are not laid on them as if they were laymen 3, tur, sic per eandem reconciliationem incipit utile esse quod extra eam inutilite datum est. Non tamen dici fas est non datum esse quod datum est, aut ut non hoc dedisse quis <quem)>quam calumnietur, cum hoc eum dedisse quod acceperat confitetur. Sacramentum enim baptismi est quod habet qui baptizatur, et sacramentum dandi baptismi est quod habet qui ordinatur. Sicut autem baptizatus, si ab unitate recesserit, sacramentum baptismi non amittit, sic etiam ordinatus, si ab unitate recesserit, sacramentum dandi baptismi non amittit. Nulli enim sacramento iniuria facienda est; si discedit a malis, utrumque discedit, si permanet in malis, utrumque permanet. Sicut ergo acceptatur baptismus, quem non potuit amittere qui ab unitate discesserat, sic acceptandus est baptismus, quem dedit ille qui sacramentum dandi cum discederet non amiserat. Il 3. That is why the Donatists are with us in some things and have distanced themselves in others. We do not prevent them from doing what they agree with us on; On the other hand, in the matters in which you disagree with us, we urge you to come forward to receive them or receive them upon your return; and we strive in all charity with the means at our disposal, so that, through correction and amendment, they may come to a decision for this. We do not say to them: "Do not give baptism", but: "do not give it in schism"; just as we do not say to those who are going to receive baptism: —“Do NOT receive it,” but we say to them: —“Do not receive it in schism.”

Even in the case of extreme need, if there were no Catholic from whom to receive baptism, and he received from the hands of someone outside the Catholic unity the same as he would receive in it, from that person, as long as he remained faithful in his spirit, we would not have him - in case of death - except for one more Catholic. And if he saw himself free from bodily death, upon reintegrating with his bodily presence into the Catholic congregation, from which he had not departed in his heart, not only would we not blame him for what he did, but with all tranquility and sincerity we would praise him. And the reason is because he had God in his heart while preserving unity, and he did not want to leave this life without the holy sacrament of baptism, which he always believed was not from men, but from God.

MI 4. We affirm these two points without hesitation: baptism exists in the Catholic Church, and it is only in her where it is legitimately received. These are the two extremes that the Donatists deny. And we still make two other statements: that baptism exists among the Donatists, but that it is not received legitimately there. Regarding these two questions, they affirm in a major tone that baptism exists in them, but they refuse to confess that it is received illegitimately. Of these four proposals, three belong exclusively to us; only one is common to both. In effect, we affirm that baptism exists in the Catholic Church, that it is received legitimately there, and that it is not received legitimately among the Donatists; but that baptism exists among the Donatists, they affirm it, and we grant it to them. cognuit, noluit ex hac uita emigrare. Si quis autem, cum possit in ipsa catholica accipere, per aliquam mentis peruersitatem eligit in schismate baptizari, etiamsi postea uenire ad catholicam cogitat, quia certus est ibi prodesse sacramentum, quod alibi accipi quidem potest, prodesse autem non potest, procul dubio peruersus et iniquus est both perniciosius and scientius. Ita enim non dubitat recte illic accipi, sicut non dubitat illic prodesse etiam quod alibi acceperit.

Suppose that one wishes to be baptized and knows that he must choose our Church to achieve Christian health, since only in it does the baptism of Christ obtain fruit, even if it had been received in another; Well, if he intends to be baptized in the sect of Donatus, because they and we together admit that baptism exists there, should he pay attention to the other three theses? In fact, if he has preferred to follow us in what they do not say, and, instead, puts what we and others say before what only we say, it is enough for us that he puts what only we say and they deny, before what only they affirm.

We say that baptism exists in the Catholic Church, and they deny it. That baptism is received legitimately in the Catholic Church, it is we who say it, not them. That it is not legitimately received in Donato's party, we say it, not them. Therefore, just as the catechumen believes what we hold to be obligatory belief, in the same way he must practice what we hold to be obligatory practice. On the other hand, as regards what some of us affirm that should be believed, believe it if you like, with greater conviction than what we alone affirm; It is logical that he believes with greater conviction that in the Donatist party there is valid baptism - which we all confess - than that there is misbaptizari et certus est iam nostram sibi ecclesiam ad christianam salutem esse deligendam et in ea sola prodesse baptismum Christi, etiamsi alibi acceptum fuerit, sed ideo in parte Donati uult baptizari, quia esse ibi baptismum non illi soli neque nos soli, sed utrique dicimus, adtendat alia tria. But even so, even if only we say so, he must believe that the baptism of Christ is valid among us, and he must not believe it invalid as only they affirm, since that catechumen had already firmly determined that, in points of dissension, he must put us before us. Therefore, about what only we affirm, namely, that our baptism is legitimate, you must believe it rather than that it is invalid, an affirmation that belongs only to the Donatists. And for the same reason, what we alone say, that their baptism is not legitimate, must be believed in preference to what they alone say: that their baptism is legitimate.

He is mistaken, then, whoever believes he is safe in receiving in Donatism what we both affirm as existing in it, but not as obligatory to receive there. We assume that said catechumen has chosen to adhere to us on points where there is dissent. The bottom line is that to safely receive baptism, you must choose not only where it is validly but also licitly administered, rather than where—according to the doctrine of those you have chosen to follow—it exists there, true, but it is not to be received there.

In case of doubt about not receiving there legitimately what he is sure of receiving in the Catholic Church, he would seriously sin by preferring the uncertain to the certain in matters related to the salvation of the soul. That a man is licitly baptized in the Catholic Church, he is assured by the fact that, having been baptized elsewhere, he has determined to pass to it; and that man is not licitly baptized among the dicitur. IV 5. It may happen that someone does not understand how we affirm that the sacrament can be administered there and yet not be received licitly. Consider that we do not even affirm its legality, as even those among them who deviate from communion admit it. On which we can resort to the comparison of the bodily sign in the militia, which deserters can maintain and receive even outside the militia, but which must not be maintained or received outside of it; and yet, it should not be changed or retired if the deserting soldier returns to the military?

Supine dementia would be to affirm this, and, on the other hand, they must recognize that a man can receive the baptism of Christ, but by persevering his heart in malice and sacrilege, prevent the remission of his sins from taking place.

They must recognize that men can be baptized in the separate communions of the Church, in which the baptism of Christ is given and received in the same sacramental celebration; but this is only useful for the remission of sins when the person reconciled with unity, rids himself of the sacrilege of dissension, which was what retained his sins and prevented their remission.

He who approached with hypocrisy does not receive baptism again later, but is purified by his sincere correction and true confession; which could not be done without baptism, in such a way that what was given before begins to be useful for health when that hypocrisy disappears through sincere confession. In the same way, whoever, being an enemy of Christ, in some heresy or schism, received his baptism - which was not lost by those who separated, whose sacrilegious crime was the cause of his sins not being forgiven - rint, sufficit nobis. The words of the Lord also say it even more clearly: But as he went out, the employee found a colleague of his who owed him a hundred denarii. He did not say: "To whom he had already forgiven the debt of one hundred denarii," because if he had forgiven it, he no longer owed it. By saying, well, I owed her it is clear that he had not forgiven her.

And it would have been better for a debtor so great that he was going to render an account and wait for his master's mercy, it would have been better for him to first forgive his fellow servant what he owed him and thus come closer to rendering an account where he had to implore his master's mercy. However, not having yet forgiven his fellow servant did not prevent his master from forgiving him, at the time of rendering an account, everything he owed him. But of what use was it to him, if through the perseverance of hatred all evil immediately returned upon his head?

In this way the grace of baptism does not fail to remit all sins, although fraternal hatred remains in the one to whom they are forgiven. Everything from the previous day is forgiven, everything that preceded is forgiven, everything from the same hour is forgiven, everything from the moment before the baptism, everything from the moment of baptism. But immediately he begins to be guilty, not only of everything that comes, but also of the days, hours and moments sic accesserat, ut ei dominus dimitteret. Hoc indicat uerba conserui dicetis: patientiam habe in me et reddam tibi (ib. 18,26). Alioquin says: «iam mihi hoc dimiseras; cur iterum repetis? Hoc et ipsius domini uerba manifestius aperiunt. 24 In the parable of the merciless debtor, which in Saint Augustine serves to explain his baptismal thesis from an allegorical interpretation, each detail contains its conclusive lesson: 1) Baptism remits sins (but the Saint notes that this debtor, before presenting himself to the king, has not remitted the debt to his companion). 2) The catechumen who receives baptism before having forgiven his brother, nevertheless receives forgiveness from God (the Saint observes that the king, seeing the inhuman debtor's behavior towards his companion, demands full payment of the debt: and then draws the following conclusion). 3) The baptized person who does not have charity has only received forgiveness at the moment of his baptism. Saint Augustine, concerned about the problem of the effect produced by baptism administered to an ill-disposed catechumen, does not realize that the parable only attempts to demonstrate the two aspects of God's attitude towards us: the desire to freely forgive us our sins and the condition that we also forgive our brother. It is impossible for God to forgive, even for a moment, those who do not have living faith. Augustine tries here, quite weakly indeed, to justify from Scripture his thesis of the revival of sins. Cf. Thus says the Apostle: And it remains for me to show you an exceptional path. I can now speak the languages ​​of men and angels, and if I do not have charity, I am no more than a noisy bell or a resounding cymbal.

Cyprian did not fully penetrate the deep secret of the sacrament; But if, knowing all the sacraments, he did not have charity, he would be nothing. And even with less penetration, he preserved this with humility, fidelity and strength, and deserved to reach the crown of martyrdom. If, due to his human condition, any darkness had crept into his lucid mind, it would be dispelled by the glorious serenity of the brilliance of his blood. It is not in vain that the Lord Christ Jesus himself, when calling himself a vine and his own as branches of the vine, said that they would be cut off and separated from life like useless branches that do not bear fruit *. And what is this fruit but the new germ of which it is also said: I give you a new commandment: cisione mortificatum diligentiam nullius curationis admitteret. Et si se ille separasset, quam multi sequerentur! Quantum sibi nomen inter homines faceret! Quam latius Cyprianistae quam Donatistae uocarentur! Sed non erat filius perditionis (cf. lo 17,12; 2 Thess 2,3), de qualibus dictum est: deiecisti eos dum extollerentur (Ps 72,18), sed erat filius pacis ecclesiae, qui tanta cordis inluminatione [172] praeditus propterea non uidit aliquid, ut per eum aliud supereminentius uideretur. Et adbuc, inquit apostolus, supereminentiorem uiam uobis demonstro. Si linguis homi(125)num loquar et angelorum, caritatem autem non habeam, factus sum aeramentum sonans aut cymbalum tinniens (1 Cor 12,31-13,1). Minus ergo ¡lle penetrauit, ut cerneret secretum abditum sacramenti; sed si sciret omnia sacramenta, caritatem autem non haberet, nihil esset (cf. 1 Cor 13:2). Cum autem minus illud perspiciens hanc tamen humiliter fideliter fortiter custodiuit, ad martyrii coronam meruit peruenire, ut, si qua in eius lucidam mentem ex humano condicione nebula inrepserat, glorious serenitate fulgentis sanguinis fugaretur. Non enim frustration ipse dominus lesus Christus, cum se ipsum diceret uitem (cf. lo 15,1ff), suos autem tamquam in uite sarmenta, praecidi dixit eos et de uite auferri tamquam fructus nisi nouus ¡lle fetus de quo item dicit: mandatum - 3% On the topic of the branches and the vine, cf. The Apostle also says: On the other hand, the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, tolerance, pleasure, generosity, loyalty, simplicity, self-control. All this begins with charity, and by coming together intimately, it forms an admirable cluster with it.

On the other hand, the Lord also rightly added: My Father cleanses the branches that do not bear fruit so that they may bear more. As men, we are exposed to the temptation to think without adjusting to reality. What amounts to diabolical presumption would be to love one's own opinion excessively or to envy the best, reaching the sacrilege of tearing apart communion and originating a schism or a heresy. On the other hand, not dissenting from reality in anything is characteristic of angelic perfection. And, since we are men, although in hope we are angels, with whom we will be equal in the resurrection, let us not allow ourselves to be infected by diabolical presumption. And yet, he said this about those who he testifies to us who had already been baptized; Thus he says to them: Was Paul crucified for you or were you baptized in his name? To these he says: I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal people, as to children in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, I did not give you solid delicacies, because you did not yet accept them. And not even now do you admit them, because you are still uerba symboli et [209] tamen non recte credat siue de ipsa trinitate siue de resurrectione uel aliquid aliud. Neque enim parua res est in ipsa intus catholica tenere integram fidem, ita ut omnino non de aliqua creatura, sed de ipso deo nibil aliter credat quam ueritas habet. Numquidnam ergo, si in ipsa catholica baptizatus postea legendo audiendo et pacifice disserendo ipso domino reuelante cognouerit aliter se antea credidisse quam debuit, denuo baptizandus est? Quis autem carnalis et animalis homo non per phantasmata sui cordis euagetur et constituat sibi deum, qualis ei pro suo carnal sensu placuerit, adque ita credat tantum longe aliter quam deus est, quantum (147) a ueritate uanitas differt? Uerissimam quippe sententiam dixit apostolus plenus lumine ueritatis: animalis, inquit, homo non percipit quae sunt spiritus dei (1 Cor 2:14). Et tamen de his hoc dicebat, quos ¡am fuesse baptizatos ipse manifestat. Eis enim dicit: numquid Paulus crucifixus est pro uobis aut in nomine Pauli baptizati estis? (ib. 1,13). Habebant ergo isti baptismi sacramentum, et tamen carnaliter sapiendo quid poterant de deo credere nisi secundum sensum carnis suae, ubi amimalis homo non percipit quae sunt spiritus dei? Talibus dicit: non potui uobis loqui quasi spiritalibus, sed quasi carnalibus. Quasi paruulis in Christo lac uobis potum dedi, non escam; nondum enim poteratis. Sed nec adbuc quidem potestis; adbuc enim

498 Treatise on Baptism 14, 19 carnal. And these are also the ones who allow themselves to be enveloped by the wind of any doctrine. Of them he says: We will no longer be children tossed and adrift by any wind of doctrine. Perhaps, then, if these have progressed until they reach the spiritual age of the inner man, and through the sincerity of their intelligence have come to know how far they are, due to their deceptive fantasies, from the authentic knowledge of God that the truth demands, should they be baptized again?

It may also happen that a Catholic catechumen comes across the book of some heretic and, without knowing how to discern error from truth, comes to believe something contrary to the Catholic faith. An error that is not in open contradiction with the words of the Symbol, under which in truth innumerable heretical errors have been born. If such a catechumen thinks that that book is from a notable and learned Catholic, and believing such things he is baptized into the Catholic Church, but then with more diligence he knows how he should believe, and clinging to the Catholic faith he rejects all that from his spirit, perhaps by confessing this he must be baptized again? Or if, before knowing and confessing him, he is discovered to think so, and is taught what he should reject and what he should believe, and it is evident that he had been baptized into that false faith, should he be baptized again? Certainly not. And why? Because that sanctity of the sacrament consecrated by the evangelical words remained intact in him as he had received it when it was given to him, even though he was carnal (ib. 3,1-3). Such etiam circumferuntur omni uento doctrinae de quibus* dicit: ut ultra non simus paruuli, iactati et circumlati omni uento doctrinae (Eph 4,14). Numquid ergo isti, si profecerint usque ad spiritalem hominis interioris aetatem et intellegentiae sinceritate cognouerint, quam longe [210] aliter per fallaciam suorum phantasmatum de deo crediderint quam ueritas postulabat, iterum baptizandi sunt? Sic etiam fieri potest, ut in alicuius haeretici librum catechumenus catholicus incidat et a ucritate nesciens discernere errorem credat aliquid contra catholicam fidem, cui tamen errori uerba symboli non repugnant; sub eisdem quippe uerbis innumerable haereticorum errors exorti sunt. Putans ergo iste catholici alicuius magni adque docti esse illum librum, si talia credens in catholica baptizetur et posteriore diligentia cognoscat, quemadmodum credere debeat, adque arrepta fide catholica illud ex animo respuat, numquid, si hoc confessus fuerit, denuo baptizandus est? Aut si, antequam discat et confiteatur, hoc sentimentale inueniatur et quid abicere debeat quidue credere doceatur manifestumque fiat in ea falsitate fidei baptizatum Fuisse, numquid denuo baptizandus est? What is it? Quia illa sanctitas sacramenti uerbis euangelicis consecrata super eum integra permanebat, sicut eam traditam acceperat, quamuis ipse in carnalis mentis

For all this, it is clear that with a defective faith the sacrament of baptism can remain intact in someone; and therefore the variety of doctrines attributed to the various heretics do not belong to this discussion. 2 For what must be corrected in each one is the evil that the one who corrects sees; What needs to be healed is what is sick; and what you have to give is what you do not have, and above all the love of peace, without which you cannot take advantage of everything else. But when all this is present, it should not be taken as if it were lacking; On the contrary, through the bond of peace and the excellence of charity, we must ensure that its possession is fruitful and not harmful.
