XVI 21. The expression that the Holy Spirit is given only in the Catholic Church through the laying on of hands *, has been interpreted by our elders referring to the words of the Apostle: The love that God has for us floods our hearts through the Holy Spirit that he has given us. This is charity, which those who have broken away from the communion of the Catholic Church do not have; And for this reason, even if they speak the languages ​​of men and angels, even if they know all the mysteries and all the science, even if they have all the prophecy and all the faith, even if they move the mountains, and even if they distribute all their goods to the poor, and give their bodies to the fire, it is of no use to them.

And those who do not love the unity of the Church do not have the love of God; For this reason it is rightly said that the Holy Spirit is not received except in the Catholic Church. For at the present fit, facta est mibi sicut aqua mendax non habens fidem (ler 15,18), si figurate adque allegorica locutione prophetiae nusquamponeretur aqua nisi quae baptismum significaret, laboraremus quaerere, quid sibi uelint haec uerba Hieremiae. Nunc autem, cum apertissime in Apocalypsi exponantur aquae pro populis positae (cf. 17-15), cur non intellegam aquam mendacem et sine fide populum mendacem ac perfidum nescio.

THE DOVE AS A SYMBOL OF UNITY

XVII 22. As a symbol of unity *, the Lord granted Peter the power to let what he loosed remain loosed on earth. It is evident that that unit was also called the only perfect Dove. Do all the misers, about whom Cyprian himself laments so much in the Catholic Church, also belong to the same dove? Well, in my opinion, these predators cannot be called pigeons, but rather hawks. How, then, do those who seize possessions with insidious fraud and increase profits with the multiplication of usury * baptize, if only that Dove baptizes, that is, that unity that can only be understood among the good, simple, chaste and perfect? Is it through the prayers of the spirit-filled saints that there is proprium donum est catholicae unitatis et pacis nec eius in omnibus, quia nec omnes sunt eius, sicut suo loco uidebimus. Practer ipsam tamen esse illa caritas non potest, sine qua cetera, etiamsi agnosci et adprobari possunt, prodesse tamen et liberare non possunt. Manus autem inpositio non sicut baptismus repeti non potest. Quid est enim aliud nisi oratio super hominem?

XVII 22. Nam quod in typo unitatis Petro dominus dedit potestatem, ut id solueretur in terris quod ¡lle soluisset (cf, Mt 16,19), manifestum est quod illa unitas etiam una columba perfection (cf. Cant 6,8) sit dicta. Numquid ergo ad eandem columbam pertinent omnes [214] avari, de quibus in eadem catholica grauiter idem Cyprianus ingemuit? Nam ut opinor, raptores non columbae, sed accipitres dici possunt. Quomodo ergo baptizabant, qui fundos insidiosis fraudibus rapiebant et usuris multiplicantibus faenus augebant, si sola illa columba, id est illa unitas quae nisi in bonis intellegi non potest, simplex et casta et perfection baptizat? That sacrament, in fact, is recognized as the property of Christ even among the wicked; but neither one nor the other of them are found in the body of the Dove, the only one, the incorrupt, the holy, the pure, the one without spot or wrinkle. It may happen that the magnitude of the crime in heresy reaches the level of the knowledge of the miser in his sin, and thus the ignorant heretic would be equated with the conscious miser; although the testimony he adduced from the Apostle does not seem to prove this. Indeed, what do we detest in heretics if not blasphemies? Wanting to demonstrate that ignorance of sin contributed to the ease of forgiveness, he adduced that testimony of the Apostle: That at first I was a blasphemer and a persecutor and a denigrator, but I have obtained mercy, because I did it out of ignorance.

VI 8. Cyprian continues saying: «And let no one say: we follow the tradition of the apostles; because the apostles have given us one Church and one baptism, which are found only in the same Church. These words do not convince me so much that I dare to disapprove of the baptism of Christ present also among heretics (as I am forced to approve the same Gospel when I find it among them, although I detest their error); I am more convinced by the fact that there were some in the time of Saint Cyprian who accepted as apostolic that custom, against which African councils were held, and of which he said shortly before: "Uselessly some, defeated by reason, blame the custom on us."

Nor do I see why this custom, confirmed after Cyprian in a plenary council of the entire world, had previously been found by Cyprian himself to be so firm that when a man endowed with such wisdom sought an authority that would authorize his change, he only found in Africa the council of Agrippinus, held a few years before him. Seeing that this was not enough to counteract the custom of munlitigator est ne intromittatur, iste uero intus callidus adsentator ne foras proiciatur?

THE TARES AND THE REITERATION OF BAPTISM

X 14. Some may reply: The tares that are within the Church very easily become wheat. It is true that it is so; But what relationship does this have with the reiteration of baptism? If someone converts from heresy and with the time and ease of his conversion he has anticipated another who inside takes longer to correct his malice and make amends, should this person not have his baptism reiterated, and, on the other hand, should the one who has been preceded by the convert from heretics be reiterated? Therefore, it has nothing to do with the question who has converted before or after his own perversity to right faith, hope or charity. It is true that the bad inside can become good more easily; However, sometimes some of those from outside anticipate the conversion of some from within, and reconciled in unity, while these remain in sterility, the former with their patience bear fruit thirty or sixty or a hundred times greater. Of course, if we were only going to call tares those who persist in their evil error until the end, we would have to recognize that there was a lot of wheat and a lot of tares inside. sacramentum diuinum et suaue est neque propter eorum sterilitatem quos etiam foris conpluit inprobandum.

THERE ARE BAD GUYS INSIDE AND OUT, WHICH ARE WORSE?

15. But are the bad guys on the outside worse than the bad guys on the inside? A big question arises as to whether Nicholas, who was already outside, was worse than Simon Magus, who was still inside, since the former was a heretic, and the latter a sorcerer. I grant that it is so, if the evil of division is considered more serious, a very clear indication of the violation of charity. But we must keep in mind that many, even if they lose charity, do not for that reason go out; They are held back by worldly emoluments, and seeking their interests, not those of Christ, they do not depart from the unity of Christ, but do not want to depart from their comforts. That is why it was said in praise of charity: It does not seek its own.

Regarding this, Cyprian himself teaches us that baptism must be considered by itself, consecrated by the evangelical words, as the Church received it, without any perversity or malice being added or mixed, either on the part of those who receive it, or on the part of those who give it. In fact, he himself reminds us of both things: that some do not keep benevolent charity inside, but rather abound in envy and malevolent dissension, about which the apostle Paul spoke, and that, on the part of the devil, there are also envious people, as he testifies very clearly in the letter he wrote about jealousy and envy *,

For this reason it is clear that there can exist, even among those who are of the devil's party, the holy sacrament of Christ, not precisely for their health, but for their damnation, not only if they pervert themselves after receiving it, but also if they were already in that perversion when receiving it, as Cyprian himself tells us, "renouncing the world with words alone and not with works." Therefore, I think it is very clear that in this question of baptism we should not take into account who is the one who gives it, but rather what it is that gives, nor who is the one who receives it, but what he receives, or who is the one who has it, but what it is that he has.

And so even the heretic, who is evidently outside, if he received evangelical baptism, did not receive it according to the error that blinded him. Therefore, if upon reconsideration he recognizes that he must leave what he had had in bad dispositions, he must not thereby abandon the good that he had received: not because his error has been reproved, should the baptism of Christ be condemned in it.

Therefore, in those who have been baptized even with false ideas about God, it is very clear that the truth of the sacrament must be separated from the error of those who have had false ideas, although both things can occur in the same person, and thus, when someone, finding themselves outside in error, has been baptized with the true sacrament, upon returning to the unity of the Church the true faith replaces the false one, but true baptism cannot replace true baptism: it cannot replace baptism to himself, because he cannot turn away either. For this, then, heretics come to the Catholic Church, and not to reiterate the good that they already have from God.

“There is no salvation outside the Church,” he affirms. Who denies it? Therefore, whatever property of the Church is possessed is not useful for salvation outside the Church. He also says that the water of the baptism of heretics is not adulterous. Indeed, neither the creature that God created is evil, nor should the evangelical words be rebuked in those who walk in error; What must be rebuked is the error of those who make the soul adulterous, even though it has the trappings of the sacrament from its legitimate husband.

Baptism can, therefore, be common to us with heretics $ just as the Gospel can be common to us, no matter how distant their error is from our faith, whether they feel something different from the truth about the Father or the Son or the Holy Spirit, whether separated from unity they do not gather with Christ, but scatter; the same as, if we are wheat of the Lord, the sacrament of baptism can be common to us with the corpus meum ut ardeam, caritatem autem non (170) habeam, nibil mibi prodest (1 Cor 13,3). "Salus extra ecclesiam non est." Quis negat? Et ideo quaecumque ipsius ecclesiae habentur, extra ecclesiam non ualent ad salutem. Sed aliud est non habere, aliud non utiliter habere. XX 27. As to whether a Catholic with terrible customs should be put before a heretic whose life, apart from being a heretic, there is nothing worthy of rebuke, I do not dare to give an opinion lightly. It is true that there will be those who say: As a heretic that he is, it will not be only this, but other vices will accompany him; It is carnal and base and, therefore, it is certain that it will be emulative, angry, envious, an enemy of the truth itself and distant from it. One can even cite the one that I judge the lightest about these evils and say that it will not be alone in anyone precisely because it is carnal and base, for example, drunkenness, which has already prevailed the custom of being mentioned without horror and even with hilarity among peoples: can it, when it is found in someone, be alone? In fact, what drunk is there who is not at the same time stubborn, angry, envious, dissatisfied with his healthy teachers, an irreconcilable enemy of those who correct him? On the other hand, it will be difficult for him to be free from fornication and adultery.

Why do we recognize the sacrament of Christ in one of them and not in the other, as if it were proper to one or the other, when in reality it is the same in both, and it is precisely from God, and it is good even if it is in the most corrupt people? And if of these two men who have it, one is worse than the other, that does not mean that what they both have is worse in one than in the other; the same as in two evil Catholics; Although one is worse than the other, he does not have a worse baptism; And if one of them is good and the other bad, the baptism of the bad is not bad and the baptism of the good is not bad, but in both it is good. Just as the light from the sun or from a lamp is not worse in sick eyes than in healthy ones, but the same in both, although due to their diversity it produces pleasure in some and torment in others. In this matter I do not hesitate to put the Catholic catechumen, burning with love of God, before the baptized heretic; Even within the Catholic Church we put the good catechumen before the bad baptized one. And with this we do no injury to the sacrament of baptism, in which this one has already been bathed and the other has not; nor do we consider the sacrament of the catechumenate superior to the sacrament of baptism, because we recognize some catechumen as more faithful and better than some baptized person *. We see that the centurion Cornelius, even without baptism, is better than Simon already baptized: the former, in fact, even before baptism was filled with the Holy Spirit, and the latter, after baptism, was swollen with the unclean spirit. Of course, if Cornelius, having already received the Holy Spirit, had not wanted to be baptized, he would be guilty of contempt for such an excellent sacrament. But, once baptized, he did not receive a more excellent sacrament than Simon: with equal holiness on the part of the same sacrament, the merits of men are diverse.

The sanctity of baptism is not increased or diminished by the good or bad merits of men. The same forte quia dicebant multo magis haereticos cum baptismo Christi posse ad regnum eius admitti quo catechumeni admitterentur, cum ipse dixerjt: nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et spiritu, non intrabit in regnum caclorum (lo 3,5). Melior enim centurio Cornelius nondum baptizatus Simone baptizato. Iste enim et ante baptismum sancto spiritu impletus est, ille et post baptismum unclean spiritu inflatus est (cf. For he who said: Whoever is not reborn of water and the Spirit cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, is the same one who said: Unless your righteousness surpasses that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. In fact, so that the catechumen would not trust in his justice, it was said: Whoever is not reborn of water and the Spirit cannot enter the kingdom of heaven; and in turn, so that those baptized would not be secure in their wickedness once they had received baptism, it was also said: If your righteousness does not surpass that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. One thing without the other is very little: one and the other together make one heir of that possession.

We must not, therefore, reproach in anyone the justice that began to exist in him before he united with the Church. Justice had already begun in Cornelius before he found himself among the Christian people: if he had to be reproved, the angel would not have said to him: Your prayers and alms have been remembered before God; and if she were sufficient to attain the kingdom of heaven, she would not be admonished to go and seek Peter. In the same way, the evangelical sacrament of baptism should not be reproved, even if it has been received outside the Church. DOES MARTYRDOM SUPPLEMENT BAPTISM?

XXI 29. Regarding the ever substitution of baptism by martyrdom, this is testified to us by what was said to that unbaptized thief: Today you will be with me in paradise, which the blessed Cyprian himself takes as an important document %. I too, considering this again and again, find that it is not only martyrdom for the name of Christ that can make up for the lack of baptism: faith and conversion of heart can also do so, if due to the urgency of the time it is not possible to attend the celebration of the baptismal mystery.

Indeed, that thief was not crucified for the name of Christ, but for his crimes; Furthermore, he did not suffer by faith, but believed while he suffered. In it it is also declared what value has, even without the visible sacrament of baptism, what the Apostle says: With the heart one believes for righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses for salvation. But this takes place invisibly, when it is not contempt for religion, but a circumstantial necessity that excludes siae, sic haereticorum errorem corrigamus, ut quod in eis non eorum sed Christi est agnoscamus.

THE GOOD THIEF AND THE BAPTISM OF CHILDREN

XXII 30. It is difficult to express the power and effect produced by the sanctification of the sacrament applied corporally to man, without which, however, the good thief was not left, because he did not lack the will to receive it, although there was no need to do so either? True, if he had not had very great courage, the Lord would not have received a baptism from the servant.

But it is necessary to consider it in itself, without taking into account the perfect holiness to which it is directed in man; That is why it clearly indicates that this sanctification is complete in the wicked and in those who renounce the world with words and not with works, although they cannot achieve health if they do not amend themselves. In the heart, which necessity deprived of bodily baptism, sanctification was accomplished by being spiritually present through piety; Likewise, when she is present, sanctification is carried out, even if necessity deprives the thief of what he did not lack.

This is the tradition of the universal Church when baptizing little children, who certainly cannot believe with the heart for justification nor confess with the mouth for salvation, which the thief could; and even more, with their cries and wails, when the mystery is celebrated in them, they interrupt crederent baptizari, when ad illum mentis habitum se peruenisse sentimental, ad quem multi baptizati adhuc ascendere conarentur.

CIRCUMCISION AND THE BAPTISM OF CHILDREN

XXIV 31. If someone claims divine authority in this matter, as it is a practice maintained by the entire Church and was not established by the councils, but has always been retained, it is rightly believed to be an apostolic tradition, although we can also conjecture truthfully what is the power of the sacrament of baptism in infants by the circumcision of the flesh which the people were the first to receive, and yet without having received it Abraham was justified. Like Cornelius he was also enriched with the gift of the Holy Spirit even before being baptized.

Of course the Apostle says of Abraham himself: He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of righteousness through his faith; He had already believed in his heart, and it had been counted as righteousness. Why, then, was he commanded to circumcise every newborn on the fourth day, if he could not yet believe with his heart so that it would be counted as righteousness? Simply because the sacrament itself had great value. This was manifested through an angel in the son of Moses, who, being carried still uncircumcised by his mother, was in eis mysterium celebratur, ipsis mysticis uocibus obstrepunt; et tamen nullus christianorum dixerit eos inaniter baptizari.

Thus, then, as in Abraham justice preceded by faith, and circumcision came as a sign of the righteousness of faith, so in Cornelius spiritual sanctification preceded in the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the sacrament of regeneration came in the bath of baptism. And as in Isaac, who was circumcised on the eighth day of his birth, the sign of the justice of faith preceded him, and in imitation of the father's faith, he followed in his adolescence the same justice, whose sign he had preceded as a child, so in baptized infants the sacrament of regeneration precedes, and if they preserve Christian piety, the conversion, whose mystery preceded in the body, will follow in their hearts. And as in that thief the benignity of the Omnipotent completed what was lacking through the sacrament of baptism, since there was no lack due to pride or contempt, but out of necessity, so in infants who die baptized it is believed that the same grace of the Omnipotent supplies what, not by impious will, but by incapacity of age, neither can they believe with their hearts for justice, nor can they confess with their mouths for salvation.

In this way, when others respond for them, so that the celebration of the sacrament has an effect on them, it certainly has value for their consecration, since they cannot respond. And, of course, it is of no value if someone answers for one who can answer for himself. According to that rule, se periculo ut circumcideretur exactum est (cf. BAPTISM AND CONVERSION OF THE HEART

XXV 32. By all this it is well proven that the sacrament of baptism is one thing, and the conversion of the heart is another, but that the salvation of man is completed in both. If one of the two were missing, we cannot think that it carries with it the lack of the other. Baptism without interior conversion can be in the infant, and this without the first could be in the good thief, as God supplies in both the one and the other what would have been lacking without will; Of course, if one of the two were missing voluntarily, the man would be responsible for the blame. Baptism can certainly exist where conversion of the heart is lacking; and there can be a conversion of the heart without receiving baptism, although it cannot exist if it is despised, since it cannot in any way be called a conversion of the heart to God when the sacrament of God is despised.

Therefore, we rightly rebuke, anathematize, detest, hate the perversity of heart of heretics; but they do not stop having the evangelical sacrament because they lack that which makes it profitable. Therefore, when they come to faith and truth, and by doing penance they ask for their sins to be forgiven, "we do not mock and deceive them after correcting and reforming them in what they have corrupted cum legitur natu(176)raliter mouet: aetatem habet, ipse pro se loquatur

LEGITIMATE BAPTISM AND ILLEGITIMATE BAPTISM

VII 8. Actually, when I read Cyprian's words, they raise some very necessary comments in me to resolve such a question. He says: "Well, if they (the heretics) saw that, according to our judgment and decision, the baptism with which they are baptized there is just and legitimate, they would think of justly and legitimately possessing the Church with the remaining property of the Church."

They do not say 'they thought they possessed the goods of the Church', but rather 'possessed justly and legitimately'. On the other hand, we grant that they possess baptism, but not justly and legitimately; we cannot say that they do not possess it, since we recognize the sibi aduersari arbitrarentur horrorem hominum de iterata tinctione quam considerationem de perdita defensione. Quod non ideo dixerim, quia humano sensu deterreri debuimus, si ab haereticis uenientes denuo baptizari ueritas cogeret, sed quia sanctus Cyprianus ait hoc ipso magis haereticos ad necessitatem ueniendi adigi potuisse, si rursus ín catholica baptizarentur, propterea commemorare uolui, quantus paene in omnium mentibus huius facti horror insidat, quem diuinitus infusum esse crediderim, ut aduersus quaslibet disputationes quas infirmi discusse nequeunt horrore ipso ecclesia muniretur.

THE LAW, THE EUCHARIST AND BAPTISM. LEGITIMACY AND EFFECTIVENESS

VMI 9. The Apostle said of the Law: The Law is good for those who use it legitimately. Thus we can say of baptism: "Baptism is good, if it is used legitimately." And just as then those who legitimately practiced the law did not annul its goodness and existence, so those who use it illegitimately, even in heresy, be it with a licentious life, do not annul the goodness and existence of baptism. Therefore, when one converts to Catholic unity or to a life worthy of such a great sacrament, one does not begin to have another legitimate baptism, but to have the same one legitimately.

Nor will the irrevocable remission of sins follow baptism by simply having baptism; It is necessary cum sacramentum dominicum in euangelicis uerbis cognoscimus. 18. Objection: “All the more reason to baptize after the heretic, since John was not a heretic, and yet he was baptized after him”?! 21. Consequently, the heretic has not appropriated baptism beforehand, since he had received it from the Church." Nor could he lose it by departing from it who we say is no longer maintained in the Church, but we know that he has baptism. Nor is anyone deprived of the birthright and granted it to the heretic; it is only said that he had risen with what he did not legitimately give, although he gave something legitimate, even if he did not legitimately possess what was legitimately his.

Birthright only exists in a holy treatment and in a good life, and to it belong all those who are members of the Dove without spot or wrinkle, a Dove that groans among the avilance of so many crows. Unless, since Esau has lost the birthright due to his desire for lentils, we are going to think that the fraudsters, thieves, usurers, envious people, drunkards and others of that type, whom Cyprian already lamented in the Church of his time through his writings, have the birthright.

Therefore, to remain in the Church is not to possess the birthright in divine things; or if everyone who remains in the Church has the birthright, all those who are unjust do not remain in the Church, although it seems that they confer baptism from within, a baptism that we believe to be conferred.

PEACEFUL SPIRIT OF CYPRIAN AT THE END OF HIS LETTER

XVII 22. We have now arrived, after going through and debating all the issues, at the peaceful words of Cyprian at the end of his letter, which I read and reread frequently without getting tired: such delight of brotherly love exudes, such sweetness of charity they overflow. He says: «I write to you, dear brother, briefly these things according to my littleness, without warning or prejudging anyone, so that each bishop can do what he thinks, according to the decision of his free will. We, as far as is in our power, looking at the heretics, do not argue with our colleagues in the episcopate, with whom we maintain concord and the peace of the Lord, especially keeping in mind what the Apostle says: If anyone likes to dispute, we do not have such a custom, nor does the Church of God. We preserve with patience and meekness the charity in our soul, the honor of the episcopal college, the bond of faith, the concord of the priesthood. For this reason also, with the approval and inspiration of the Lord, and taking into account the scope of our Jimitation, we have written the booklet on the “Advantages of Patience”, which we have sent to you as a pledge of mutual affection»?, baptismum dare et habere a nullo nostrum negantur. 23. In these words many things are worthy of consideration. In them shines the radiance of the Christian charity of this man, who loved the beauty of the house of the Lord and the place of his presence in the tabernacle.

Firstly, he did not hide his thoughts; Later he expressed it with admirable peace and meekness, he maintained ecclesial peace with those who had a different way of seeing things, he understood the saving force that was contained in the bond of unity, he loved it greatly and kept it with prudence, he saw and agreed that those who did not agree with him could think differently, leaving charity safe. I could not say that he maintained divine concord and the peace of the Lord with the bad, since the good can have feelings of peace towards the bad, but he cannot maintain with them the peace that they themselves do not have. Finally, by not preventing or judging anyone, so that each bishop acts as he thinks, having the free decision of his will, he offered all of us, whoever we are, the opportunity to peacefully discuss these issues among ourselves.

He is present among us, not only because of his letters, but also because of that charity that shone in him with such ardor and could never die. I would really like, then, to unite myself closely with him, and if my sins do not prevent me and his prayers help me, I will try to learn, if I can, from his writings, with what peace and comfort the Lord governed his Church through me.

23. In his uerbis plana consideringa sunt, quibus in hoc uiro, qui dilexit decorem domus domini et locum tabernaculi habitationis eius (cf. And clothed in the bowels of humility by the anointing of his word, if I have some truer ideas in union with the entire world, I will not regard him with superiority even in that which he thought otherwise, without separating himself—it is true—from the Christian world.

Certainly, when this question, not yet discussed, was in suspense, when many of his colleagues dissented, he behaved with such moderation that he did not mutilate with the stain of schism the holy communion of the Church of God, the strength of his virtue shone out to a greater height than if he had given full consent to all the truths with others, but without this virtue. And it would not please him if I tried to put his intelligence, the power of his word and the abundance of his doctrine before the sacrosanct council of all nations, which he surely attended in the unity of the spirit, especially being now enlightened by the truth, in which he discerns with complete certainty what he sought here with such great peace.

Surely in this plethora of light he will smile as if at children's games at these our speeches: there he already sees the rule of piety that governed him to have nothing more appreciated in the Church than unity; He also contemplates there with ineffable delight with what most merciful providence, seeking to cure our swelling, the Lord chose the foolishness of the world to confuse the wise, and so salutarily ordered all things in the hierarchy of the members of his Church, so that men would not be considered chosen for the propagation of the Gospel by their wit or their learning, whose dominus et quanto solacio gubernquerit, et per eius sermonis adfectum uisceribus humilitatis indutus si quid uerius sentio cum orbe terratum, non ei praeponam cor meum nec in eo ipso, quod aliter sentiens non tamen diremptus est ab orbe terrarum. Maius quippe in eo robur uirtutis eminuit, cum ista quaestio nondum discussa nutaret, quod aliter sentiens quam multi collegae tantam moderationem optinuit, ut ecclesiae dei sanctam societatem nulla schismatis labe truncaret, quam si omnia non solum ueraciter sed etiam pariter sine ista uirtute feel. Neque enim ei placeo, si eius ingenium facultatemque sermonis et doctrinae ubertatem sancto concilio cunctarum gentium, cui profecto interfuit per spiri- [282]tus unitatem, praeponere adfectem, praesertim iam in tali ueritatis luz posito, ubi certissime cernit quod hic pacatissime requirebat. How Cyprian will rejoice, with what serenity he will contemplate in this light the great good that follows to the human race from finding something reprehensible in the Christian and pious writings of the orators, although not in those of the Fishermen! Absolutely sure as I am of this joy of his holy soul, neither do I dare in any way to affirm or hold my writings as free from all error, nor do I dare to prefer my opinion to that of his, according to which those who came from heresy should be treated differently from that of before, according to his own testimony, or as they are received now, according to the custom that has been consolidated in the plenary council of the Christian world. I do not put mine before that opinion, but that of the holy Catholic Church, which he so esteemed and loved, in which he produced such abundant fruits with his tolerance: he was not alone the universality of that Church, although he did remain in its universality; nor did it ever abandon its root, but rather fertilized that root, it was purified by the heavenly vinedresser* with even greater fertility; and for his peace and his health, so that the wheat would not be uprooted with the tares, he rebuked with the freedom that truth gives and endured with the virtue of charity such great sins of men established with him in unity *. inde pestifera inflarentur superbia. With an abundance of doctrine he gives us this warning *: there are many dead in their crimes and sins who, although they do not belong to the community of Christ or to the members of that one innocent and simple Dove (which if she were the only one to baptize, they, certainly, would not baptize); It seems, however, that they are inside, that they baptize and are baptized. In them, certainly, although dead, lives the baptism of those who do not die and whom death will never dominate. There are, then, within the Church dead people not hidden (since Cyprian would not say so many things about them), who do not belong to that living Dove, or who do not yet belong; and there are dead people outside as well, whose non-belonging to it is more clearly seen, or who still do not belong; and it is true that one cannot receive the life of someone who does not have it. However, it is very clear that those who receive baptism among such subjects, if they approach with genuine contrition of heart, receive the life of him who is the owner of baptism. On the other hand, if they renounce the world with words and not with deeds (as Cyprian says there are within them), they do not receive life if they do not convert, although they have true baptism, even if they do not convert. Therefore, it is also manifest that those dead from abroad, although neither baptizarent, specie tamen intus uideri et baptizari et baptizare, et in eis quamuis mortuis illius tamen baptismum ujuere, qui non moritur et mors ei ultra non dominatibur (cf. XIX 25. Therefore, to those who then received those coming from heresy, baptized with the baptism of Christ received outside the Church, and claimed to follow the ancient custom, as the Church still practices today, they would be answered in vain by telling them that in ancient times the heresies and schisms were still as in their beginnings, and that among them were those who distanced themselves from the Church and had been baptized into it before, and It was not necessary to baptize them when they then returned to the Church and did penance*,

In fact, as soon as a heresy was born and it left communion with Catholic unity, that same day it could baptize those who came to it. SHEEP LOST IN HERESY, AND THE GOOD ONE INSIDE

26. What text of the Holy Scriptures shows that it is against God's command not to baptize those who come from heretics, if they have already received the baptism of Christ there? On the contrary, it is clearly demonstrated in them that many false Christians, although they do not have the same charity as the saints—without which all the holy things they possess are of no benefit—nevertheless have common baptism with the saints, as I have already demonstrated ad nauseam.

The Church, the Spirit and baptism cannot be separated from each other, and thus those who have separated themselves from the Church and the Holy Spirit, Cyprian claims, are also separated from baptism *. Just as on a fruitful branch there is something to be pruned so that it bears more fruit, so on a dry and sterile branch there is usually some cluster hanging *. It would be foolish to appreciate the filth of the fruitful branch; utility is sought by not rejecting the beautiful fruits wherever they are hanging. Likewise, he who, apart from unity, rebaptizes precisely because it seemed to Cyprian that it is necessary to baptize again those who come from heretics, acts foolishly: he thereby rejects what is admirable in a man of such greatness, and practices his errors, without achieving the very thing he seeks. In fact, Cyprian, profoundly rejecting those who separated from unity out of zeal for God, judged that they had also separated from baptism; and the Donatists, considering it a small crime that they had separated themselves from the unity of Christ, strive to demonstrate that there is no longer baptism in it, but that it came out with them. Now, since it is said "we believe in one baptism, which is in the holy Church", so that it is affirmed that it is certainly in the holy Church, but it is not denied that it is also in another place, it is not necessary to dispute against those words, even if he thought otherwise,

In fact, if I were asked separately if there is only one baptism, I would answer that there is only one. If I am then asked if this is found in the holy Church, I would answer that it is, indeed. If I were still asked if I believed in that baptism, I would answer that I did; and that answer would imply that he believed in only one baptism, which is in the holy Church. But if you ask me if it is found only in the holy Church and that it does not exist among heretics and schismatics, I would answer with the entire Church that this is not my faith.

But since he did not put this into his opinion, it seems to me not honest to attribute to him words that I have not found in him, in order to refute them. As if he said “one is the water of the river Euphrates, which is in paradise”, he would certainly say a truth. But if, when asked if this water is found only in paradise, he answered affirmatively, what he said would be a falsehood. In fact, it is also found outside of paradise, in those lands through which it flows from that source. But is there anyone so reckless that they claim to have answered a falsehood, while perhaps being able to tell the truth? For this reason there should not be ecclesia sancta credimus, Si autem dixisset: «quod est in sola ecclesia sancta credimus», responderdum erat sicut ceteris. Answer: If the reason for wanting to baptize him is because he did not receive forgiveness of sins, suppose that you find someone within the church who is baptized having hatred towards his brother; and since the word of the Lord cannot fail: If you do not forgive, you will not be forgiven either; when this man makes amends, will you command that he be baptized again? In no way. Well, the same must be done with the heretic. It is true that it should not be overlooked why Dativeus did not simply say "we have no communion with the heretic," but added: "as far as it depends on us." In fact, he saw that many agreed with this opinion, from whose communion, however, in order not to break the unity, they could not separate themselves, and he added: "as far as it depends on us." With which he showed that he did not voluntarily communicate with those who he thought did not have baptism, but that everything had to be endured for the sake of peace and unity; which huius sententiae non debent habete contradictionem, quia nihil inpediunt ueritatem...

Wouldn't this answer have the appearance of truth? And yet, it is a falsehood. In effect, they baptize the wicked, since the thieves who were with Cipriano in the unit and whom he refuted were wicked. That is the reason - it will be said - for adding outside." Why, then, can't these baptize outside? Perhaps because they are even worse for being outside? But the greater or lesser malice of the one who gives it matters nothing for the integrity of baptism. In fact, there is not as much difference between the bad and the worse as there is between the good and the bad; however, when the bad baptizes, he does not give anything different from what the good gives. Therefore, when one baptizes worse, he does not give anything different from what a less evil person gives when he baptizes.

Would it be necessary to pay attention to the merit of the man and not to the sacrament of baptism so that it could not occur outside? If this were so, one could not be kept outside, and it would be necessary to baptize as many times as one, leaving the Church, returned to it again.

66. What it means to be baptized for a dead person, without prejudging a more careful consideration of the same Scripture, we have already said elsewhere *, I ask, however, why they understand only heretics as dead, when the apostle Paul has said generically of sin: The wages of sin is death, and also: To desire according to the flesh is death. And* What profit, then, does the bathing of one who is baptized by these? If he is a sinner, he certainly has a bath, but it does nothing for his health.

On the contrary, if the one who baptizes him is a sinner, but he converts to God with a sincere heart, he is not properly baptized by that dead person, but by him who lives and of whom it was said: This is the one who baptizes, regardless of the minister who baptizes bodily.

He says of heretics: "If those who receive baptism among them obtain eternal life through the remission of sins, why do they come to the Church?" To this I answer: they come precisely because, although they received the baptism of Christ in the celebration of the sacrament, they do not obtain eternal life except through the charity proper to unity. In reality, the holy Catholic Church, in all peoples, faced with a certain darkness that may arise from some points of this question of baptism, that is, whether that of heretics and schismatics can be the same as that of the Catholic Church, is protected with the authority of primitive custom and a plenary council. However, there were respectable men, and above all Cyprian, who within the same unit saw things differently, and now intend to use that authority against us, those who are so far from their charity. Therefore, being offered the opportunity to discuss and examine all the points that we find on this question in the council and in the letters, we are forced to consider this issue again and again more carefully and to show that the universal Catholic Church is completely right in determining that heretics and schismatics, who have already received the baptism of Christ in the sect from which they come, be admitted with him into the Catholic communion, corrected from their error, established and founded in the charity; so that, as regards the sacrament of baptism, they do not receive what they did not lack, but rather take advantage of what they already had. INTRODUCTION I. THE «BREUICULUS COLLATIONIS» AND THE CARTHAGE CONFERENCE OF 411!

The great inter-church event of Carthage 411 goes beyond the limits of any introduction. With him the Catholic-Donatist controversy culminates and this Augustinian work deals with him. Its context is double, namely: a remote one, which dates back almost to the time of Optatus of Milevi and which could be traced back to the edict of the Emperor Honorius, on October 14, 410?; and another close and even immediate, in which it is necessary to include the circumstances of the date, the place, the arrival of both episcopates to Carthage, and the documents that follow one another during the days between the arrival in the city, May 18, and the opening, June 1? Here I will say only what is essential so that the reader has a rough idea that allows him to understand Augustinian writing.

The emperor Honorius ordered in the edict to place at the disposal of the proconsul, or tribune and notary of his in Africa, Marcellinus, all the administrative apparatus necessary to carry out such a very delicate mission, a mission that must have ended on February 14, 411 and that, in reality, only began on January 19, 411, when the imperial commissioner ordered the edict of convocation to be established in Carthage and spread throughout the Province of Africa *. According to the imperial rescript, the Conference had to be held within a period of four months: quam rem intra quatuor menses praecipimus explicai5, that is, we are faced with the famous chronological difficulty of the lapsus temporis, so exploited by the Donatists during the debates. Together with the famous documents or gesta municipalia *, it demonstrates how difficult Marcellin's task was, whose edict of immediate convocation contrasts, by the way, in terms of style, with that of the emperor.

C) Purpose. It is very clearly expressed in these words from the preface of the BC: "That is why it seemed good to me to cover everything in this summary, so that with the numbering of it and the facts, each one can easily find what he wants to investigate." An analogous judgment is made by the author in his self-review of the BC when, having declared the method followed in the writing, which was the chronological method of the three days of the Conference (=litterisque comprebendi secundum tres dies... consultis numeris, quos rebus singulis annotaui)", he adds: idque opus utile existimaui, quo quisque commonitus uel sciat sine labore, quid actum sit, uel consultis numeris..., legat in eisdem gestis ad locum, quodcumque uoluerit "? The fundamental purpose of the BC, then, was to make the official Acts intelligible. In what way? Proceeding to write them in a style that, without deviating from that of the official ones or Gesta (=hence the collationis of the title), would introduce the synthesis factor, or the quality of concision and summary: hence, also, the title Breniculus or breviary or compendium or summary. And along with this novelty, which the official ones lacked, which were cumbersome, another no less important note: that of clarity, To achieve this note, Saint Augustine prefers to respect the chronological order of the Acts, which, after all, was the one followed during the debates of Carthage 411. And then also respect the punctuation, in the hope that whoever deemed it appropriate to verify the official ones and those of Augustine, that is, the BC, could do it with ease (=uel consultis numeris..., legat in eisdem gestis ad locum)”.

A purpose, as can be seen, that begins with being methodological, since it is intended to save energy for the reader, who was surely fatigued by the prolixity of the official ones (=quoniam fatiguent illa nimia prolixitate) *, who in this way can comfortably know what was debated in Carthage 411. IV. BC Division The tripartite division corresponds to the three days of the Conference. The division into chapters of the first two books is from Saint Augustine. The one in the third book is purely arbitrary. In fact, the author only indicates five chapters that, according to the current distribution, begin with the summaries of the following citations: 1,1; 2.2; 7.8; 8,10; 12,24. Monceaux represents a sixth chapter for the judge's ruling: 25.43 *%, The BC limits itself to summarizing the Minutes, explaining the tenor of

the same, indicate the consequence of the ideas by establishing the sequence of events through a summary presentation of them. It is not true, as Lancel wants, that the BC is devoid of any documentary value, since there is no shortage of occasions in which it alludes to or refers to certain documents. And regarding the fact that "it does not provide any indication that would allow the original order of the documentation to be restored" 7 it must be specified that this was not Augustine's purpose when writing the Brewiculus. It is obvious that Augustine's interest was not so much in the documents, easily consulted in the Acts after all, as in clarifying what was obscure in said Acts, that is, in eliminating the clutter and making the text understandable. One thing is that for our modern research a precise Augustinian report of the documentation of Carthage 411 would have been great, and especially from the criteria of a comparative study between Gesta and BC, and quite another that it would then be necessary to provide them. Day, then, spent reading documents; tentative; of preparation; without dialectic yet, although the first symptoms of blockade of the Conference by the schismatic side made an appearance in the room through the question of lapsus temporis and the question of number. The question arises: Were the Donatists sure that they were right? If they were so sure they had the truth on their side, why did they start acting that way?
The second session opened, as agreed, on June 3. The summary of it in the BC is very simple and brief:
1.) Request from the Justice of the Peace for both parties to take a seat in the courtroom. Positive response from Catholics and negative from Donatists (c.1).

2.) Reading of the demand that the Donatists had delivered the previous day asking that "the mandate of the Catholics be shown to them, with whose careful examination they could attend and be instructed on the appointed day", to which the Judge agreed (c.2).

3.) Question from the Judge about agreement or disagreement with the proposal to each sign their own interventions. Donatist demand for a delay, so that the drafted Minutes could be shown to them, to which the Judge had to agree by ordering the codices to be brought. The Donatists, likewise, complained about the publication of the Minutes, "because the secretaries did not arrive to collect the entire process." Finally, after insisting, "they were granted a delay of six days, based on the response of the secretaries regarding the publication of the Minutes, and they promised that, when the Minutes were published, they would sign their interventions" (c.3).
In short: short session, of pure procedure, more than a session.

Important, because it deals with true theology, because it addresses the underlying issue, which is the discussions about the very cause of the Church. There they were, finally, after so many years, face to face the two ways of understanding the Church, the two ecclesiologies, from whose clarification flowed the baptismal theses and everything else.

The debate on this matter of Ceciliano forced not only an exhaustive documentary contribution, but also to stick to historical data. The summary of the BC constitutes one of the best synthesis of the main historical events of Donatism. In Carthage 411, in fact, the unavoidable evidence of the brief archival data had to be resorted to to prevent the many signs that there were distortions and manipulation of the facts.

IV part (n. 43): Conclusive, Disarmed and without arguments, Donatism failed to react to the Judge's request in the sense of adducing new evidence. "In the end the Judge already said: If you have nothing to read against it, please come out so that we can write a complete ruling on this whole issue." The final paragraph of the BC is quite eloquent in itself: «He made them enter again and it was read

the previously drafted sentence: it covered everything he could remember from the prolonged debates of the three sessions. The third session of the Conference of Carthage, on June 8, 411, is, without a doubt, the most substantial of the three, the most interesting, the truly doctrinal; simply, the one that ended up analyzing the substance of the Catholic-Donatist question. Of the four parts into which this third session is divided, those of greatest interest are, clearly, the second, due to the ecclesial argument, the pillar of the entire controversy, and the fourth, since, although short on words, it was powerful, of all the scope that the proconsular and imperial ruling, favorable to the Catholic cause, entailed.
VI. Texro A) Editions

1. After our debate with the Donatists I briefly recalled the issues that were discussed there and compiled them in writing, arranged over three days, in which we debated with them. I considered this work useful, since it teaches each one to know without effort what was discussed there, or to read, seeing the numbers assigned to each point, the place they want in the same minutes; In fact, the minutes presented at such length tire the reader. The title of the book is: "Summary of the debate."

SUMMARY OF THE DEBATE WITH THE DONATISTS DEBATE OF THE FIRST DAY! Preracio: PURPOSE OF THE WORK The Catholic bishops and those of the sect of Donatus, by order of the emperor, engaged in a discussion with interviews carried out in the presence of the tribune and notary Marcellinus, as Justice of the Peace?. A very lengthy account was written about all of this, which could well have been done more briefly. But those who knew that they were not defending a worthy cause, made every effort, first, to ensure that no such debate took place or that the issue was not even discussed. Not being able to achieve this, they described it with such clutter that it was very difficult to read. That is why it seemed good to me to cover everything in this summary, so that with the same numbering in this summary and in the original minutes everyone can easily find what they want. Cum catholici episcopi et partis Donati iussu imperatoris disputing inter se gestis apud tribunum et notarium Marcellinum cognitorem habitis contulissent, multum prolixa eorundem Gestiónrum est facta conscriptio, quamuis posset totum multo breuius agi. Sed qui causam bonam non se habere sciebant, id egerunt primum quantum potuerunt, ut nec ipsa collatio ièret et ut prorsus causa ipsa non ageretur. ADDITIONAL NOTES

[1] Protocol of Cirta.—On March 5, 305—Lancel prefers 307—a synod of eleven bishops met in Cirta of Numidia, today Constantine of Algeria, to ordain the new bishop of that city (Breu. 111 17,32; LereLLeY, 11 3835). This improperly called council of Numidia, or also council of Cirta, or, said from the minutes, Protocol of Cirta, is presided over by the oldest of the group, Second of Tigisi (compl. no. 46). When Segundo questions those present about their honorability in the crime of fraditio, almost all of them admit to having handed over the Scriptures and ask for forgiveness. Purpurio de Limata, however, violently rebukes Segundo for investigating a crime of which he himself is guilty. As the hostility becomes unanimous, he decides that each one will be accountable directly to God (Brew. 111 15,27; C. Cr. 111 27; Orraro, I 14), authorizes everyone to sit down and proceeds to the ordination of Silvanus, recently elected successor of Paul and, like him, translator of the Scriptures during the investigations carried out on May 19, 303 (C. Cr. III 26,29; PAC 1, 1078-1080). S. de T. has been held responsible for the first act of dissidence at the origins of the Schism. The reproach of Catholic tradition became especially intense during the Carthage Conference of 411: suspected traditor and acquitted in 305 by the fraditores present in Cirta, and with him consecrators of the traditor Silvanus, he had had no scruple in condemning with them in Carthage, and on suspicion of this same crime, the absent Caecilian (C. Ep. Parm. 13,5; C. Cr. MI 27,31; De a. 17,31;

For the origins of the D. we depend essentially on a single dossier, composed unilaterally by the Catholics in the final stretch of Constantine and used in Carthage 411. Some of its points have not infrequently been the subject of conflicting opinions within critics. The Protocol of Cirta is a unique verbal process, partially preserved, of the meeting held in the Numidian metropolis to ordain Silvanus, and which in itself demonstrates that Christians enjoyed authentic freedom at that time. We know its records from Optatus and Agustín, who offers the almost entire text in C. Cr. 11 27,30 (Breu. 1 15,27; MoNncEAUx, IV 13s; Von SODEN, 7s; DUCHESNE, 629; LAMIRANDE, 75; BARNES, 12). The minutes of the verbal process seen during the improperly called Council of Cirta are, therefore, those designated with the title of Protocol of Cirta. Once its authenticity was contested by Volter, Seeck vigorously defended it and it was later recognized by Duchesne (LAMIRANDE, 729).

During the Conference of Carthage, the Donatists attempted to demonstrate the inauthenticity of the Protocol and for Marcellin to reject it, alleging that the piece—decretus is usually the name by which it is mentioned—was false due to its consular date, contrary to ecclesiastical customs; On the other hand, meeting a council during the persecution of Diocletian would have been impossible, to which the Catholics replied saying that it was not impossible, since the acts of the martyrs (acta martyrum) demonstrated that the Christian communities had met at that time.

The date of the Protocol was certainly falsified, but the Donatists, instead of working on this argument, insisted on the impossibility of holding meetings under Diocletian, and thus they soon found themselves cornered by the Catholics. [4] Osio of Córdoba.—Born around 256, by 300 he was already bishop of Córdoba, and as such he attended the council of Elvira. In Constantine's letter to Caecilian, his name appears: "Constantine Augustus to Caecilian, bishop of Carthage: 1. Since in all the provinces, particularly in the Africas, the Numidias and the Mauritanias, I was pleased that something should be granted for their expenses to some distinguished ministers of the legitimate and most holy Catholic religion, I have dispatched a letter to the most perfect Ursus, general director of the finances of Africa, instructing him to arrange for pay your firmness three thousand folles.—2. You, therefore, when you acknowledge receipt of the indicated amount of money, order that this money be distributed to all the above-mentioned people according to the document that Hosius has sent you" (EUSEBIUS, HE X 6,1-2: BAC 350, p.631s). When Constantine writes this letter, Hosius is already part of his court. They must have met, therefore, before April 313 (VeLasco, 632, n.170; V. C. DE CLERCO, 140150). He accompanies Constantine to the East in 324, and in 325 he is the main character of Nicaea, as revealed by the records, headed with his name. Faithful to the Nicene creed during the Arianism of Constantius (350-357) and declared supporter of the champion of orthodoxy, the great Saint Athanasius, the Arian bishops manage, however, to make him come, an old man, to the emperor, and sign a letter in which the homousios is not used (357). Perhaps recognizing that he had not condemned

Augustine does not seem to know much about Hosius on this matter, but he did know, and at length, about the Donatists. Hence, when replying to Parmeniano, it is necessary from the outset: first, to prove that it was just as they say; then, that it manifested itself as they claim (C. Ep. Parm. 14,7). The fact is - he continues - that the Spanish, after a time, also agreed to forgive, like the French, Osio, condemned, apparently, for intrigues very similar to those used by the D. But there is more: the case of the Spanish bishops serves to condemn the D. once again, because they knew how to understand and forgive. If in the first part they could resemble the Donatists by allowing themselves to be carried away by the condemnation, and perhaps through intrigue, in the second part they differ completely, since the Spaniards did not act like those of the party: sicut isti miseri fecerunt (C. Ep. Parm. 14,77: CSEL 51, p.26). [51 Donatist Bible.—The Bible is common basis for Catholics and Donatists. They go to it constantly, but it is also a point of litigation. The schismatics will not cease to accuse Caecilian and his followers of having handed over (=+tradere: traditores) the Scriptures (compl. n. 71). It is rather the Donatists - Augustine replies - who, by not wanting to listen to them, commit something worse than handing them over or burning them (Ep. 129,3). Furthermore: with their attitude contrary to Scripture, they show that they do not know how to read or understand it, nor interpret it (C. Ep. Parm. 11 1,2; C. Gaud. 1 30,34; Ep. 185,1,2; LAMIRANDE, 693s). Catholicity is one of the recurring biblical themes. Augustine also understands that the use of the Bible consists of more than just instructing and edifying. It is, above all, about convincing. Hence the rigorous choice of texts when

Additional notes 853 comment or argue (L. DE MonDaADoN, 441ff). Hence also, although the Bible is common, the interpretations are not so common. Catholics and Donatists sometimes work in very different ways on the texts contributed to the debate. This has been highlighted by Congar, Bavaud, Quinot and A. C. de Veer in his complementary notes (cf. in Bibl.). The important thing in cases like this will be to determine who is right: the Bible is, without a doubt, the best arbitrator (P. pe Lurs, 3ff). It is worth remembering that the legitimate bishop speaks in the name of Christ, Shepherd of the shepherds, and is linked to the fides Ecclesiae, of which he is a minister, which, in turn, is linked to the holy Scriptures. The preacher and the doctor of the faith are fundamentally commentators (+tractatores) of the Holy Scripture: «Tractator loquitur; if it were loquitur, Christus loquitur» (Serm. 7,1: PL 38,124). In what Scripture has not expressly determined anything, we must abide by what the Church says, since Scripture does not formally contain the definition of everything, but it establishes the right that the Church has, by virtue of the assistance of Christ and his Spirit, to clarify the points not settled by the sacred text (CONGAR, 749).

Augustine knows how to take advantage of the good of D in the use of the Bible. For example, the rules of Tyconius (MorEau, 271, n.31; cf. compl. n. 24). It pronounces on the canonical books (De d. ch. 1I 8,12), on whose canonicity, in its time, not all the Churches were in agreement (Morzau, 289; La BONNARDIERE, 289). Faithful to the end to the biblical version of the Seventy (ib., 312). In their controversies they all highlight a common characteristic: from the Manichaeans to the Pelagians, passing through the Donatists, it is noted that those who live outside the Catholica question the Word of God, even when the Bible itself is not the object of the confrontation, since it always provides the arguments for dialogue or debate (ib., 329-352: 331). Studying his scriptural citations, however, is difficult, understanding the topic at hand, since neither Augustine of Hippo has transmitted in their entirety all the Donatist writings that came into his hands, nor do we preserve all the works he wrote to the schismatics; To glimpse the biblical contributions of his works, one must often refer to the brief news of the Retractions (ib., 3325).

By preserving the texts of certain heterodox people, Augustine has also transmitted their bibles, that is, the biblical quotations that these texts reaffirm. We have, therefore, a batch of biblical documents of which he is a witness without being the author. Here it is necessary to resort to, among other sources, when preparing the Donatist Bible, which is still to be done, although we already have meritorious studies with the Augustinian Bible, which La Bonnardiére is in progress, and the good studies recently dedicated to Tyconius by S. Barcellona and R. Pose (cf. compl. n. 24 and 25; in bibl. gen., n.4. Donatism: Ticonius). We will have to do something similar to what Decret and Gryson contributed with their splendid studies on Manichaeans and Pelagians respectively (La BONNARDIERE, 336, bibl.).

Another chapter to take into account is that of the biblical versions (GrrBOMONT, 231ff), which, despite their variety, present as a common characteristic that they are prior to the Hebrew translation of Saint Jerome, and which in no case should be judged and criticized based on the Vulgate. Globally they belong to the Vetus latina or, rather, to the Veteres latinae (old Latin women), of which the Institute of the Vetus latina (Die Reste der Altlateinischen Bibel) has become a prestigious editor in Beuron. The Latin term Vetus includes the set of

854 Complementary notes loans provided by the manuscripts and scriptural citations collected, one by one, in the works of the Fathers of the Latin Church. Augustine, as is the case with the other Latin Fathers, constitutes a testimony of the versions of the Bible that he had in hand and, therefore, also of the versions of the heterodox that he collected in his writings, the Donatists included, of course (La BONNARDIERE, 3365; GRIBOMONT, 231ff). The variety of versions depends not only on the authors of these writings, but also on each of the biblical books themselves. More and more light is being shed regarding the Veteres latinae, thanks to the Bulletin de la Bible latine, edited annually by Father Maurice Bogaert in the RBén, in the abbey of Maredsous, but in the Donatist Bible there is still much to be done. It is becoming increasingly clear that Donatists and Catholics stuck at the beginning to the famous Bible used by Saint Cyprian, but that later the Catholics enriched it with data and contributions from the Italic versions, coming from the transmarine Churches, while those of the party preferred to cling to the original of Cyprian and not admit additions. And, within themselves, there were their pluses and minuses as reflected in the confrontation between Tyconius and Parmeniano (compl. n. 27 and 25). This simple fact shows how, while the Catholica preferred to open itself to transmarine imports, thus proving to be a Church of the Fathers in accordance with the times, the Schism preferred to remain clinging to the traditional, revealing itself as a closed and monolithic Church up to sectarian limits.—BIBL.: G. [6] "Extra Ecclesiam nulla salus."—The meaning of this formula of the baptismal controversy of the 20th century. 111 goes beyond the Catholic-Donatist and even patristic spheres (WILLEMs, 114ff). Appeared in an inadmissible context

Additional notes 855 sible for orthodox criticism and in a parousian perspective. Fruit of a rigorous attitude and a true postulate. The baptism of heretics, invalid, because outside the Church there is no salvation. How can we conceive that a baptism is valid outside the Church? God has given salvation to the world in Christ, who prolongs it by founding the Church: the unity and communion of the Church gathered around the bishop is salvation, since the community of Christians is precisely the place where the Father, the Son and the Spirit communicate. Outside of this unity, also constituted by the fides integra, there is only room for the work of the antichrist. It is impossible to have God as Father if you do not have the Church as Mother. It is not possible to be a Christian without belonging to Her (Ep. 55,24; QuasTEN, 667). She is the only way of salvation: Extra Ecclesiam nulla salus (De unit. 6: CSEL 3/1, p.204); Salus extra Ecclesiam non est (Ep. 73,21; cf. Ep. 74,7; 4,4; 55,24; CreEsPIN, 2525). The rigorism of Tertullian takes over the disciple Saint Cyprian in these and other phrases. Led by a rigid, rectilinear methodology, he will force even the texts so that the argument bends towards the thesis of unity, and will proceed, as if it were a theorem, from the one God to the one salvation in Christ, and to the one Church, to the one bishop and one baptism (Lana, 746). The formula is linked to a scheme of inclusion or exclusion contained in expressions such as in Ecclesia, or intra (extra) Ecclesiam, or also intus/foris (Epp. 55,8; 63,14; 66,8; 69,3; 70,1; 73,1,1.2,2; 7,2; 9,1; 11,2). And this scheme, in turn, linked to the monolithic and rigorous sequence of one God, one Church, one baptism. We are faced with the theology of yes or no, inside or outside, light or darkness. Rigorism prevents any middle ground (De unit. 11; Epp. 69.3; 73.5; 66.2; 68.2; 71.2; 52.1).

Donatist ecclesiology was strongly inspired by that of Saint Cyprian. Those of Donato also advocated that the Holy Spirit and salvation have a very close relationship, and with them baptism, only possible in the Church: only a minister in communion with her can validly celebrate the sacraments and communicate grace, since only what one has is given. "Augustine understands this position as if the Donatists made the sacraments and grace depend on the personal moral sanctity of the minister, although the veil of ambiguity with which they wrapped this point prevents us from knowing whether Augustine's argument was valid for them" (ConGarR: BAC II 4; Ip., in BA 28, p.53).

Saint Augustine raised the same argument in another way: the sacraments are valid wherever faith exists and the form instituted by Christ is kept; but although valid, they are only received with usefulness and benefit (utiliter, ad salutem-salubriter, ad salutem) in the unity (unitas) of the Church, to which the Holy Spirit is linked (De b. 11,2; V 8,9; VI 1,1; C. Cr. 1 29, 34; Epp. 61,1; 54,1; passim). He distinguishes, therefore, between valid sacraments and beneficial sacraments, and demonstrates that baptism and orders are valid even outside the Church, although they only benefit in the Church, "for it is one thing not to have it (b), another not to have it with benefit" (De b. IV 17,24). The reason for the first is because "baptism has its own holiness and truth" by virtue of Christ who has instituted it (C. Cr. IV 16,19) and is its main minister (/m lo. 6,7) and who prints its character (In lo. 6,15-16; In lo. ep. 7,11); that of the second, because he cannot possess the grace of baptism who does not have charity, and he who tears unity lacks it: "Those who do not love the unity of the Church do not possess the charity of God" (De b. [71 "Nibil innouetur nisi quod traditum est."—Two great ecclesiastical traditions, the African one (ceclesiological) and the Roman one (Christological), confront each other through Saint Cyprian and Pope Stephen 1 over the question of the baptism of heretics (Laca, 371ff; NEUNHEUSER, 42f; BrissoN, 114). What about such baptism and how to treat eventual converts from apostasy and heresy? The practice was diverse: in the African Churches and quite a few in the East, rebaptism had begun some time ago. Rome and Alexandria, on the other hand, only demanded the laying on of hands as a sign of reconciliation. The validity of the baptism of heretics had already been denied by Tertullian (De bapt. 15). Like him then (198-200), the bishops of Africa and Numidia later thought and acted (S. CrP., Ep. 71,4,1). The issue became complicated when Magnus, homo laicus (MANSI, 1921), asked Cyprian if heretics should be rebaptized in the name of Christ as heretics and schismatics. "About this problem," Cipriano replied,

Supplementary Notes 857 as far as the capacity of our faith and the holiness and truth of the divine Scriptures inspire us, we say that all heretics and schismatics have no jurisdiction or right” (Ep. 69,1). The council of Carthage in 256, presided over by Cyprian himself, ratified this response and the decision to rebaptize (Mater, 235; MuniEr, 602).

Communicated to Stephen (Ep. 72), he wrote two letters on the matter: one to the Church of Asia Minor, in which he threatens to excommunicate the bishops of Cilicia, Cappadocia, Galatia and neighboring provinces if they continue rebaptizing (EuseBio, HE VIT 5,4; S. Cir., Ep. 75,25); another in the same 256 (Ep. 74) to Cyprian, where he categorically rejects the rebaptizing practice of Africans: «If, therefore, some come to you from any heresy, do not innovate anything, but follow tradition (nihil innouetur nisi quod traditum est), that is, lay hands on them to receive penance, since the heretics themselves do not baptize anyone of one or another. another sect that comes to them, but only admits them to their communion" (S. CIP., Ep. 74,1; J. Campos, 693).

The words nibil innouetur nisi quod traditum est have been the subject of controversy among specialists (DOLGER, 7958; (QUASTEN, 538; CONGAR, 71ff). It is clear, of course, that Stephen intends to say: «Let nothing new be introduced, rather let tradition be followed. Which indirectly means that the rebaptizing practice has been, and continues to be, an innovation (inmnouetur). In fact, Cyprian protests that he is being treated as an innovator (Ep. 74,2). Having calmly examined the matter, Stephen, in the end, does not express his own opinion so much as that of Roman tradition; he cites an ancient principle of Roman tradition, according to which the matter must be settled. Supported, then, on this Roman tradition (Ep. 74,1-2) and referring to his Petrine succession (Ep. 75,17) Stephen originates the confrontation. With his appeal to the immutable tradition he clearly demonstrates, in any case, the extent to which the Roman Church had already realized its primacy in the universal Church (Sruner, 3309s). to Cyprian on behalf of the clergy of Rome: Nibil innouandum putauimus (S. Cip., Ep. 30,8; QUASTEN, 539.5165s; DESIMONE, 508). [8] "Integer"-"profanus" in Donatist ecclesiology.—The D. advocated and wanted a Church, from the essentially ecclesiological point of view, pure, of upright and irreproachable men. Such is the meaning of the adjective integer, which is often used in opposition to profanus or adulter. The word integer, with the sense of intact, irreproachable, appears in the sacramental-baptismal jargon of Saint Cyprian (De unit. 6; Epp. 67,25; 68,2; 72,3; 73,1; cf. references in BrIssoN, 138, n.5; 220, n.3). Even more difficult to express its proper meaning in canon 33 of the council of Elvira of 300-303 (integer=inviolate: Manst 2,12; P. De Luis, 1144). It also appears with some frequency in the Donatist writings or those relating to the D. (Gesta apud Zenophilum: CSEL 26, p.192; S. Ac., Epp. 43,9,25; 93,10,43; De b. II 15,20; C. Ep. Parm. III 1,1; cf. n. compl. 1 and 46). "It is a sacrilegious person," the Donatists affirm, referring to the Catholic minister, "who erects an altar, a profane who officiates, a guilty person who baptizes, a wounded person who signs, a persecutor who venerates martyrs, a traditor who reads the Scriptures" (Passio Saturn. 19). The Bishop of Hippo also specifies: «Non est autem aqua profana et adultera super quam dei nomen inuocatur, etiamsi a profanis et adulteris inuocetur, quia nec ipsa creatura nec ipsum nomen adulterum est. baptismus uero Christi uerbis euangelicis consecratus et per adulteros et in adulteris sanctus est, quamuis ¡lli sint impudici et inmundi, quia ipsa eius sanctitas pollui non potest et sacramento suo diuina uirtus adsistit siue ad salutem bene utentium siue ad perniciem male utentium» (De b. 111 10.15: CSEL 51, p.205).
The Donatists spoke without specifying or distinguishing even once,

and they boasted of being not only the holy Church, but the Church of the saints. But they did not consider any sins other than those excising the Church as destroyers of the sanctifying virtue of the minister: heresy, schism, traditio - the surrender of the Scriptures was equivalent, in fact, to having renounced the faith -, persecution of the Church; in short: sins, so to speak, ecclesiological (CONGAR, 56; KORNYLJAK, 57.62). In his letter on baptism Donatus approached the terms pure and impure, holy and profane through the prism of ecclesiology and not through that of personal morality (MonCEAUX, V 125). The following expressions of Saint Augustine are revealing in this regard: «interesse qualis sit macula et guale uitium» (C. E. Parn. 11 7,13); «peccator qualem nostri describunt..., ius sibi baptismatis non usurpet» (C. Cr. 11 29,37). The Donatists, finally, attributed to this pure, integral, irreproachable Church, Bride of Christ, the Pauline statement Ecclesia sine macula et ruga (Eph 5,27), without economizing a margin, a tension, between its present historical state and its eschatological state (ConGAR, 63, n.3). Saint Augustine does know how to introduce the appropriate ecclesiological distinctions: between the Church here below and the eschatological one, as explained in the Augustinian ecclesiological theses of the general introduction.—BrBL.: P. [9] The authority of Saint Cyprian for Donatism.—Saint Cyprian was an exceptional figure and of great veneration for any Christian in Africa. On the anniversary of his martyrdom, the Donatists danced around his tomb (S. Ac., Serzz. 311,5). They invoked his great authority especially in matters of ecclesiology and rebaptismal practice (C.

Saint Augustine also professed respectful veneration to him, even consecrating a considerable part of the De baptismo and significant references in Ep. 93 and in Contra Cresconium (WiLxis, 121; Concar, 592.597.615.619; LAMIRANDE, 713). The entire Augustinian syllogistic emphasis is focused on demonstrating to those of the Schism that they have no right to use the authority of Saint Cyprian - no matter how much they try to put forward their thesis of the rebaptizing practice - since the schismatic attitude is in no way contrary to the Saint, who remained in the Church and was an ardent defender of its unity (De b. II 3,4). The Augustinian insistence consists above all in highlighting that the Donatists have broken with the Church, causing a detestable schism, while Cyprian preferred to maintain communion with those who thought differently from his own, and, although he advocated rebaptism, the issue was then in need of being settled in a plenary council (Arles 314; cf. n. compl. 10), so he preferred to take the case without any sectarianism rather than forcing the Church of Africa to submit to his personal conviction in a matter that, after all, was still debatable (De b. 1 18,28; 11 5,6; 6,7; 1IT 3,5: main text where the Hipponense cites Ep. 73,23 of Saint Cyprian; IV 8,11; V 17,23; C. Cr. II 38,48s; Ep. 93,10,41). The argument discussed here, then, gave Augustine the opportunity to outline a beautiful theology of communion in diversity or plurality. The accurate formulas used credit him as one of the great exponents of unity within the apostolic tradition; unity, by the way, which is something very different from pure and simple leveling uniformity (CoNGAR, 70; BATIFFOL, 616ff). Contrary to the Donatists, who supported their theses on the ecclesiological and baptismal statements of Saint Cyprian, and despite their declared admiration, and even verbal juggling to save him in what could be saved, Saint Augustine has no choice but to declare the error of the holy bishop of Carthage on the rebaptismal issue, and this is stated in his De baptismo (cf. criticism of Ep. 73 of Cyprian to Jubaiano: III 13-V 23; criticism of Ep. 71 of Cyprian to Quintus: V 23-27; criticism of Ep. 70 of Cyprian and the synodality of the autumn council of 255: V 27-30;

74 from Cyprian to Pompey: V 31-39; and criticism of the Sententiae episcoporum of the council of 256: VI 9-VII 99). The authority of Saint Cyprian, therefore, is not for Saint Augustine the supreme norm, unlike the Donatists. Before there is that of the Scriptures. And that of the universal Church, which after the death of the Saint pronounced itself clearly in a council (Arles 314). Furthermore, the tradition to which the Donatists want to adhere is not that old, rather it is recent (compl. note 7). That they invoke the authority of San Cipriano, very well; but let them first imitate the love of unity that the Saint demonstrated so many times (S. C1rr., Ep. 73,26,1s; S. Ac., De b. IV 11; V 22; VI 10; C. Gaud. 11 8; C. Cr. 11 42-48; 111 2; De un. b. 25). That in support of their elitism, and their theses of the holy and irreproachable Church, they affirm that Saint Cyprian remained pure, intact (n. compl. 8), agree; but that they also add that by preferring to maintain unity and not separate themselves from sinners and reconcile apostates, they deny with their sovereign authority the fundamental theses of the Donatist schism (De b. 18; MI 3; V 1; C. Cr. TI 41). It is to be admired with what skill Augustine withdraws the benefit of tradition from his adversaries and takes advantage of the arguments of Cyprian himself to reinforce his anti-Donatist doctrine and conclude that that of Arles in 314 is the authentically traditional doctrine.
