[101 Arles and the rebaptization.—Expressly summoned by Constantine, on August 1, 314, a good number of bishops met in Arles under the presidency of Chrestus of Syracuse to examine the Donatist question. Also present were Caecilian of Carthage and his accusers, who, despite everything, failed to prove their accusations. Arles confirmed and fully endorsed the sentence of the Council of Rome of 313 (DPAC II 3023). Cecilian's innocence, then, was once again recognized, and his accusers were either condemned or exiled (PAC 1,170). Regarding the baptism of heretics, he preferred the Roman tradition of Stephen (c.9) and not the African one, defended by Saint Cyprian and continued by the Donatists (LANGA, 743.7315.751s; compl. nm. 9), against whom he declared equally valid the ordinations conferred by traditors (c.14). Due to the range of topics, Arles offers a wonderful overview of the pastoral and disciplinary problems of the Church as a result of the Constantinian peace. Many of its resolutions were collected in 325 by Nicaea (Munter, 3655). On the other hand, it does not seem that African law later included it in the number of its authorities. Optatus does not even mention it to evoke the acquittal judgment of Caecilian, and Augustine refers to it, apparently for the first time, in Ep. 43, dated by Goldbacher between 396-397; In any case, he never claims to have had knowledge of it from the texts (CRESPIN, 24, n.3, citing BATIFFOL: PAC 1,170, n.55, doing the same with L. DE TILLEMONT).

Although Augustine does not consider it a plenary council (ERNST, 288ff), in the Donatist quarrel it occupies a prominent place. Of great interest also for the primacy of the bishop of Rome. These are no longer the times of Pope Victor trying to impose his will on the entire world. Miltiades had made the best possible use of it in Rome the previous year, even though the pacifying measures correspond to the emperor, who is the one who decides to hold this council, summons the bishops and provides them with the means for the meeting (Euskemio, HE X 5,21-24; LAMIRANDE, 732s). Arles continues an issue settled in Rome the previous year. Here we would be faced with the recourse of one council to another in disciplinary matters, although the emperor, arbitrating ecclesiastical issues, sets a precedent of notable consequences. In fact, Arles communicates to Pope Sylvester the result of his deliberations in a respectful letter.

Supplementary Notes 861 in which his absence is deplored and his authority is recognized in terms that amount at least to an implicit supremacy over the entire East. Rome will stop intervening for decades in the great affairs of Christianity, and this must have a significant impact on the Donatist, since the intervention of the emperors, sometimes creating confusing situations, will favor, despite severe measures, the development of the Schism (LAMIRANDE, 733),

The Donatists, not satisfied with the sentence of the Council of Rome, appealed the case to the emperor, to whom they wished to inform in person about what, in short, had already been reported by the vicar of Africa, Elaphius (PAC 1,43). They accused Pope Miltiades of partiality and presented two complaints in particular: 1.*, Gallic judges had been requested and there were only three against seven Italian bishops; 2.*, the council had not studied the case of Félix de Aptonga (n. compl. 67). Ignorant of the rules of the Church, Constantine committed the imprudence of giving in to Donatus's demands, as he ordered proceedings against Felix, which were completed in Carthage on February 15, 314 with a ruling by the proconsul Aelianus (PAC 1,44), who proclaimed his innocence. The process had made clear the bad faith of the Donatists in resorting to falsehoods.

This council denounces in canon 8 the old African custom of rebaptizing, but with the following precision: if the convert has already been baptized in Patre et Filio et Spiritu Sancto, let him be content with having the hand imposed on him ut accipiat Spiritum Sanctum; If he cannot prove that he is baptized with a baptism received in the Trinitarian faith, baptize him (CRESPIN, 31, n.6; TURNER, 3875). Neither the holiness nor the quality of the minister, therefore, intervenes in this judgment on the value of baptism. Canon 13 explicitly contemplates the case of apostate clerics during the persecution of Diocletian: traditors of Scripture, sacred vessels and other religious utensils. Once their guilt has been proven by official documents (public record), they must be deposed (ab ordine cleri amoucatur). Regarding ordinations conferred by guilty bishops, do not question whether the ordained subjects have remained faithful. There is, however, an important distinction here: traditio renders clerics guilty and subject to destitution, but they do not lose pso facto all sacramental power, so that the sacraments conferred by them before being judged remain valid (CrEsPIN, 315). If they have truly apostatized, exclude them from the clergy. In this, Arles and Nicaea follow Saint Cyprian (CRESPIN, 48).

A new appeal was filed by Donatus, Constantine admitted it to processing and decided to personally examine the matter, which he did - "when leisure permitted" - in November 316. The sentence was notified on the 10th of the same month to the vicar of Africa, Eumalio (PAC 1,366), it declared, once again, the evident innocence of Caecilian while at the same time censuring the hypocrisy of his adversaries. Not even because of these did the Schism give way, and as time went on—Parmeniano himself (C. Ep. Par. 16,11)—even accused Constantine himself of partiality, according to them influenced in this regard by Hosius of Córdoba (Concar, 7265; compl. n. 4).

[11] The rebellion of Gildon.—The Moorish prince Gildon, son of Nubel, powerful tribal chief of the Kabyles of Mauritania Caesarian, brother of Firmus, who revolted in 372 against the Roman authorities, and of Mascezel (PAC 1,785,457,712), served with honor to the Romans, which is why in 386 he was rewarded with the appointment of comes et magister utriusque militiae per Africam (CYh 1X 7.9). Later disillusioned with Theodosius 1 - who sent him aid during his revolt against Eugene (392-394) - he became a supporter of the Donatists and became close friends with Optatus, schismatic bishop of Tamugadi, therefore also called Optatus Gildoniense (C. Ep. Parm. 11 4,8; 15,14; C. litt. Pet. 11 92,209; Finally revolting against Honorius at the beginning of the autumn of 397, he was declared a public enemy (bostis publicus) by the Senate of Rome at the end of that season. During the winter there is a great movement of ships and troops. The war begins to turn against Gildon at the beginning of 398. Gildon escapes on a ship. A storm forces him to land in Tabraca (Thabraca), today Tabarka of Tunisia, where he is taken prisoner by the army led by his brother Mascezel, whose son had been murdered by Gildon. On July 31, 398, he died by strangulation: Strangulatus interiit (OrosI0o, Adu. Pagan. 7,36,11: CSEL 5,535). His friend Optatus Gildoniense, or Gildonian, was executed with him (DPAC 11 1515).

His supporters (satellites) continued after his death to be subject to repressive measures (CTh VII 8,7; IX 40,10; 42,19). During the ten years of his power, Gildon had caused great bitterness among the Catholics: totius Africae gemitus (S. Ac., Ep. 87,4s) thereby favoring, like Firmus, the Donatists, which, from Augustine, earned those of the Schism the adjective of Gildonis satellites (C. Ep. Parm. II 4,8; C. litt. Pet. YI 92,209; 11 101; C. Cr. TI 13,16), whose most genuine prototype was, precisely, Optato of Tamugadi, also him

Supplementary notes 863 Gildonian or Gildonian (C. Ep. Parm. 11 15,34). Gildon owned so many large properties in North Africa that upon his fall a special commissioner was appointed to intervene. Despite the above, his family maintained ties with the Roman aristocracy. Salvina, his daughter, for example, married Nebridius, grandson of the empress Flacilla (S. JeroN., Ep. 123,17; DPAC I 1381). Had the ambitions of this powerful and unscrupulous indigenous tribal leader been realized, "they could have had far-reaching consequences for the fortunes of Donatism and Catholicism in North Africa" ​​(FrewD, 1515). The poet Claudius Claudianus celebrated the victory of Honorius' troops in his De bello gildonico. Before gaining the limits of the Proconsular with his troops to fight his brother Gildon there, General Mascezel passed through Capraria, today Capraia, an island in the Tuscan archipelago, where he recruited monks to follow him on the way to Africa (Orosto, Adu. Pagan. 7,36,5: GSEL 5,534). One of them died on African soil. C. did not respond (S. Ac., Ep. 51,1-5).

Under the form of an emphyteutic lease, and in exchange for a large sum of money, C. took over at the end of 401 the estate of the Mapalians (fumdus Mappalians), which belonged to the emperor and fell in Hiponian territory (C. litt, Pet. 11 83,184; 1l 99,228; Ep. 66; J.-L. Marer=PERLER, 227, n.5). This type of lease granted the signatory a possession for an unlimited period, with the power to bequeath and sell the property, marking the rights of the owner (in this case, the emperor) for a rent (LereLLEY, 11 123). To begin with, C. forced the Catholic settlers of the estate with his family to be baptized: about eighty people. This case contains several significant data: for example, the power of the owner over his domain, even in the hypothetical case that he was nothing more than a simple emphyteutic possessor of an imperial domain; also, that the administration of the res priuata was only concerned with the rent, leaving the tenant to act at his leisure, even if it was against imperial law, as in this case; also shows
864 Additional notes in this case, in short, the importance of large imperial and private properties in Africa (LePELLEY, 11 124).

Augustine of Hippo protested vigorously (Ep. 66): he knew that he could have C. sentenced to a fine of ten pounds of gold, according to the law of June 15, 392 (CTh XVI 5,21; compl. n. 37). He preferred, however, to place C. in the face of his responsibilities before God, suette that if it was demonstrated that the colonists had chosen him that way, then well; but that there would be a confrontation on the farm, before the Mapalienses themselves so that they could demonstrate it, and that there would be an interpreter so that those people, who only knew Punic, could express themselves in a way that could be understood. C. didn't do anything this time either.

In accordance with the resolutions of the Council of Carthage on August 25, 403, and through a magistrate (apud acta), Possidius invited C. to a colloquium (C. Cr. III 45,49; MarEr, 41). C. responded first that he had to consult his colleagues. Then, to a second invitation, his response (apud acta) was negative, adding some considerations that provoked general laughter and sneering (C. Cr. III 46,50). Deeply wounded, he soon took revenge: a priest named Crispin, like him, a relative of his, gathered a few armed men and ambushed Possidius one day when he was due to visit his Figuli estate. Possidius had to take refuge in the Oliuetensis estate, where he was persecuted, abused and mistreated, barely escaping death (C. Cr. TIT 46,50; Ep. 105,4; Postplo, VA 12). As a result of the incident, Posidio sued C. before the authorities of Calama, to punish his priest as contemplated by ecclesiastical discipline. In this case, too, C. did not want to do anything; On the contrary, he rather encouraged his faithful to make life impossible for the Catholic bishop. Thus, Possidius demanded a full-fledged process against C. in accordance with the provisions of the antiheretical law of June 15, 392 (CTh XVI 5,21; compl. n. 37).

C. denied being a heretic before the proconsul, and urged the Catholics to prove otherwise. The matter was not with the defender ecclesiae, a layman, but with the bishop (A. C. DE VEER, citing HARTMANN: BA 31, p.818). C. was cornered in the often rejected debate on the problems of a schism in the Church. The Bishop of Hippo, who always supported Possidius, wanted him to convince his adversary of heresy, although he would later be forgiven as to the penalty. Possidius succeeded after a third attempt (Posipio, VA 12; S. Ac., C. Cr. 111 47,51). Sentenced to the well-known fine of ten pounds of gold, C. escaped it thanks to the intervention of his Catholic adversary (Ep. 88,7; 108,2,4). He was uninspired when he appealed the sentence against the opinion of even his own colleagues. The truth is that he appealed to the emperor and was condemned again to the famous fine, which he did not pay this time either thanks to the intervention of the Catholic bishops, mainly Augustine (Posibius, VA 12,9; CTh XVI 5,39; XVI 6,4; C. Cr. III 47,51). The objective of Possidius, inspired in this case by his friend Augustine, was not so much to defeat a personal adversary as, rather, to obtain that the Donatists were, before the law, officially recognized as heretics (A. C. DE VEER, 819). Already of advanced age when he was the protagonist of the episode of 403/404, C. died shortly before the Carthage Conference of 411: "Crispinus proximo tempore exiuit de corpore" (Gesta 1 139, SCh 195, p.788). Of the four letters from Augustine to C., which Posidius mentions, only two have reached us (PAC 1,253; Mater, 284; A. C. DE Ver, 817).—BIBL.: J.-L. MalrEr,

[13] The Catholic bishop Maximian of Bagái.—Of Maximian, Catholic bishop of Bagái, we only know with certainty the circumcelionic outrages of which he was a victim and his immediate trip to inform Honorius of what had happened (C. Cr. 111 43,47; Ep. 88,7: documents contemporary to the incident, which occurred in 404). Agustín returns to the character in 417 without providing new information (Ep. 185,7,26s). The news consecrated to Maximian on October 3 is based on it (Acta Sanctorum, Oct., II, p.160s). We also have evidence of a Maximian of Bagái, or of Vega, who in 402 wrote to the council of Milevi to notify his intention to resign from the episcopal office for the good of his community, a resignation accepted by the council, which invited its faithful to provide themselves with a bishop. The Ep. 69, common to Augustine and Alypius, details that he had converted from the schism with his brother Castorius (PAC 1,1975), but not whether he was already a bishop when he converted or was so later. Occasion of a scandal among Catholics (Ep. 69,1), it does not seem to be related to his conversion; At least, the faithful appreciated his brother Castorio, also converted. It is unknown, in short, if that occasion of scandal ended. It is true that no Castorius is mentioned as a Catholic bishop in the documents of the time, which prevents taking sides when it comes to identifying or not this Maximian of Bagai, or Vega, with Maximian of Bagai in Numidia, today Ksar Baghai of Algeria. When the Bishop of Hippo refers to the circumcelionic mistreatment of which Maximian of Bagái was a victim, he does not adduce as the main or secondary cause of the same his conversion of the D., but only the having judicially obtained the restitution of the basilica of the Calvian estate, occupied by the Donatists (C. Cr. 111 43,47; Ep. 185,7,27). Can the identification of both characters be deduced from Augustinian silence? There are authors who think this way. Others, like R. Crespin, prefer to distinguish them (CrEsPIN, 65, n.4). After explaining both possibilities with their respective bibliography, A. C. de Veer concludes by stating that the distinction of the two Maximians and their sees would be viable if it were possible to prove that Maximian Bagaiensis and Vaginensis really resigned their position in 402, "mais il ne me semble pas possible de le prouver" (p.816).

Maximian of Bagai was in a rural basilica in the fundus Caluianensis when the Donatists broke in: attacked and severely beaten and wounded with a dagger on the altar, he would have surely bled to death if his executioners had not dragged him on the ground: the earth thus covered the wound and the bleeding stopped. Finally taken to a tower, he was thrown from it into the void, but chance wanted him to fall precisely on a dunghill. A night passerby noticed that strange figure and called his wife, and with the help of a flashlight they recognized the poor bishop, who, unconscious, was still breathing. Like good Samaritans, they were in charge of transporting him and healing him. Against all hope, and when the news of his death had begun to spread, Maximian escaped from danger. As soon as he regained the necessary strength, he left for Italy to ask the emperor for protection (C. Cr. TIL 43,47; Ep. 185,7,278).

The news of the events shocked public opinion inside and outside Africa and unleashed indignation against the Donatists. When he arrived in Italy, where there were already other African bishops, Servant of God
866 Additional notes

(Servus Dei or Seruusdei), for example, also victims of the circumcelions, the spectacle of their wounds intensified the widespread anti-schismatic indignation. Servant of God, he was bishop of Thubursicu Bure, in the Proconsular, today Teboursouk of Tunisia, and he had also been seriously insulted by the Donatists. In Italy and in 404, Maximian and Servant of God found other bishops victims of the salvationism of the schismatics. There was a widespread belief among them that they would never be able to return to their African homeland. However, Servant of God appears in the Carthage Conference of 411, where, curiously, he appears without complaining about the mistreatment received some years ago (C. Cr. TI 43,47; LanceL, 17, n.3).

Before Theasius and Evodius arrived, commissioned by the Council of Carthage on June 16, 404, to ask Honorius to apply the Theodosian legislation against heretics, the aforementioned circumstances were already working in their favor. The insecurity created in Africa, which prevented Maximian and his colleagues from returning to their respective headquarters, or in any case from carrying out their duties with tranquility, as well as the request raised by Maximian to the emperor, "not so much for revenge as for the defense of the Church entrusted to him", contributed to the resolution by Honorius taken on February 12, 405, that is, to the famous edict of union with which he imposed sanctions that went beyond the limit of conciliar demands (no. compl. 43). According to the Roman Martyrology, it seems that Maximian of Bagai did not survive his wounds for long (PAC 1,725).—BrBL.: R. CrESPIN, Ministere et sainteté, 65.72s; S. [14] Saint Augustine and the IX Council of Carthage.—There is no unanimity regarding the date of this council. On the common basis of the month of June 404, some go for June 6, others for the 16th and there are also those for the 26th, depending on whether one reads the instructions given to the synodal mission sent to the emperor (Codex Canonum ecclesiae africane, Can. 93: MANSt, 3,794-798) or whether one refers to Ep. 88.7 of Saint Augustine (LancEL, 18; CRESPIN, 70s; MUNIER, 607; MAIER, 41; MANDOUZE, S. A. L'aventure, 369, n.3; PAC 1,1319.369). It took place in the basilica of the second region of Carthage: «Carthagine in basilica regionis secundac» (MANSt, 3,794; J.-L. Marer=PErtER, 251, n.2). He confirmed the failure of the policy of religious pacification and considered the measures to be taken against the intensified violence of the Donatists (A. C. DE VrER, 809). Unanimity of its participants that only civil power could effectively remedy the situation; discrepancy in the measures to be taken.

The oldest councilors – the majority – wanted an outlaw pure and simple; an edict of union that would impose on the Donatists their forced return to unity. The minority, inspired by the Bishop of Hippo (Epp. 93,17; 185,25), believed that it was not necessary to go that far: it was enough to request protection by resorting to the Theodosian legislation of June 15, 392 (n. compl. 37), applying it against those who disturbed public order, but without disturbing others. No one would be forced, in this way, to be Catholic, and Catholics, on the other hand, could practice their religion in peace, also avoiding the risk of malingerers: "My first sentence was that no one should be forced

Supplementary Notes 867 to accept the unity of Christ; that we had to act by word of mouth, fight in the dispute, triumph with reason so as not to turn those we knew as declared heretics into feigned Catholics” (Ep. 93,5,17: BAC 69/VIIT?, p.560). The persuasive weapons of gentleness and reason seemed the best to the minority group of the council led by Augustine. There was no reason to give up on them. It was only necessary, however, to ensure the indispensable conditions for peace. This moderate sentence is the one that prevailed. It was requested that the penalties imposed against heretics who were stubborn in continuing ordaining be applied again, restricting above all their power to make a will. The suggestions that the Donatists be spared all physical punishment had their most important supporter in Augustine of Hippo (Ep. 185,7,29; MUNIER, 607).

Theasío and Evodio (PAC 1,1105.369) were in charge of the council to introduce and maintain the claim before the court. According to the commonitorium that was sent to them, they had to describe the climate of insecurity created with the circumcelions and request the return of the antiheretical legislation of Theodosius, and specifically against the Donatists the fine of ten pounds of gold imposed on the authors of violence of a similar nature (Epp. 88,7; 185,7). Upon their arrival in Rome they found that their mission was already accomplished: impressed by the testimonies of Maximian of Bagai, Servant of God and other bishops who were victims of Circumcelionic-Donatist savagery, Honorius had decreed on February 12, 405, sanctions that went even further than the points demanded by the council, and which Augustine summarizes thus in C. Cr. 111 43,47: «ita factum est, ut et praeteritae omnes contra uos leges excitarentur et istae conderentur nouae» (CSEL 52, p.455; compl. n. 13).—BiBL.: R. CRESPIN, Ministere et sainteté, 70s; S. LANCEL, Actes de la Conférence, 18; J.-L. Mater, L'épiscopat de l'Afrique romaine, 41; J.-L. Marer=PERLER, Les voyages...(Paris 1969) 250-252; A. MANDOUZE, S. A. L'aventure...369; Ch. MuntEr, Cartagine. V, Council: DPAC 1 607; A. C. DE See, 35. Les violences des circoncellions d'apres le temoignage de saint Augustin: BA 31, p.809s; Ip., 36. L'état de la législation antidonatiste dans le «Contra Cresconium», p.810-814; Tb., p.366s.

[15] The "Mandatum" of the Catholics.—On May 30, 411, the eve of the solemn opening of the Conference of Carthage, the Catholic part carried out the last of the so-called preliminary acts: drafting a manifesto—titled Mandatum—to which they attached, in a separate annex, the signatures of the full episcopate stamped in the presence of the imperial commissioner Marcellinus (Gesta 1 55). It is an important document, since the Catholics advance in it to the Donatists the bases of dialogue that allow reaching an understanding within the Conference. It is also a very complex memorandum, based entirely on a catalog of scriptural testimonies (testimonia) whose selection of quotes, for the purposes of enriching perspective, must be compared with that presented by the Donatists contributed during the third session (Gesta 1 55; 111 258; Mandatum, 2-3: PL 43,822-824). With this document, the Catholics intended, on the one hand, to speak clearly to the faithful a few hours before the great debate, and on the other, to convey to the hierarchy of the Schism the rules of the game, so to speak, "ad gerendam huíus causae defensionem" (Mandatum, 1, col. 822); «... ad disputandum episcopis catholicae ecclesiae est inuncta defensio aduersus criminationibus Donatistarum. hoc manda iterum, sicut in superioribus litteris breuiter tota causa comprehensa est” (Brew. 1 10: CSEL 53, p.43).
Its content is simple and fundamental: we must distinguish well the
868 Additional notes

causa Ecclesiae of the Caeciliani cause (compl. n. 65), something of utmost importance both from the historical point of view and from the doctrinal and specifically ecclesiological point of view. From the first, because the Catholic bishops went ahead to respond in advance to the presumed maneuvers of their adversaries: both causes were called to be debated through their own documents and according to a particular method; practical reason, therefore, that forced the distinction to avoid unfortunately confusing these causes. From the second, due to the so Augustinian and so repeated desire not to mix ecclesiological argumentation with historical controversy and to grant priority, whenever possible, to the ecclesiological argument (Ep. ad Cath. VII 5-6; Gesta 11I 155.101.197). The Bishop of Hippo's recourse to the divine Word was very frequent (C. litt. Pet, 11 85,189; C. Cr. 111 67,77). In addition to the most solid ground, Scripture was common to both parties, which explains why the Saint intended from the beginning to center all possible dialogue on the divine Word (Epp. 23,6; 33,5). There was in the Mandatum, along with the scriptural reason, others of a historical nature, especially in order to make it clear once and for all that the cases of Felix and Cecilian had been ruled since ancient times in favor of the Catholics (Gesta 1 55; 111 227-231; LanceL, 485.232; LAMIRANDE, 1025). The Mandatum reveals, in short, the clarity of attitudes that reigned in the Catholic Church on the eve of the Conference. The irresolution and disorder of the Donatist episcopate contrasts, by the way, with the "solid preparation" of the friends of Aurelius and Augustine in the hours immediately preceding the holding of an in-depth debate (LancEL, 50). The Catholics feared that those of the Schism, faced with the doctrinal solidity of their adversaries, would dedicate themselves to entanglement and dark maneuvering, as in fact happened. The spirit of the Mandatum is completely Augustinian.—BIBL.: E. LamIRANDE, Augustine and the Discussion...11. The Mandate if the Catholic Council, 101-106; Ib., L'offre conciliatrice des Catholiques aux Donatistes relativement á Vépiscopat (Gesta collationis cartbaginiensis, 1, 16): Église et Théologie 2 (1971) 285-308=A. C. DE VeEr: REAug 18 (1972) 321-323; S. LANcEL, Actes de la Conférence, 45-50.

[16] Saint Augustine and the tragic end of Count Marcellinus.—The summer of 413 caused great bitterness to the Bishop of Hippo. As a result of the Heraclian uprising, Count Marinus unleashed an apparently arbitrary and strong repression in Africa that affected the brothers Apringius and Marcellinus, the latter a great friend of Augustine (PAC 1,5525.704). The true cause of the unjust accusation that ended the lives of these brothers is unknown. Public rumor then spoke of the envy of Marinus (Oros1o, Adu. Pagan. 7,42,17), the animosity of some colleagues (S. Ac., Ep. 151,4) and the hatred of the schismatics against the former president of the Conference of Carthage (Ep. 151,10). Saint Jerome accuses the heretics, read Pelagians (Dial. adu. Pelag. 3,19), and Orosius also mentions the gold of the Donatists (Adu. Pagan. 7,42,47). We know what happened thanks to Ep. 151 of Saint Augustine.

The Catholic side, especially Augustine, moved feverishly to save the two brothers. In his captivity, Marcellin demonstrated great firmness of mind, willing to accept evils, including death, in forgiveness of his sins on the day of judgment (Ep. 151,9). During one of those visits that Augustine made to his friend, he declared to him in prison that throughout his life he had always respected marital fidelity (ibid.). Marino promised the Catholic hierarchy not to act until the delegate bishop returned with the emperor's response, but he did not.

Supplementary Notes 869 fulfilled the promise (Ep. 151,5). When the order came, not only to forgive those imprisoned, but to give them complete freedom, Count Marino, gratis igitur crudelitate nulla necessitate (Ep. 151,11: CSEL 44, p.491) had summoned the two brothers, had listened to them again and had ordered them executed on Friday the 12th or, more probably, on Saturday the 13th of September, the eve of the feast of Saint Cyprian. (J.-L. Marer=PerLer, 321, n.10; PAC 1,687).

It was a terrible blow for Agustín's bosom friend. Fraternal friendship had reigned between Marcellin and him, as confirmed by the letters exchanged (MOREAU, 3ff), the Retractationes and the treatises dedicated by Augustine to Marcellin, namely: De peccatorum meritis et remissione et de baptismo paruulorum; De spiritu et littera, and the first books of the City of God (De pecc. mer. 11,1; De spir. et litt. 1,1; De ciu. Dei 5, praef.; Ep. 143,2). Deeply afflicted by that tragic end of his friend, offended by such an unjust sentence, disgusted by Marinus' clumsiness, the Saint could not stand it any longer in Carthage. The day after the bloody event, he left for Hippo with the firm intention of never setting foot in the town that had served as a theater for such a horrible crime (Ep. 151,3.12; J.-L. Marer=PeErLEr, 323). The arrest of Marcellinus, apparently, deeply divided the diocese of Carthage, of which certain eminent members, perhaps out of opportunism, who knows if in good faith to save what could be saved - even if it was with the death of both brothers -, tried to gain the sympathies of the perfidious imperial commissioner. They even pressured Aurelio himself to humiliate himself in front of that man. For the Bishop of Hippo it was too much; He could not bear the spectacle of that Church (Ep. 151,3).

Augustine paid warm tribute to Marcellin, "in whom the Church has been mainly persecuted" (Ep. 151.4: BA 99a/Xla?, 150; cf. Ep. 151,85), evoking with as much admiration as emotion the memory of this Catholic immersed in the very heart of the most worrying African religious issues of the moment, of profound spiritual convictions translated into an edifying moral life (Ep. 151.8). Informed of what had happened, Honorius did not hesitate to dismiss Marinus, who, despite the services provided in the fight against the Heraclian uprising, ended his days in total darkness (Orosius, Adu. Pagan. 7,42,17). An imperial edict of August 30, 414 ordered that Marcellin's anti-Donatist policy be maintained and continued throughout, spectabilis memoriae uirum (CTh XVI 5,55, ed. Mommsen, 1-2,874; S. Ac., De nat. el grat. 23,25; De gest. Pelag. 11,25). The Roman Church, for its part, inscribed in its martyrology, dated April 6, the name of the executed: "Carthagine sancti Marcellini martyris qui ob catholicae fidei defensionem ab haereticis occisus est" (DELEHAYE, 127), a formula with Hieromonian resonances: "qui postea sub inuidia tyrannidis Heracliani ab haereticis innocens caesus est» (Dial. adu. Pelag. 3,19: PL 23,588s). And Saint Augustine writes “ad sanctae memoriae Marcellinum” (De nat. et grat. 23,25: CSEL 60, p.252).—BrBL.: H. DeLrmaYE, Martyrologium Romanum (Bruxelles 1940) 127; G. Lanocs1, Marcellino Flavio: DPAC 11 2087s; E, LAMIRANDE: BA 32, p.48-54; J.-L. Marer=PERLER, Les voyages...(Paris 1969) 320-324; M. Morkau, Le dossier Marcellinus dans la correspondence de s. Aug.: REAug 9 (1973) 3-181.
[17] "Compelle intrare" or theory of coercion in Saint Augustine.— It is one of those classic arguments in which the Bishop of Hippo changes over the years. His pastoral life was presided over by a
870 Additional notes

enviable balance, which, in this circumstance, is configured by these two texts: 1. «... if you have received the power to judge, if they accuse him before you and he is convicted of sin through true evidence and vestiges, punish him (coerce), correct him, excommunicate him, degrade him, in accordance with ecclesiastical norm» (Ser. 164,11: BAC 443/XXIHL 606); 2.2 «We are lazy to excommunicate, to separate from the Church. We also frequently fear that the punishment will worsen the one who has fallen" (Serm. 17,3: BAC 53/VI1l 286). With its compelle intrare, the Middle Ages will insist more on the energy of the former than on the pastoral concerns of the latter (BORGOMEO, 372; MAISONNEUVE, 49ff). To correctly interpret Saint Augustine, it is necessary to resort to this sense of balance, as, for example, Borgomea (372, n.96) and Mandouze (387. 337, n.4) do compared to Courtois.

As a priest, and in his first episcopal years, Augustine flatly rejected the use of force in religious matters. Then, in a short space of time, he begins to accept and defend it (MONACHINO, 89ff; P. pE Lurs, 8315). Thus he writes regarding the Contra partem Donati books, published around 397 and lost: «In the first of them I have written that I do not like that schismatics are forced to enter into communion by any kind of violence coming from the force of secular power. It is true that I did not like them then, because I had not yet experienced the evil that their impunity caused or how much timely correction could serve in order to change them for the better" (Retract. 11 31 [5]). He maintains this position in the IX Council of Carthage, in 404 (compl. no. 14). On the other hand, he already accepts the edict of union of February 12, 405, which imposes the union with quite severe penalties (n. compl, 14), In his Ep. 93,5,17-19, Saint Augustine explains the causes of change.

Naturally, not only his brothers influence the episcopate, convinced that they must accept the help of the secular arm, and the intensified violence unleashed by the circumcelions even in Tagaste, their hometown. There are also the conversions of people to the Catholic Church, before the intervention of the constituted imperial force, subjugated and under the pressure of circumcelionic terror. The Saint turns to Scripture to support his new theory, mostly Lk 14:23: "force them to enter" (compelle intrare-cogite intrare); «Go out into the paths and hedges and force everyone to come in – compelle intrare – so that my house is full. Notice that of the first who arrived it is said: Bring them here, and it is not said: Force them to enter—compelle—» (Ep. 173,10: BAC 99a/XTa, 380); «And then he replies: Go out into the paths and hedges, and force those you find to enter – cogite imtrare –. He brought the first ones gently, and thus obedience was completed; but he forced the latter, and thus repressed their disobedience: ¿n istis autem qui coguntur, inoboedientia coercetur» (Ep. 185,6,24: BAC 99a/Xla, 471; MANDOUZE, 384, n.3; 387).

Compelle intrare, the Middle Ages repeated. Cogite intrare, he had read Augustine in the African version of the Bible, which presents, in relation to the Vulgate, certain literary variants (n. compl. 5). It is necessary to note that this Augustinian version seems to be ignored by some modern authors, who, however, and as if they had had first-hand knowledge, do not hesitate to assign to Saint Augustine the responsibility of the doctrine of the medieval compelle intrare (cf., for example, A. JULIEN, 227; and more cases reported by MAISONNEUVE, 381ff; cf. more authors in MANDOUZE, 383, n.4; 385, n.4).
Additional notes 871

Despite appearances to the contrary, the change is not abrupt. Supported by Pauline theology (Rom 13,1-4), he detects in power a minister or instrument of God to repress evil (C. Ep. Parm. 18,13ff). And in imperial legislation, an aid at the service of justice and truth, so that, although these laws do not achieve good for anyone, they can at least prevent evil from being done. The Augustinian anti-Manichean struggle, which puts him in contact with the Old Testament, which he has to defend, and specifically his pedagogy of fear, provides great services on this issue (Brown [Torino 1972] 245-263). Finally, it is necessary to specify: 1.2, that Augustine devised this theory for that specific case, in no way for an indiscriminate and universal application, as the compelle intrare medievalists have later insisted on making us believe; 2, that said theory should not be dissociated from its way of acting in each case (Apringio-Matcelino-Crispin, etc.); 3.", that the same dry and hard theologian of the cogite-compelle intrare is the shepherd of souls, defender of his diocesans, threatened with death by the club of the circumcelions, as Mandouze rightly writes, "the same defender of the Truth threatened by an erroneous ecclesiology in which theoretical Puritanism is radically invalidated by the deeds and gestures of the Donatists" (361-364; 3845); and 4., who, as an apostle of Africa, also feels responsible for schismatics and Catholics and wants by all means to rescue them from eternal death, trying to combine the two attitudes represented in the previous texts with the healthy balance to which he always aspired.—BiBL.: 'T. van BAvEL, Répertoire bibliograpbique de saint Augustin 1950-1960 (La Haye-Steenbrugge) 1963) 703705; P. [18] Saint Augustine and his concept of martyrdom against the Donatists. —The concept of martyrdom is key to understanding the Donatists, who always boasted of being the Church of martyrs, persecuted by traditors (MONCEAUX, IV 464ff; V 35ff; VóLtTER, 5-10). They began by taking over the martyrs of Abitina, tortured in Carthage on February 12, 304 (DPAC 19); They then denounced in Caecilian the executioner of the confessors of the faith and the enemy of the cult of relics, thereby confronting Lucilla and thus provoking a hardening of positions (OpTaTo, 1 16; S. Ac., Ep. 439,25; C. Ep. Parm. 13,5; C. Cr. III 28,32; PAC 1,649; DPAC II 2135-2140); His council of 312 accused Catholics of weakness in the face of persecutors and, on the other hand, of severity, if not cruelty, towards confessors who resisted the test. Their resort to violence, such as the battles of 317 to maintain their basilicas or confront imperial repression, often became a weapon used against Catholics; thus, the cases of Bishop Donatus, killed in Bagái in the course of a revolt, and of Marculo (MONcEAUxX, IV 27.35-37, V 38-40; PAC 1,6965), and not to mention those caused by Macarius, whose black memory the Donatists remembered to the Catholics as an insult when speaking of Macariana tempora, or of Macariana persecutio, and also pars Macarii, as opposed to pars Donati that Catholics foist on them; or, finally, Macariani, without forgetting Macariana Ecclesia (MoNcEaAUux, IV 375; PAC 1,655-658; BA 32,719). Of course, those responsible for such persecutions were, for their denigrating hatred, the Catholics (C. litt. Pet. 1 18,20; TI 64,143; 92,202; TII 25,29; C. Cr. 1V 15,17; G. c. Em. 3,9; C. Gand. 1 12,12; 16,17; 19,20). Such persecutions were a sin as great as that of traditio (C. litt. Pet. 11 42,139; LAMIRANDE, 7195). Fanatics of circumcelionic sectarianism, they considered even suicides martyrdom. The Donatists believed they would secure unparalleled martyrdom glory by paying executioners to be executed, rushing down ravines, throwing themselves into the void, into water or into fire (C. litt, Pet. YI 20,46; De haer. 69; Ep. 185,4,15; C. Gaud. 1 22,25; 31,36-39; C. Cr. TI 49,54; The bodies of martyrs proliferated so much in Africa that it was sometimes difficult to distinguish a Catholic from a Donatist. To define the question of their alleged martyrs, the schismatics held provincial councils. Recent archaeological and epigraphic discoveries have revealed numerous martyrdom inscriptions with Punic or Libyan names that are not cited by Augustine, the martyrology, or the Carthage calendar. His martyr literature is composed of sermons, letters and tracts classifiable into common martyrs (before 312) and own martyrs, with long lists of those who fell in the repression of Macarius (347), when the edict of union of 405 and the various fights between circumcelions and agents of imperial authority (R. PosE, 1027).

Contrary to the profusion of honorific titles and the concept that the Donatists had of their martyrdom, full of confusion and fanaticism, Augustine specified that the punishment of authority is not enough to be a martyr for the truth: that the Donatists must first prove that their heroes have not been condemned for the crime of heresy or schism, because, otherwise, all the heretics that authority has mistreated, even the pagans and demons, would have to be called martyrs. whose idols have been burned. A true martyr is he who suffers persecution for justice or because of the true faith, of which precisely the Donatists are enemies. Saint Cyprian had already denied those separated from the unit the honorable title of martyrs, alleging that the death of a schismatic, rather than the crown of faith, was a deserved penalty for betraying said faith (De lap. 8; De unit. 14,12; 19,17; Epp. 55,17; 59,13; 60,4). In accordance, then, with its principle regarding acts performed outside of ecclesial communion and according to the distinction that in martyrdom must be made between punishment and cause, the Donatist martyrs are nothing other than common law criminals, false martyrs and fools (Ad Donat. p. coll. 17,28; C. Gaud. Í 26,29; LAMIRANDE, 741).

The thesis had been advanced by Optatus (III 8). Augustine perfects it, advocates and applies it fully: "The martyr is not made by the punishment, but by the cause": Christi martyrem non facit poena, sed causa (C. Cr. 111 47,51: CSEL 532, p.459); itaque martyres non facit poena, sed causa (In Ps, 34

Additional notes 873 1 13: CC 38, p.320); tu ostendis poenam, ego quaero causam (Serm. 329,4: PL 38,1453). A martyr, then, is he who dies for a just cause—for Christ, for faith, for justice—not for the simple fact of dying, or suffering, since one can suffer the same for the cause of Christ as for an ignoble cause (P. De Luis, 776; LAMIRANDE, 747). This explains why Augustine accepts, on the one hand, that atrocities have been committed against the Donatists, which he, of course, condemns, and flatly refuses, on the other hand, to grant such victims the title of martyrs. Nor is the argument of quantity acceptable, because if the anti-Donatist imperial repressions were numerous and harsh, the Circumcelionian ferocity was even more so. The Saint distinguishes very well between causa iusta and causa iniusta, as well as between persecutio iusta and iniusta, to always insist, as a determining martyrial element, on the usta causa (Ep. 185,2,11; MANDOUZE, 383, n.3; more texts in CONGAR, 728). He compares the suicidal practices of the Donatists, condemned even by Tyconius himself, to the gesture of Judas: the Donatists preferred any type of suicide except that of the rope, precisely so as not to resemble Judas. There is no shortage of occasions when he has to defend Catholics from false accusations: the Donatists sometimes blamed Catholics for deaths that were later proven to have been genuine suicides. The Christian martyr is made not only by his external victory (foris uincebant), but above all by the struggle waged in the heart (intra se pugnabant; cf. Borcomeo, 132).

That a martyr is made not by the torment, but by the cause, Augustine proves with Calvary, where Christ—he says—was crucified between two thieves. From the point of punishment—being crucified—Christ was in no way distinguished from them (Serm. 331,3), but he was, of course, due to the cause: equally hanged, but not equally debased (Serm. 327,2). The cause gave in the person of Jesus a positive value to the fact, in itself negative, that God suffered the ignominy of the cross. Underlying this Augustinian thesis of cause and punishment is a way of thinking different from the one that prevails among us today, a world dominated by the idea of ​​truth and justice in themselves, not by that of subjective conscience in which Augustine is a master. His is a point of view evidently justified if one tries to analyze with fully theological rigor the title of martyr (ConGar, 728).—BiBL.: P. BorcomEo, L'Église de ce temps, 1318; "Y. Concar, 19. [20] Tyconius and Optatus of Milevi in the doctrine of baptism.— T. advocates universality as a constitutive note of the true Church and denounces the Donatist presumption of incarnating the Church of the perfect, since also in the schismatic community there continue to be good and bad. Baptismal efficacy, furthermore, cannot in any way depend on the moral dignity of the minister (C. Ep. Parm. 111 3,17; Sr MONETTI, 138; Concar, 7185). All of this, which was the very denial of the schismatic system, was maintained by T. in De Bello Intestinal, around 370, the time when Rogato broke with Parmeniano and took with him a good number of colleagues. Vigorously attacked by the party, T. responds in Expositiones diuersarum causaum. In 378, Parmenianus wrote to the great exegete a letter that we know today in some way thanks to the refutation that the Hipponense made of it twenty-two years later (cf. his analysis in Concar, 719). But T. does not allow himself to be convinced and ends up excommunicated by a council that those of his party held in 380. T. does not have the logic of Newman, returned to the universal Church (n. compl. 22), although he does have enough wisdom not to found another sect. Busy in scriptural studies, he published his famous Liber Regularum in 382, ​​and around 385, the translation and commentary on the Apocalypse. He must have died around 390. T. discusses the baptismal theory of his party from the platform of his ecclesiology (compl. no. 24); Methodologically, like Saint Augustine, he affirms that the sacraments of Catholics are valid, as is the baptism of heretics, if it is conferred according to the proper rites; He justifies his thesis with the Bible and from the inconsequential history of his own party, since a schismatic council of 336 had agreed not to rebaptize Catholics; Finally, it establishes the need for the good to tolerate the bad in the Church (S. AG., Ep. 93,10,43s; Monceaux 1V 333ss; Brisson, 218ss; CRESPIN, 153. 232). Saint Augustine had great esteem for this unique character. From him and Gennadius (De uir. ill. 18) come many Ticonian news: for example, that Donatus, in communion with Bishop Deuterius, welcomed traditors without rebaptizing, and that he remained in communion with the bishops of Mauretania, themselves in communion with the non-rebaptized traditors until the intervention of Paul and Macarius in Africa (SIMONETTI, 1378).

As for Optatus, he addresses the baptismal question in book V, and considers that baptism is a gift from God that should not be repeated (17; V 13-11; PAC 1,796; compl. n. 19). Against the Donatist praxis, in accordance with Saint Cyprian, who had also not considered the baptism of heretics to be valid, O. observes that the baptism administered by heretics who alter the profession of faith is not valid, but that between Donatists and Catholics an escclesiastica conuersatio (c.1) and, therefore, valid is the one administered by both. Three elements (species) must be distinguished in baptism: prima in Trinitate, secunda in credente, tertia in operante (the first two are essential); not so the sanctity of the minister: Operarii mutari possunt, sacramenta mutari non possunt (c.4). Making the validity of baptism depend on the holiness of the minister is like admitting that the will of man can hinder the saving will of God, who infuses the baptized with the divine Spirit; Not, of course, the minister. [22] "Securus iudicat orbis terrarum."—This Augustinian phrase (C. Ep. Parm. 111 4,24) is part of the anti-Donatist theological scope of the universal catholicity of the Church. In his reply to Parmeniano, Augustine accentuates the lack of logic of the D. in the sacramental (baptism) and ecclesial (unity) themes and his confrontation with the Catholic (III 4,22-5,28). Are transmarine Christians guilty of what has happened in Africa? Who can assure the Donatists—from their puritan separatism—that before them there were not other groups that broke with sinners, anticipating and forming the Church of the pure? The Schism ignores it. The universe also ignores what has happened in a corner of Africa. And as for its internal schisms? That the Sect has had to put up with sinners from its surroundings so as not to separate itself from the crowd of innocent Donatists? Why, then, not extend this argument for favor to the universe? Do you also know if those who have reported are really bad? For the universe the thing is doubtful ("incertum est orbi terrarum": C. Ep. Parm. 111 4,24; CSEL 51, p.130).
878 Additional notes

What is not, however, is the reckless blindness with which the Donatists have separated themselves from the transmarine Christians, whose life they do not know; nor the meritorious patience with which known sinners are endured so as not to condemn the good unknown. The crescendo tone culminates in the famous phrase: «quapropter securus judicat orbis terrarum bonds non esse, qui se diuidunt ab orbe terrarum in quacumque parte terrarum» (IT 4,24, p.131).

The excommunicated Tyconius did not have the logic to return to Catholicism, but Newman did, many centuries later with this decisive Augustinian phrase, the goal of a patristic itinerary (ConGaAr, 719; compl. n. 25). It was in September 1839, reading the August number of the "Dublin Review", in which Wisseman, already a bishop, signed a work on Anglicanism and the Donatists, when a friend pointed out to him - he clarifies - "some impressive words from Saint Augustine, mentioned in one of the extracts from the magazine, which had escaped my observation: Securus iudicat orbis terrarum. The words gave the article a strength that had suddenly escaped me. They decided ecclesiastical questions by a rule simpler than that of antiquity; What's more, Saint Augustine was one of the oracles of antiquity; here, therefore, antiquity decided against itself” (Newman, 96s). The final judgment of the Church, "pillar and support of the truth", is formed by the general intelligence of the Christian world. Because the securus iudicat supposes, in effect, an orbis terrarum. It was his tolle lege, like the one who had converted Saint Augustine (Newman, 97; NÉDONCELLE, 271; LANGA, 55858).

In Newmanian biography, the securus iudicat overflows the glorious limits of a "supernatural biographical incident" of conversion. Newman returned to the Augustinian phrase many years later, in a more repetitive way, if possible, and with another meaning: sociological and doctrinal in 1839 (the universal Church cannot but be right regarding heretics); ecclesiastical and infallibility in 1870. Newman was convinced that the scriptural interpretation was preserved from corruption during Arianism thanks to the sensus fidelium of the orbis terrarum. Hence, two infallibilities stand out: the active or the hierarchy, and the passive or the faithful. Therefore, the faithful enjoy infallibility because they constitute that orbis terrarum, although to exercise it they always need the regulatory intervention of active infallibility (STERN, 180ff; LAnGa, 560ff).

The Bishop of Hippo continues and completes this demonstration by putting catholicity as a criterion of ecclesiological truth: "Nulla est igitur securitas unitatis nisi ex promissis dei ecclesia declarata, quae super montem ut dictum est constituta abscondi non potest et ideo necesse est omnium terrarum partibusnota sit" (C. Ep. Parm. 1II 5,28, p.136; for a good batch of texts in this same line, cf. Concar: BA 28, p.744, citing some from Batiffol).—BiBL.: Y. GONGAR, 38. «Securus iudicat orbis terrarum»: BA 28, p.743s; P. [231 Augustinian casuistry of extra-Catholic baptismal reception.—The distinction between the sacrament and its grace allows Saint Augustine to recognize sacramental validity in schism and heresy, preserving only the Church of Christ, however, all the truth of the Holy Spirit. A nuance, this one, unnoticed by San Cipriano and the Donatists. Because one thing is what is seen of the sacrament (species) and another is its spiritual reality (uirtus). Having (baptism) is not the same as having (it) fruitfully: habere utilitatem, ad utilitatem and babere salubriter, ad salutem (De agon. chr. 30,32; In lo. 26,11; De b. VI 1,1; Concar, 91). Between the schismatic communities and the Church there exists, therefore, the bond of the sacraments, which demand, due to the demands of their own spiritual fruit, the return of the former to unity. Hence, Saint Augustine denounces the evil of separation and does not see in the sacraments of the dissidents a truly objective internal link with the Church, since outside the unity of charity neither sacrament, nor prayer, nor virtue, not even martyrdom benefit man, since everything that is possessed outside the Church falls outside the unity and charity of the Holy Spirit (De b. 1 14,22; 111 10,13; IV 20,27; V 7,8; C. Chr. 11 28,36; In this he agrees with Saint Cyprian (ConGAR, 727; compl. n. 6). The Donatists had sacraments, but not the unity and charity of the Spirit (Ep. 185,42; Serm. 269,2). For the return of schismatics and heretics to the Church, therefore, Saint Augustine requires only an imposition of hands, which, of course, was neither a penitential rite (which in that case would have separated the priests from the exercise of their functions) nor a sacrament of confirmation (since it was repeatable, and the Bishop of Hippo did not attribute it to the Donatists, in whom he honored, moreover, his sacraments). Rather, it was a rite of the gift of the Holy Spirit convenient to the ecclesial incorporation into peace and charity and unity of those who already had the communio sacramentorum, but not yet the societas sanctorum, that is, the communion of the Church as unity and charity by the Spirit (De b. V 23,33; C. Ep. Parm. 11 13,28; Serm. 269,2; HormaANN, 3365; CONGAR, 925). Membership in the Church can be apparent or real, and only the latter guarantees health. So it may happen that Christians baptized outside the Church are considered baptized within it, while others, apparently baptized within, are considered as if they were baptized outside (De b.

V 39). Unity must be adhered to by the heart, and it happens that it is possible to be adhered corde intus without having been baptized, and vice versa: baptized within and adhered corpore intus only, but not corde intus, which is the case of sinners not separated from the Church by schism or excommunication and who, consequently, belong externally to Her, but not internally, not through the heart: corde intus (CRESPIN, 2535). Catholic doctrine, being this way, by recognizing the sacramental power of those separated, both in body and heart, avoids the contradictions incurred by Cyprian and the Donatists (De b. V 29; VII 103). And recognizing that power does not imply in any way admitting that the unworthy or separated can give health: «Sacramentum gratiae dat Deus etiam per malo; ipsam uero gratiam non nisi per se ipsum uel per sanctos suos” (De b. V 29: CSEL 51, p.257). Approving the baptism received in the schism is not approving the baptism of the schismatics, since they use the sacraments of the Church as a good that does not belong to them. Augustine and Cyprian agree that it is illicit and illegitimate to preserve and give baptism outside the Church, which does not mean that it is impossible, since the baptism of Christ, despite its use in the hands of usurpers,
880 Additional notes
fathers and enemies of the Church, has its own holiness and truth, unaltered by the sins of men (De b. 111 13; V 9; VI 25; CRESPIN, 23358).

Separation from the Church does not entail loss of baptism or the impossibility of validly baptizing. Now: not even when the split is aggravated, totally or partially, by the rejection of the Catholic faith? Can heretical ministers validly baptize? Saint Augustine had to answer these questions in the Donatist controversy (CrespIN, 269-273). A follower of San Cipriano, the D. did so negatively. Even at the cost of disagreeing with Cyprian, Firmilian and those of Donatus, specifically Parmenian, Augustine replies that baptism can exist where faith is lacking. No one among us, says the Saint, has ever thought of repeating baptism to repentant apostates (C. Ep. Parm. JI 29). It would be utopian to expect a perfectly clear faith from every baptized person. Hence it is necessary to distinguish between sacramental truth and the errors of a deficient faith, even though they may coexist in the same man (De b. IV 22). For baptism to be valid, all that is needed is conformity of the formula with what is determined by the Lord in the Gospel: in nomine Patris et Filii er Spiritus sancti (De b. VI 15,20, p.211=Mt 28,19 BA 29, p.206-209; CrespIN, 277). Like that of the unworthy, then, the ministry of the separated schismatics can produce true sacraments, even in the case of separated heretics who profess serious errors regarding the dogmas of the Christian faith. It is enough that they respect the formula.

And what about baptism administered without any reference to the Christian faith? The Bishop of Hippo posed the question regarding a borderline case: that of baptism conferred by a non-Christian, by someone who, without being baptized, knows the rite by chance. Without attempting to find the definitive solution to the problem, which would require - he says - the opinion of a plenary council, and to date not even a provincial one has given, Augustine, on his own, considers valid the baptism given in the evangelical form by a non-Christian, provided that the baptized person is animated by a sincere desire and a certain faith. He does not approve, of course, the conferred, for example, for play, fun or pure theatrical staging. The case is different for those who also come without true faith and without sincere desire to be Christian, and ask to be baptized in the Church or in a sect that they believe to be the Church: in that case, there is true baptism, since there is a society of believers. The situation, in summary, presents a certain connection with the Christian faith, given that the sect—Augustine recalls—although it does not adhere to orthodox doctrine, has emerged like all the heresies of the true Church (De b. VII 101-102; C. Ep. Parm. 11 30; CRESPIN, 279). In any case, the presence of the "society of believers" gives the rite a religious character and guarantees it a seriousness that it would surely lack in the previously contemplated case of the theatrical ceremony (VILLETE, 230; CRESPIN, 278s).—BIBL.: Y. [24] Tyconium.—T. He is a star of the firmly Donatist for his vast scriptural knowledge and his independence of judgment in the face of the Schism. «Natione Afer...—Genadio qualifies—... in diuinis litteris eruditus, iuxta historiam sufficienter, et in saecularibus non ignarus Fuit» (De «ir.ill. 18). Great thinker and hard-working analyst of his own faith, sincere with himself and with others, a scholar with a profound interior life, determined and convinced to the end (Monceaux, V 165-171; BRrISSON, 222), with a penetrating spirit and great expressive force according to Augustine, he defended the universality of the Church against Parmenian, to the point of ending up excommunicated from the party by a schismatic council of 380 (C. Ep. Parm. 11,1, DPAC 11 3447; His works are divided into three classes: 1.* Polemics: De beautiful intestine and Expositiones diuersarum causarum (PAC 1,1122; m. compl. 20); 2.* Of exegesis: Liber Regularum (PAC 1,1124; DPAC 11 34475; RATZINGER: REAug 2, p.173ss; Cazier: REAug 19, p.241ss; SIMONETTI, 112); 3.* Of applied exegesis: a version of the Apocalypse and a commentary on the Apocalypse (R. PosE: Salmanticensis 32, p.35-48). The Bishop of Hippo used his writings and recommended them, with the necessary prior nuances. He used, in particular, the Liber Regularum and the commentary on the Apocalypse, from which he highlights some observations (De d. chr. TUI 30,42-47,56). Gennadius completes his references and cites two more works—Jas polemics— (De uir. ill. 18), while highlighting the spiritual interpretation, the corporeality of angels, millenarianism and the resurrection. They also speak about T. Quotvuldeus, Primasius, Cassiodorus, Bede, Saint Ambrose and Beatus of Liébana (DEPAC 1 514s; 11 3448; R. Pose: Bolletino dei Classici, 221-231).

Universality is the foundation of his ecclesiology. In front of his people he demonstrates with Scripture that the Church cannot be limited to Africa nor be reduced or suffer damage because of sinners, since, no matter how great a sin may be, it can never stop the course of divine promises (C. Ep. Parm. 11,1; Ep. 93,10,44; PINCHERLE: RR 1, p.355s.443ss; R. Pose, Symbols ecclesiastical...(Rome 1978) passim; Ib., Compostellanum 24, p.293ff). He discusses in depth the baptismal theory of D. on this ecclesiological platform (compl. no. 20). The authentic Church is the persecuted one, as was Christ, its Head. Ecclesiology and Christology always go together. Only the elect enter the ChurchKingdom. The universal judgment will be in charge of exposing and unmasking hypocrisy, the worst of evils, now latent. According to T., the sum of saints plus sinners is not admissible, but rather the option of saints or sinners. Rather than leaning towards an intensive catholicity as opposed to an extensive one, he prefers to admit both. We know a good part of his ecclesiology thanks to Augustinian quotations: cf., among others, C. Ep, Parm. 11.1; 11 13.31, 2242; III 3,17; Epp. 93,4,14.10,43s; C. lite. Pet. 11 83,184; C. Ep. Parm. 1 10.16; 11 22.42; Epp. 87.10; 93.1s; 249 (on ecclesial symbols, cf. works by R. PosE, in Bibl. gen., n.4).

Each verse of the Apocalypse serves to demonstrate that the holy, universal and bipartite Church walks through history in the midst of hypocrisy, persecution and the harassment of the Antichrist, the latter an idea very much from the author of The City of God, which includes No. 8 of Lumen Gentium: "The Church goes on a pilgrimage between the persecutions of the world and the consolations of God" (BAC 252, Madrid 51967, p.52; De cin. XVIII 52,2; With the supposed division of the commentary on the Apocalypse into three books, T. would have attempted to recapitulate his ecclesiological conception.” Exegete par excellence, everything
882 Additional notes

it subjugates it to ecclesiology", including the anthropological: thus unity (unum corpus), bipartitism (dextra et sinistra). Even the human body (anima-caro) allows him to distinguish, Pauline style, the celestial man from the carnal man (the double Adam, the celestial and earthly Church: R. Pose: Aug 19, p.470.481).

Much of his biography remains in shadow. We do not know when he was born. In 366 he had not yet written anything (MoncEaux, V 170). And when he died: perhaps around 390, because Augustine descends into the anti-Donatist controversy in 393 and never speaks of T. as still alive. Even on the spelling of the name, criticism remains divided: Tichonims, Tychonius, Thiconius, Thyconins. Recent Augustinian editions give Tychonius, (cf. MANDOUZE, who writes Tycomius: PAC 1,1122, n.1).—BimL.: cf. the Bible gen., n.4.

[25] The strange case of Tyconius.—The confrontation between Parmenianus and Tyconius leads to a somewhat strange situation for the latter (compl. n. 27). Even the Bishop of Hippo, who does not spare praise for his qualities and his vigorous anti-Donatist literature, recognizes that T. has absolutely absurd convictions about not wanting to radically depart from the Schism (C. Ep. Parm. 11,1; De d. cb. VI 30,42). It may be that for an adequate approach to the topic it is necessary to have, simultaneously, the writer, polemicist and exegete. In any case, his is a well-made ecumenical step in the sense of wanting to reconcile the two parties through the search for a new face of the Church. The Catholic was precisely walking there, in front of a D. anchored in his purest tradition. A step that probably helped him take his brilliant intuition and his masterful exegesis and mastery of Scripture, in which "the most banal citations of the Bible dévenaient des armes foudroyantes" (MOoNCcEaUx, V 168). It happens, however, that T., an excellent connoisseur of Gnostic traditions and exegetical techniques, failed to carry out his analysis with flexibility, so that, attacking the Catholic and the D. for being schismatics, he ended up even expelled from his party. Purely not wanting to understand either Catholics or Donatists, he ended up being misunderstood by both. His ecclesiology (compl. n. 24) reveals the great strength that T. granted to reason, the same reason that he presumed to have against the Schism and against the Catholic Church. Saint Augustine never ceases to be surprised by what he considers the inconsistency of T., who opposes his party, defends fundamental Catholic theses and, nevertheless, prefers to remain completely apart from Catholics (De d. ch. YI 30,42; Ep. 249).
Parmeniano tried in vain to persuade and convince T. When the

failure was evident, he tried to reduce him to silence: «I am going to remind you of what T., a certain author who belongs to your communion, recorded in his writings. He seems to have written rather against you in favor of the Catholic Church. And then, why did he separate from the Catholic Church? With just this question Parmeniano puts him down» (Ep. 93,10,43: BAC 69/ VIII, p.585). The Augustinian testimony is that he ended up excommunicated from the party by a Donatist council held around the year 380 (C. Ep. Parm. 11,1). The condemnation, however, left T. indifferent. With the serenity of a philosopher, believing that he alone, in possession of the truth, continued independently and uncommitted on his path, fully dedicated to the great exegetical work, convinced that neither the D. nor the Catholic Church embodied the Church of Christ and, instead, the one outlined by him from his exegesis (Monceaux, 1V 337; V 166).

Why, once excommunicated, does he not allow himself to be carried away by the humble logic of entering the Catholic Church, like Newman centuries later? (n. compl. 22). Here is the mystery that some specialists have tried, with mixed success, to clear up. In this sense, A. C. de Veer's comments reviewing L. J. van der Lof's study are interesting (REAug 14, p.356). E. Romero Pose affirms, for his part, that "the misunderstood Donatist" does not adhere to the decadent theology (exegesis) of the schismatic movement, but prefers to start from far back to assert himself in tradition and thus give a new face to Donato's party: too much time had passed since his appearance for him to be listened to and for all to accept his approaches. «The former could not understand -——due to the progressive aging of the party— the breadth of the Tyconian scores. The Catholic Church could discover the use and conclusions that T. made of exegetical traditions that once belonged to the Great Church” (4845). [26] Parmenianus, Donatist bishop of Carthage.—Donatist bishop of Carthage from c. 362 to 391/2, P. is chosen to succeed Donatus as soon as this great leader dies, in the year 355, in exile (S. Jerón., Chron. ad ann. 355, Opraro, 11 15; III 1.34). The optatian expression bispanum aut galum (11 7: CSEL 26, p.44) is difficult to interpret due to the rhetorical nature of the passage. More than the Milevitan's hesitation, one could see in it a deliberately vague phrase to signify the foreign nationality of the character, after all the first European called to govern an African religious movement as markedly nationalist and closed as the D. (PAC 1,816, n.2). He embraced the Donatist cause probably during the exile of the leader, whom it is believed that he met, even standing out among his most fervent followers, which is why those of the party, once the leader died, would have set their eyes on him (Monckaux, V 222). However, he still had to wait a while to enter the headquarters. The ban of the Schism decreed by Constans in 347 lasted in 355. His was, therefore, in those years a rather honorific primacy [Opratus, II 7; III 3; S. Ac., Retract. 11 43 (17); Serm. 46,8,17].

The situation changes completely in 362, when Julian the Apostate comes to the throne. Within the package of tolerance measures was the order to return the confiscated property to the Donatists (OPTATO, II 16; 111 3; S. Ac., Epp. 934,12; 105,29; C. litt. Pet. 11 97,224). That was a hard blow for Catholic. In those of the Schism, on the contrary, it represented the beginning of a vigorous and rapid reconstruction (Oprtato, 1 16-17, HI 3-V1L,7; S. Ac., C. Ep. Parm. 1 12,19; C. litt. Pet. YI 92,203; cf. CTh XVI 5,37; n. compl. 36). Despite his initial disadvantage, the new primate will end up playing a decisive role in the development and consolidation of the Church of Donato. In fact, the Donatists were known in their time as Parmenianists or Parmenians (C. Ep. Parm. 14,9; De haer. 41;
884 Additional notes

Serm. 46.17; PAC 1,816, n.7). At his death he left a well-organized D., flourishing in the various African provinces, and even with a majority in North Africa (Oprato, VII 1; S. Ac., Epp. 22,2; 129,6; 209,2; In Ps. 21,26; Serm. 1l; In Ps. 36,19). In the absence of other testimonies, these data would suffice to underline his indisputable pastoral activity, his talent as an orator and the success achieved with numerous writings - psalms, sermons or commentaries (tractatus) - composed to reinforce the cohesion of the Donatist community and neutralize the constant Catholic efforts to return it to unity (OpTATo, Í 4; S. Ac., Ep. 55,18; C. Cr. 12,3). On June 26, 363, Julian died. The Schism had taken advantage of those years of favor and managed to maintain its strength during the following years.

Dated surely before June 24, 393, he sends to the famous Tyconius the Epistula ad Tychonium, unfortunately lost, a key point to understand the confrontation between one and the other and its subsequent consequences (C. Ep. Perm. 11,1; De b. 11,1; compl. n. 25 and 27). Throughout his thirty years of episcopate, he knew how to maintain firm control of the Donatist Church. In Mauritania, with the Rogato schism. Also, in some way, with the circumceliones. Not so much the Claudianist split, which hit the D. of Rome in 385 (S. Ac., Serm. II in Ps. 36,20; PAC 1,990s.210; DPAC II 3008s). His prestige rose to heights as high as that of his predecessor Donato. For his ability as a theologian and administrator of the party, he earned the respect of Augustine, who, like Optatus, recognized in this schismatic leader the brilliant and mordant orator (OpTaTo, 11 14): «The arrogance of Donatus was exalted and a party was formed. Parmeniano, who followed him, consolidated the error. The first is the mountain; the second, the hill» (S. A., Serm. 46,8,17: BAC 53/VII, p.631). He died on an uncertain date, although certainly prior to the council of Cabarsusa, which met on June 24, 393 (Mater, 33s), since the person condemned as holder of the schismatic primal see of Carthage in that Maximianist council was already Primianus (compl. n. 31). Against him Saint Augustine wrote the Contra Epistulam Parmeniani—BrbL.: Y. ConGar, 10. Parménien et Tyconius: BA 28, p.718-720; To., 24. Citations scripturaires de Parménien, 733-735, W. H. C. FreND, Parmeniano: DPAC 11 2696-2687; J.-L. Mater, L'épiscopat de l'Afrique romaine, 33-35; A. ManbouzE: PAC 1,816-820.

[27] Parmeniano and Ticonio, confronted.—The controversy between P. and T. mainly affected the ecclesiological and baptismal issues (Monceaux, V 231ff; ConcaAr, 7185). Thanks to Julian the Apostate's policy of tolerance, P. was finally able to enter Carthage as a Donatist primate. And between 363-366 he wrote his first work, Aduersus Ecclesiam traditorum, known for the refutation that Optatus of Milevi carried out in 366 (PAC 1,8175). In the midst of this almost euphoric atmosphere of reorganization, T. suddenly appears with his two polemical works (compl. n. 24), whose main theses dealt with: 12 Donatist pride and intransigence (C. Ep. Parm. 1 13,31; Ep. 93,4,14.10,43); 2. The universality of the Church: it is absurd that true Christianity is only in Africa (C. Ep. Parm. 11,1; Ep. 93,10,44); 3.” The holiness of the Church: which is neither stained nor can perish outside or inside Africa (ibid.); 4. The separation of good and bad: which will not happen until the end, with the judgment; so that the Donatist incoherence is notorious in not wanting to put up with the guilty (C. Ep. Parm. 11 22,42; II 3,17); 5.0 The rebaptismal practice, through which the Donatist incoherence appears once again, since the D. does not

Additional notes 885 was as intransigent in the ancient synods, nor in that of Carthage in 336, in admitting Catholic turncoats without rebaptism. And the same can be said of the case of Deuterius and the Mauritanian bishops (Ep. 93,10,43s; GENN., De uir. ill. 18).

These Ticonian theses were pure antidonatism coming from D. himself, from an ideologue, theologian and distinguished exegete belonging to the Sect. A hard blow for the party, in the process of reorganization. It was necessary to intervene. P., then, wrote in 387 the Epistula ad Tychonium, the content of which we know thanks to Saint Augustine. In it he invited T. to withdraw the ideas expressed in his writings, ordering him, on the one hand, not to give his version of the history of the D. again, and on the other, "to renounce the audacity of proclaiming that the Church is extended throughout the universe" (S. Ac., Ep. 93,10,44; C. Ep. Parm. 11,1). The strategic error was tremendous, because the Catholics were right from the schism itself. P., therefore, objected: 1.%, T. shows himself to be inconsistent in reasoning as he reasons and, nevertheless, remaining a Donatist; 2.2, T. does not take into account in his argument of the universality of the Church certain facts that refute it: Gallic, Spanish and Italian bishops, who, by remaining in communion with the traditors, have become their accomplices; 3." Milan; Since then, the Church of the Innocents has not known the slightest blemish; 5.” As for breaking with the guilty, remember T. the abundant scriptural texts that condemn Catholics, whose faults corrupt all who join their society (C. Ep. Parm. 11 8,15; 9,18; 19,38; 21,40s; C. Cr. IV 6971); and 6., T. must also warn that Catholics lack true baptism, since it is not possible to have it without having first received it, nor to receive it if no one confers it, which is impossible in carnal men, incapable of begetting children according to the Spirit, since divine law will never allow a dead person to give life or a wounded man to heal wounds.

As to the objections made to the party, it is evident that one can be baptized by a bad minister as long as the malice is hidden, and that the Holy Spirit, although not with those who appear to confer the sacrament, is in reality with those who have faith to receive it; and, finally, that in any case it is God himself who fulfills the sacrament through the hand of the minister (PAC 1,820).

P. concluded by exhorting T. to remain in the party and endure the persecutions until the end, without ever joining the persecutors (PAC 1,820.1123). But T. did not allow himself to be convinced and ended up excommunicated by a Donatist council held in the year 380, or 385 according to Frend (C. Ep. Parm. 11,1; Concar, 719; MoNcEaux, V 232ss; R. Pose, 3447; FREND, 2687). It cannot be considered a success for P. that T. did not abandon the D. or enter the Catholic Church, as Frend maintains citing C. Ep. Parm. IT 6.29. Although it is true that it did not cause a new schism between the Donatist ranks, the end of that confrontation, as noted in n. compl. 25, is far from being a success attributable to P.—BrBL.: Y. [28] Parmenian and the Rogatist and Claudianist schisms.—Rogato was Donatist/Rogatist bishop of Cartena, in Caesarian Mauritania, today Tenés of Algeria, in the 15th century. Eponym of a fraction called Rogatista within the D.: Rogatistae a Rogato; Rogatus auctor uester (S. AG., Ep. 93,3,11: CSEL 34/2, p.455s). He broke with his people in the time of Parmenian - 370 more or less - and founded the sect of the Rogatists. It was these same people who went to Julian to demand their rights, believing themselves to be authentic heirs of Christ and Donatus (Ep. 93,3,11; 4,12; 8,24). Parmeniano's henchmen did not sit still either. With the help of Firmo, they attempted to eliminate the Rogatists "through the barbarian kings" (C. list. Pet. 11 133,184; C. Ep. Parm. 1 10,16; Ep. 87,10; compl. n. 35).

The Rogatists were characterized: 1., in terms of behavior: by a rejection of the violence admitted or practiced between Circumcelions and Donatists; 2.", in terms of its justification: for an ideal of trying to embody the "Church of the pure"; 3.", in terms of troops: for the small number of faithful, practically limited to Mauritania. Rogato withstood the attacks of Firmo and his friends the Donatists, and in the processes between primianists and maximianists he allied himself with the latter (G. c. Em. 9; C. Cr. 111 62,68; IV 70,73; C. Ep. Parm. 1 11,17; R. Pose, 3008; Mater, 405). As the urbanistae or urbanenses were in Numidia, so the center of the rogatistas was Cartena of Mauritania. Grouped together with nine bishops who had separated from the rest, back in 370, in open opposition to the violence of the circumcelions, and faithful to the emperor when the Gildonian revolt, around 408 only ten or eleven bishops remained (Ep. 93,11.49). Rogato must have died for 407/408. Vincent, a former classmate of Augustine in Carthage, came to take his place (Ep. 93,1,1). which places us in the years 420-422, from which it is impossible to speak of rogatistas (Monckaux, IV 1285; A. C. De VEER, 828s; CoNGAR, 740; PAC 1,9908).

The Donatist bishop Claudian, Lucian's successor at the head of the schismatic community of Rome, called by his adversaries the community of the Montanians, was the sixth chief bishop since its foundation when his desire for rebaptism and his declared opposition to Pope Damasus, with the consequent disorders, forced him to be expelled from Rome and return to Carthage in 380 (Orrato, 11 4; A. C. DE VzER, 84755). Things did not go well in the African metropolis either: opposed to Parmeniano, with whom he could not reach an understanding, he decided to lead a group of followers and thus open a new schism within the party, called Claudianist. Primiano admitted them to the Donatist communion in 392, an intolerable decision in the opinion of the Maximianists, who used it in 393 as one of the justifying causes of their own schism (C. Cr. IV 9,11; Concar, 740; PAC 1,210).

In addition to the Rogatistas and Claudianistas—groups that do not reach the magnitude of the Maximianists—there were still other particular and minority schisms within the D. Augustine judges them severely, especially the rogatistas (Ep. 93,6,20s.7,23.8,245.10,36.11,49), and de-
