IV 58,69. 69,73; De b. 16,8; In lo. 10,6; J-L. Mare, L'épiscopat de V Afrique romaine, 405; E. Romero PosE, Rogato: DPAC 11 3008s; A. C. DE Vrer, 45. Rogatus et les rogatistes: BA 31, p.827-829; lo., 54. An episcopal siege donated to Rome, 847849, Cf. n. compl. 26,27 and 29.

[29] Primianus and the Council of Bagái.—Successor of Parmenianus from 392 to 412 (C. Ep. Parm. 11 2,11), the Donatist bishop Primianus had to face numerous internal crises in the party, caused, precisely, by his autocratic and radical way of being. He presided over the schismatics in Carthage 411, like Aurelius over the Catholics. He was only a newly ordained man when he sat in the primal chair (S. Ac., In Ps. 36 II 20). For reasons that are still unknown to us, he had his presbytery condemn four deacons, himself excommunicating Maximian, one of them, whom he considered his main offender (G. c. Em. 9; C. Cr. IV 4,4). Maximian was a descendant of the great Donatus, and may well have been his opponent in the race for the primal see. The sanction was imposed not only without regular prior notice, but also in the absence of the accused. To this scandal he added that of not pursuing the demand that the seniors of the Carthaginian Donatist community had presented to him in order for him to renounce admitting sacrilegious Christians (incesti) into his community, probably the Claudianists (mn. compl. 28).

The schism occurred in the agonies of 392. Primianus was condemned as cruel and despotic. It was done first in Carthage by a council of forty-three bishops, and on June 24, 393, that of one hundred bishops in Cabarsusa (n. compl, 31). Elected in his place and consecrated in Carthage by twelve bishops (PL 11,1185-89), Maximian took possession and installed in the present see only a part of the clergy and the Donatist community (S. Ac., Epp. 108,2,5; 185,/4,17; C. lit. Pet. 1 10,11; C. Cr. UI 52,58; 1V 6,7; 31,8; G. c. Em. 9 PAC 1,720, n.16-17;907).

As the majority of the party was with the leader, it was not difficult for Primianus to assemble on April 24, 394, in Bagai of Numidia, today Ksar Baghai of Algeria, a council of no less than three hundred and ten bishops (MatEr, 265.110). For the D. this figure was a symbol of plenitude, perhaps due to similarity with that of Nicaea: three hundred (Saint Athanasius) or three hundred and eighteen (Saint Hilary). In any case, a symbolic figure—servants of Abraham (Gen 14:14)—that soon became traditional. It should be known in any case that the Donatist statistics are not very reliable, and the most approximate and certain that we have on the matter belongs to Carthage 411 (ConGaR, 743; compl. n. 58). There were councilors from all the African provinces, mostly Nmumidians and Mauritanians; Without prior debate, and recognizing Primianus' innocence, they ended the excommunication without remission or possible moratoriums against Maximian and his twelve consecrators, granting the others an extension to return to the Church. The numerous Augustinian sources of this council denounce the anti-Maximian persecution that Primian's party unleashed everywhere. This schism meant the collapse of the official theories of the Sect, since those of Primiano appealed to secular power - exactly what they always accused Catholics of - and before the magistrates they claimed the Maximianist basilicas as their own, declaring against this group the

[30] Saint Augustine and Maximianism.—Maximianism takes its name from Maximian, Donatist/Maximianist bishop of Carthage at the end of the 4th century: «... aut Maximianistas aut Maximianenses aut quodlibet aliud quod a Maximiani nomine deriuetur...» (C. Cr. IV 6,7: CSEL 52, p.52; PAC 1,719-722; compl. It is a movement closely related to the events that took place in the schismatic councils of Cabarsusa and Bagai, and whose most notable characteristics, according to Augustine, were: 1.*, rejection of violence admitted or practiced between Donatists and circumcelions (C. Ep. Parm. 11 3,7; C. litt. Pet. YI 15,35; In Ps. 54,26); 2.*, conviction of representing the true Church of Donato (C. Cr. IV 6,7; In Ps. 36 11 19); 3.*, a small number of faithful, dispersed throughout Byzacena and Tripolitania—provinces where this schism had arisen—and in the Proconsular (C. litt. Pet. 11 58,132; Ep. 93,8,24; In Ps. 54,26).

Although it is not the first open schism within the D., its history provides Saint Augustine, perhaps like no other, with a rich series of decisive arguments against the doctrinal positions of Donatus's party, especially in book IV of the Contra Cresconium. Augustinian's sharp observations, moreover, will be precious and will count not a little among the Catholics of the Carthage Conference of 411, when the time comes for the debates (Gesta 1 16: SCh 195, p.600; 1 18, p.610612; 1 55, p.662.665). Here are the most common arguments that Augustine extracts from this story: 1.2 Why reject Caecilian, first condemned and later recognized as innocent, and not Primianus, whose vicissitudes are the same or at least very similar? 2. Why take it against the Catholics by saying that they have resorted to imperial justice against the Donatists and forget, on the contrary, that those of Primianus have also appealed against the Maximianists? 3. Why reject the validity of baptism conferred among Catholics and accept,

Additional notes 889 on the other hand, without any scruples that of the Maximianists, administered before they returned to the great Church? 4.2 Why be suspicious of the alleged stain of Caecilian and not, on the contrary, of that which, after Bagai, was admitted in Maximian and his consecrators, two of whom at least—Felician and Pretextatus (PAC 1,722, n.37; compl. n. 33)—have been readmitted to the great Church while retaining their episcopal dignity?

The Bishop of Hippo, in short, does not cease to exploit the dialectical strategy that this schism provides him, drawing the logical conclusion that follows from it, namely: the abandonment, by the D., of his essential theses and his alleged reason for being (In Ps. 36 11 19s; C. Cr. MI 18,21; Cowcar, 725). Conclusions, after all, drawn from a premise of inconsistencies. Something that T. himself, not only with Maximianism, but with the council of 336, for example, also knew how to wield against the hierarchy of his party.—BiBL.: P. BrisSON, Autonomisme, 223-225; Y. CONGAR, 15. Le schisme maximianiste et Vabandon des théses donatistes: BA 28, p.724s; A. C. DE VER, L'exploitation du schisme maximianiste...: RAug 3 (Paris 1965) 219237; Io., 43. Les origines du maximianisme: BA 31, p.825-827.

[31] Maximianism and the Council of Cabarsusa.—On June 24, 393, a council of one hundred Donatist bishops, meeting in Cabarsusa, the unlocated seat of the Byzacena, closed ranks with Maximian, definitively condemning and deposing the leader Primianus. Perhaps the choice of an obscure place in the Byzacena, whose true location is unknown and whose spelling there is no unanimity: Cabarsusa-Cabarsussi-Cebarsussi, responds to the fact that the Tripolitania, the Proconsular and especially the Byzacena were the places where Maximian had the most followers. In fact, only the presence of one Numidian bishop is safely attested: Perseverance of Teveste (S. Ac., In Ps. 36 11 20; A. C. nz Veer, 7865; Mater, 335.120.380; PAC 1,855). It was presided over by the primate of the Byzacena, Victorinus of Munaciana (Mater, 442; PAC 1,1196). Although the minutes have not reached us, we can get a very approximate idea of what happened thanks to the synodal letter Tractoria, with which the faithful were informed of the transcendental agreement and its reasons, a letter preserved in Saint Augustine (Ir Ps. 36 11 20), reproduced in PL 11,1189-1191 and Mansr 3,845-850, and analyzed by MONCEAUX, IV 355-361. The number of synod members is not certain. The list of signatories, as it has been preserved, is incomplete, it is true, but so is that offered by Augustine: cemtum vel amplis (C. Cr. 1V 6,7: CSEL 52, p.307; cf. centum: C. Ep. Parm. 14,8; C. Cr. 1I 13,16; Epp. 108, 2,55; 141,6; De baer. 69), the primianists never answered it, so fond of exploiting the argument of number in favor of their council of Bagai (Mater, 34s; A. C. DE VERR, 787; n. compl. 29). According to Tractoria, Cabarsusa completely reopened Primiano's summary. Other charges were added to the charges determining his conviction (A. C. DE VEER, 825ss; compl. n. 29): Primianus had made episcopal elections to replace bishops still alive; He had ordered the priest Fortunato to be thrown into a sewer for having baptized the sick; he had denied ecclesiastical communion to the priest Demetrius so that he would disinherit his son; He had outraged Demetrius himself for his hospitality to some bishops at the time of the first investigation; had sent a pack of wicked men to demolish the houses of
890 Additional notes Christians; Finally, he had occupied many properties by force (C. Cr. IV 47,57).

The bishop - it could be read in a clear verdict, without invective or rhetorical phrases - is a true mediator, the very source of the holiness of the faithful. He must, therefore, be holy under penalty of compromising ecclesial holiness (a thesis rejected by Saint Augustine, for whom holiness comes from God and the Church is holy regardless of whether its ministers are: Im Ps. 36 11 20; C. Ep. Parm. 11 4,8; 8,155; C. Cr. 11 7,7). Primianus, on the other hand, the verdict continued, is a criminal, a minister deserving of excommunication according to Saint Pabius (2 Thes 3:6). The faithful have to break with him, otherwise they would be contaminated by their sins. This separating the faithful from their leader is one of the most important points of Tractoria.

Finally, let us highlight the following points: 1.*, the geographical opposition of two parties in conflict; 2.", on the one hand, the dignified and serene tone of the presentation of the charges that Primianus is accused of, as well as that of the conviction in Cabarsusa; 3.*, on the other, the diatribes, invectives and violent condemnation with which Maximianus and his consecrators are punished in Bagai; and 4., the contrast in behavior: generally moderate that of the Maximianists; brutal and excessive that of Primianus at the beginning and his supporters later. Specialists like Frend wonder if rivalries of race, temperament and civilization would not play an even more important role in this matter than that of religion (FREND, 21558). his candidate in the succession of the late Parmenian (A. C. DE VEER, 7888). BrimL.: W. H. C. Freno, The Donatist Church...(Oxford 1952) 214217; maximianist council of Cabarsussa: BA 31, p.786-789. Cf. the bibl.
[32] Optatus and Parmenianus.—Through the seven books against Parmenianus, Optatus intended to refute the Donatist theory on the sacrals.

ments and their effectiveness, and at the same time demonstrate that the D. could not in any way be the true Church. Unnoticed, however, were such essential ecclesiological aspects as the concept of the body of Christ, the mysterious character of the Church or the link between the Church and the Eucharist, which St. Augustine was in charge of exposing in detail when the time came (CoNGAR, 78s; compl. n. 19).

Optatus demonstrates that the sanctifying effect of the sacraments does not depend on the holiness of the dispenser, but on God himself, Saints and sanctifiers in themselves, the Church is not, therefore, the reason for their holiness; On the contrary, they are, as a gift from Christ to his Church, the cause of ecclesial holiness. Optatus also distinguishes between the essential holiness of the Church, received from Christ, and the holiness of its members, who, even so, can, of course, be sinners. Saint Augustine will enrich this doctrine with the timely and subtle distinction societas sanctorum -communio sacramentorum. Obptato defines the characteristics of the true Church from his controversial anti-schismatic analysis: there can only be, he says, one Church; the only wife; the only dove; called Catholic because it is rationalis (111 1), and is universally extended (11 1): "una Ecclesia quae est in toto orbe terrarum" (III 3); «in

Additional notes 891 toto orbe terrarum diffusa» (IT 2). Decisive argument for Optatus is geographical catholicity, which Saint Augustine also endorses (De b. 15; p. 52,1,2; compl. n. 22). Optatus goes further than Saint Cyprian in stating that the one cotbedra is no longer just that of the bishop, on which the unity of the local Church is founded, but the cathedra Petri, the foundation of the unity of the Catholic Church, of the universal Church (11 2). The cathedra Petri, therefore, guarantees the unity of catholicity. An optatian ecclesiology, as seen, of communion, and communion built on Roman primacy, clearly affirmed by that of Milevi (Concar: BAC III 236, n.29).

It was 394 when Parmenian published the Aduersus ecclesiam traditorum, with the purpose of justifying the schismatic legitimacy of his Church in the face of the indignity of the Catholics, that is, traditores (14-6). From Optato de Milevi (compl. nos. 20 and 32) we know that the five books that made up the work deal specifically with: 1., baptism; 2.” of ecclesial unity; 3. of the origin of the Schism as well as the unworthiness of Catholics as traditors and instigators of the persecution unleashed by Paul and Macarius; 4., on the motivation for the rejection of the Catholic sacraments: the oil and the sacrifice of the wicked (Ps 141,5; PAC 1,818). Clear influences of the Cyprianist De unitate Ecclesiae catholicae can be perceived in these books, although the theory of the gifts, attributed to the Bride of the Song of Songs, gives the work an air of originality from which Western theology should benefit.

Parmeniano claimed these dowries for the Donatists. These were: 1.%, Catbedra: sign of the authority and unity of the bishop; 2.*, Angelus: spiritual power of the baptismal waters, so titled in memory of the angel who descended into the pool and stirred up the water (Jn 5:4); 3.2, Spiritus: third Person of the Trinity, principle of our sanctification; 4.s, Fons: sanctifying water of baptism; baptismal font; 5.2, Si gillum: seal of baptism and the altar, a sign of the importance that the Donatists gave to baptism and the Eucharistic sacrifice through the main article of their Trinitarian profession; and 62, Umbilicus: the same altar, umbilical cord, center of the fertility of the Church. In his emphatic rejection of imperial interference in ecclesiastical affairs, Parmenian did nothing more than follow Donatus the Great (I 22). The Parmenianist writing, finally, received a complete response around 365 with the Milevitano's De schismate Donatistarum (n. compl. 19).— BrsL.: Y. Concar: BA 28, p.78s; Io: BAC 111/3a-b, 234-236; A. Manbouze: PAC 1,816-820. Cf. the bibl. of nos. compl. 19-20 and 26-28.

[33] Pretextato Asuritano and Feliciano Maustitano.—Pretextato of Asuras, city of the Proconsular, today Zanfour, in Tunisia (Mater, 106), was first a Donatist bishop, later a Maximianist and finally a Donatist-Primianist bishop. With Feliciano Mustitano he composes living proof of the denial that the Donatists had given to their own disciplinary doctrine, readmitting two bishops who had split from their communion without withdrawing their episcopal dignity or contesting the validity of the baptism they administered during their schismatic-Maximianist era (G. c. Em. 9). Participating in the ordination of Primiano, after the latter's condemnation inflicted in Carthage, he went to Cabarsusa, among whose signatories he appears (C. litt. Pet, 1 12,13; In Ps. 36 11 20), being one of the twelve consecrated.
grantes of Maximian, later condemned with him without possible remission in Bagái (n. compl. 29 and 31). On March 2, 395, he was accused before

the proconsul Herod, in Carthage, to imitate Feliciano, sheltered in his church, and like him, the object of a demand for expulsion. It is presented by the lawyer Titian on behalf of the semiores of Asuras, as well as those of the church of Mustis, including the priest Peregrino, all of them primianists (De b. 11 12,17; C. Cr. III 56,62; IV 4,5.39,46; C. Gaud. 1 39; PAC 1,5535.1115s). Pretextato resists, but on December 22, 396, the Asuritan clerics and semiores, who claim to act in the name of Rogato, the consecrated bishop "in place of the condemned bishop," demand his expulsion from the proconsul Theodore (Epp. 88,11; 108,5,14; C. Cr. III 56,62; PAC 1,991.1108).

Just on the threshold of 398, he returned to Donatist unity under pressure from the Asuritan locals, themselves victims of the force of Optato of Tamugadi. His re-entry into the party, like that of Feliciano, is made official with his presence at the ceremony with which the anniversary of Optatus was celebrated, which must have occurred between December 396 and January or February 398, in Tamugadi naturally, and which Primianus attended with other Primianist bishops (Ep. 108,2,5; compl. n. 29). Only after this double unconditional readmission became effective was Saint Augustine using the case of P. and F. as a typical exponent of the incoherence that the Donatists incurred in rejecting the return to Catholic unity (PAC 1,902, n.19). The Bishop of Hippo alludes to P. dying "shortly afterwards", both in C. Ep. Parm. TIT 6.29, that is, after the final stretch of 404 and before June 411, as in Ep. 108,2,5, dating between 409 and 410. Asuritan Pretextato, of course, is presumed dead, although without mentioning his name, at the Carthage Conference of 411 (Gesta 1 120: SCh 195, p.709; Mater, 386).

Musti, city of the Proconsular, today Henchir Mest, a city on the route from Carthage to Sica Veneria, near the current Krib, in Tunisia, was the seat of Feliciano, a Donatist bishop first, then a Maximianist and finally a Primianist. He also took part in the ordination of Primianus, and was later a signatory of Cabarsusa and one of the twelve consecrators of Maximian. Same as Pretextato: they are very similar biographies. The Mustitan Donatists strongly supported his opposition to the condemnation of Maximian and his consecrators. His reconciliation with the Primianists and the circumstances that surrounded it, like that of Pretextatus, gave rise to Saint Augustine - as has already been said - to denounce the blatant incoherence of the Schism (R. Pose, 1350). Absent from the Conference of 411, he is nevertheless mentioned by Victorianus, Catholic bishop of Musti, as his Donatist rival at the same time as Donato, bishop of Turris Rutunda, today Sidi Khalifa, in Algeria (PAC 1,1189s. 317). A piece of information that Alypius will take advantage of at the Conference of 411 to place on the Donatist-Primianist orthodoxy of F. a question to which, on behalf of the Donatists, Petiliano refuses to answer because it is unrelated to the ongoing procedure. Petiliano will insist on the refusal during the third session (Gesta 1 122; SCh 195, p.434; 131136; S. Ac., Breu. YI 11,22). In the opinion of Catholics, the case of F. is revealed to be at least the root of a split of see (Breu. I 12). St. Augustine refers to F. as still alive in Ad Donat. p. col. 4.5; that is, before February 28, 412 (PAC 1,402).—BrBL.: CL LereLLEY, Les cités de l' Afrique romaine 11 147-150; J.-L. [34] Salvio Membresitano.—Salvio of Membresa, city of the Proconsular, today Medjez el Bab, on the Medjerda valley, about 60 km southwest of Tunis, was a Donatist-Maximianist bishop, holder of the Membresitana see already before joining Maximianism (C. Cr. IV 4,5; 49,59; LerELLEY, 141ff). Signatory of the synodal letter of Cabarsusa and one of the twelve consecrators of Maximian, later condemned with him in Bagái (n. compl. 35), he refuses to give up the see to whom Primianism has just ordained in his place before the end of the year, that is, to Restituto (C. Cr. 111 56,62; Ep. 108,5,14; PAC 1,9708), a rebellious attitude that Well, before March 2, 395, a full-fledged process carried out by the lawyer Numasius before the proconsul Herod (PAC 1,788). Accused of sheltering himself in a kind of sacrilegious secret thanks to his episcopal power, his expulsion is requested without further consideration (C. Cr. IV 4,5; Ep. 108,4,13). Despite the above, Restituto instructs him in the 397 new process before the proconsul Serano, whose jurisdiction in the matter seems to have been admitted (PAC 1,1060s). In accordance with a law of Constantius that reserved to bishops the privilege of judging bishops, and given, consequently, the sentence of Bagai, Salvius is summoned, by virtue of the interlocutory sentence of the proconsul, before the following dilemma: either return to communion with the primianists or expulsion from his see, leaving Restituto loca omnia, up to the cellula(e) and agell(i) (C. Cr. IV 48.58; 66.82). It is guessed from a fragment of the minutes that Salvius did not consent to the first part of the dilemma and that, once condemned, he did not agree to leave the places either (C. Cr. IV 48,58). Salvius is, in the eyes of Augustine of Hippo, the prototype of the persecuted Maximianist, victim of the repressions that Primianism obtained from power; also an exponent of the heretic who, unlike Feliciano Mustitano and Pretextato Asuritano, at all times was inflexible, refusing to return to the Donatist-Primianist communion (C. Ep. Parm. 14,22; C. Cr. 51,61; compl. n. 35).

Given his popularity among the members, the proconsul preferred to entrust the inhabitants of Abitina, a nearby town of the Proconsular, today Chouhoud el Batin, in Tunisia, to carry out the expulsion trial. The elderly Salvio was the object of mockery and ridicule, forced to dance with obscene airs and dead dogs around his neck (C. Cr. TV 49,59; 51,61; Ep. 118,6,16; Monceaux, IV 3025). Of course, the proconsul had not even remotely thought of ordering such an atrocity, but the incident is, from the outset, revealing: on the one hand, the proconsul did not have agents to execute his order; On the other hand, intervention outside the geographical limits of its jurisdiction was contrary to law. This singular behavior may have responded to the attitude of the magistrates of Membresa, favorable to Salvius, who could oppose, at least by inertia, an order from the proconsul without any risk of reprisals, which, on the other hand, indicates the extent to which what some modern historians have called totalitarianism of the late Empire reached (LePELLEY, 60s). Salvio, however, obtained from his people the construction of a basilica. When Augustine writes the Contra Epistulam Parmeniani, years 404/405 according to the dating recently advanced by Schindler, he makes it clear that Salvius was still alive. In the Conference of 411, however, it is his old adversary Restituto who occupies the seat of Membresa, without the slightest mention of Salvio.—B1BL.: Cl LePELLRY, Les cités de l' Afrique romaine 11 141-144; J.-L. [351 The Moorish king Firmo.—The Moorish prince Firmo, son of Nubel and brother of Gildon and Mascezel, and apparently also Mazuca, revolted in 371 against Romano, count of Africa, numerous non-Romanized indigenous tribes of Mauretania, dragging Roman officials and imperial troops to his cause, specifically the fourth cohort of the Sagittarii and the legion Flauia Victrix Constantina (LepeLLEY, 11 516; PAC 1,9975; He also gained the support of the Donatists to such an extent that the schismatics of Rogato did not hesitate to describe the Donatists as Firmians (Firmiani; m. compl. 28). Catholics and Rogatists from the Punic town Rusicade in Numidia, today Skikda, a city 87 km north of Constantine, are his victims in Caesarian Mauretania, whose coastline he invades - already proclaimed king -, taking over Caesarea, the capital, today Cherchell (C. Ep. Parm. 1 10,16; C. litt. Pet. 11 83,184; Ep. 87.10; LereLLeY, 1 525; We know of the coalition between Firmo and the Donatists through Saint Augustine, although it seems that the phenomenon was rather limited (C. Ep. Parm. 1 11,17; TENGSTRÓM, 79-83).

Caesarea suffered greatly from these incidents: surrounded between the end of 371 and the beginning of 372, it soon fell prey to the rebels, who took it using fraud and bribery, according to Orosius (Hist. VII 33,5). Valentinian I then sent Count Theodosius, father of the future Emperor Theodosius, to the scene of the events, who, once landed in Igilgili, immediately went to the field of operations, reaping without delay some resounding successes; It does not take long for them to reach 'Tipasa and take Caesarea, about 27 km from each other, where they defeat Firmo, who flees in retreat across the desert. Caesarea had actually been sacked by Mazuca, who was wounded and taken prisoner. Theodosius orders him to be returned to the city that he had recently sacked, but he dies, probably from his wounds, and his head is sent to the Caesarians. Firmo, meanwhile, seeks refuge with lgmazen, king of the Isaflemses, whose location is still, prosopographically, very hypothetical (DESANGES, 56).

Following his victory over the Isaflenses, which in 373/374 cost Firmo's brother the life, Theodosius had a notable municipe (potentem municipem) named Evasius, his son Fioro, and other people "convinced of having helped the disturber of the peace by secret industries" burned alive, which shows that Firmus sought with the aforementioned rebellion something more than being a simple leader of rebellious tribes in the mountains. Kotula, however, maintains that Firmo did not seek to usurp the imperial title (KoruLa, 137-146; LrereiryY, 1 515-517). Mandouze notes that it was precisely in Tipasa in Mauritania, in the sanctuary outside the walls dedicated to Saint Salsa, where Firmo implored in vain the intercession of the local martyr to seek refuge in the town that was already besieged (PAC 1,457, n.6). Firmo ended up hanging himself when in the town of the Isaflenses he was about to be handed over to the Romans. The suicide of this barbarian king caused the Donatists, his allies, more than displeasure, and they would not take long to take revenge on Theodosius, who, accused of aspiring to the Empire, was beheaded in Carthage in the year 376 (ConGar, 730).—BIBL.: Y. [36] Julian the Apostate and the Donatists.—It was the year 360 when Julian was acclaimed august with the unconditional support of the troops. Deposed without delay by Constantius II, and after his unforeseen death when preparing to march on the West, Julian was once again acclaimed, this time emperor, in Constantinople. "Greek among Greeks", he soon undertook a series of reforms. Particularly important are the edicts ordering the return of the exiled bishops of Constantinople and those of religious tolerance and paganism, opportunely taken advantage of by the Donatists, ready again for excesses, about which Saint Augustine writes referring to Julian: "sacrilegious dissensions liberas esse permitteret" (Ep. 105,9; Opraro, 11 16-26; VI 5-8; Brisson, 2615; MARTROYE, 79s).

Julian was recognized by Africa only after the death of Constantius TI, in November 361. The notary Gaudentius had been in charge of maintaining obedience to Constantius in African lands during the events of 360, a loyalty that later cost him his life. Julian died on June 26, 363. His empire in this part of Africa therefore lasted only twenty months (LePELLEY, 1 98.283). In the city of Thibilis, today Announa, about twenty kilometers southwest of Guelma, the ancient Calama of Saint Posidius, there is a statue dedicated to Julian with the following ordo written: restitutor sacrorum. It seems, therefore, that the restorative measures of paganism were well received in Thibilis, as well as in Casae, where Julian is described in an inscription as restitutor libertatis et Romanae religionis. The fact that no governor is mentioned in the text indicates that the ordo of Thibilis proceeded to this dedication spontaneously. As can be seen, paganism retained its influence in these cities during the years 361-363 (LePELLEY, 11 477-487: 4825). The Donatist leaders were able to return to Africa; Parmeniano, finally entering the primal seat (n. compl. 26); and the basilicas and other properties confiscated in 347, be returned to the schismatics. That return meant the intensification of their anti-Catholic violence, so that an even more insurmountable wall was built between both ecclesiastical groups (LAMIRANDE, 559, n.3; FREND, 18755).

It is clear that the "Church of the Martyrs" knew how to take advantage of Julian the Apostate's hatred against the Catholic Church. In 362, very soon therefore, Bishop Pontius and the bishops Rogatian and Cassian went to Julian to demand justice: that the heads of the Donatist Church return from exile and the basilicas be returned to them to exercise their ministry (C. litt, Pet. 11 97.224; Ep. 105,2,9; Opraro, 11 16; PAC 1,885). Juliano attended to all their requests. Which gave rise to his adversaries, Augustine of Hippo above all, to reproach the Schism not only for the recourse to self-determination.

[37] Imperial anti-Donatist legislation from 317 to 400.—It is singularly copious. In one way or another, all emperors except Julian the Apostate legislated against the Donatists. Saint Augustine expounds it briefly. But the documents abound all the more because these laws were sometimes applied intermittently. For the period defined here, the distribution according to the following headings is sufficient:

1) From 316/317 to 337 (death of Constantine). Fed up with so much Donatist interpellation, Constantine made public at the end of 316 or on the threshold of 317 an edict of unity ordering the confiscation of the Donatist basilicas and their allocation to the Catholic Church. And in the same way with the assets of those obstinate in separation, who were threatened with exile. Parmeniano's complaints suggest that there were even death sentences (C. Ep. Parm. 18,13; Epp. 105,8; 141,10). In any case, this "very severe law" (Ep. 105,9) was the cause of closed attacks against the Donatist assemblies" (Passio Donati: PL 8,753ff; S. Ac., Epp. 105,5; 88,3; 89,14; 93,14, etc.; cf. Von SoDEN, 26; SEECK, 5555; VoGr, 3325; BRISSON, 2575; The error, however, remained uneradicated. Constantine sent his vicar of Africa, Verinus, another law dated March 29, 319 with which he ordered the search and punishment of the authors of "defamatory libels", in clear allusion, no doubt, to the false accusations of the Donatists against the Catholics (CTh IX 34,1; PAC 1,1146s). With a rescript of April 25, 320, he reminded the proconsul Aelianus that such libels, even those preserved in the proconsular archives or the vicar of Africa, should not bother the accused persons. On May 5, 321, he sent his Epistula ad Universos Episcopos per Africam (CSEL 26, p.212s), giving the impression of granting a respite of consecutive tolerance to the investigation of the Donatists before the emperor and that, in reality, it was only a temporary suspension of its effects, in no way an abrogation of the edict (Gesta 111 543-551: SCh 195, p.548-550). Two of his rescripts return to the defamatory issue, one from December 4, 320, and the other from October 21, 328, and in the years between 326 and 330, Constantine excluded
Supplementary Notes 897 the Donatists of fiscal immunity, which they reserve for the Catholic clergy.

2) From 337 to 391 (death of Parmeniano). Despite the truce of 321, skillfully used by the Schism to consolidate itself, as clearly demonstrated by its council of 336, "Constantine's sons imitated their father, promulgating similar laws" (Ep. 105,9: BA 69/VITI2, p.701). With an edict made public in Carthage in the year 347, Constans, in effect, reactivated the legislation of 317 (CoNGAR, 732). His most notable intervention was through Pablo and Macario, his commissioners, operanii unitatis (Orraro, 1 10: CSEL 26, p.96), executors of his policy of unity undertaken in Africa (Passio Maximiani et Isaac: PL 8,768B; MarrroYE, 54.655; BrIssoN, 258ff; VoN SODEN, 51, n.30; This edict was in force until Julian abolished the anti-Donatist measures. If this had not been the case, the D. would in no way have been able to return from exile and rebuild himself (compl. no. 36). From Julian to Theodosius, anarchy. Theodosius will restore imperial unity. Another period that the rioters took advantage of to reorganize. In fact, we will have to wait for Honorius for repressive measures as strong as those of 347 to be issued again. Once Julian's rescript was abrogated, without us knowing why, Valentinian 1 and Valens dictated two new constitutions, one on November 9, 368 on defamatory libels. And on February 20, 373, Valentinian I, after the defeat of the Moorish king Firmus, an ally of the Donatists, published another in Trier prohibiting the rebaptismal practice and ordering the dismissal of any bishop who refused to abide by it (CIh XVI 6,1; S. Ac., Ep. 105,9; MONCEAUX, IV 244s; BrissoN, 262). On April 23, 376, Gratian confiscated all the meeting places of heretics and threatened with penalties anyone who facilitated or tolerated such assemblies. A new edict of his on October 17, 377 came to confirm or aggravate, as the case may be, the preceding laws (CTh XVI 6,2; on the date indicated, cf. MARTROYE, 89 - which seems unacceptable to him; BrIssoN, 263; the edict is addressed to Flavian, vicar of Africa: S. AG., Ep. 87,8; PAC 1,462s, n.4s; CONGAR, 732).

3) From 391 to 400. It is the time of Emperor Theodosius (379-395). In 376 the Donatists had intrigued until they had his father executed in Carthage (compl. no. 35). Among its abundant antiheretical legislation, that of August 3, 379, stands out, in which it outlawed all heresies, prohibiting schismatics from spreading their rebaptismal practice as well as holding assemblies. And that of February 27, 380, which ordered all subjects to profess the Catholic faith. And that of January 19, 386, threatening with capital punishment those who disturbed the peace of the Church. And that of June 16, 388, prohibiting, also under penalty of death, discussing religion in public. Both laws, dated November 26, 389, one and May 19, 391, prohibited the meetings of heretics, although without yet reaching the point that their schism was assimilated to heresy, an important circumstance that would come with Honorius on February 12, 405 (compl. no. 43). The most severe of the Theodosian laws corresponds to June 15, 392, when it punished heretical clerics and anyone who had facilitated illicit assemblies with a fine of ten pounds of gold (CTh XVI 5,21). Saint Augustine refers to it repeatedly (Ep. 88,7: Crispín case - compl. n. 12 - 185,26; C. Cr. III 47,51). Catholics rarely demanded its application: in 395, when

On July 18, 392, Theodosius threatened anyone who disturbed the Catholic Church with deportation. On April 15, 394, he forbade heretics from ordaining bishops. On July 9 of the same year, all heretical meetings, ordinations and propaganda. On March 30, 395, Honorius and Arcadius confirm those of their father, who died two months earlier, and continue legislating. This was the situation when Augustine began his reply to Parmenian. [38] Optato Gildonieno—Optato of Thamugadi, in Numidia, today Timgad, a city 20 km from Lambesa, in Algeria, is one of the most famous bishops of the D., whose biography we know thanks to Augustinian documents, some of prosopographical interest. For a dozen years (388-398) his episcopacy was closely linked to Gildon. Hence the nickname Gildonian or Gildonian. The adjectives that this "mitrated barbarian" received from Saint Augustine are extremely revealing: unjust, thief, blackmailer of other people's property, oppressor of orphans and widows, breaker of families, murderer, tyrant, criminal, traitor and serpent (C. Ep. Parm. YI 15,34; C. litt. Pet. 11 101,232; 103,237; C. Cr. TIT 13,16; Monckaux, IV 65.120; With the help of the Circumceliones, he fueled the Gildonian rebellion (compl. n. 2 and 11). The Numidian Catholic bishops tried to complain in 395 before the vicar of Africa, Serano, demanding that the fine of ten pounds of gold prescribed by the Theodosian law of 392 be applied, but he did not even deign to appear (PAC 1,1060s).

For ten years he "reigned" in southern Numidia with terror and brigandage, having Gildon's troops on his side. The splendid Tamugadi Cathedral was built. His prestige in the region was great. The accusation that he was the one who had destroyed Maximian's basilica is denied by Cresconius, who attributes the fact to a popular movement (C. Cr. IV 46,55; Ep. 44,4,7). By force of "persecution" he imposed the return to the great schismatic Church of numerous Maximianists; Pretextato Asuritano and Feliciano Mustitano were two of the most notable cases, since their return was made public between December 396 and the beginning of 398, on the occasion of the anniversary of Optato, in which Primiano and other bishops of the party were present within the grandiose framework of the cathedral, built—as an inscription read—Haec Inbente / priest Dei Op/tato (PAC 1,800, n.26; C. Cr. TI 59.65;
As a result of his tragic end, like that of Gildon, he achieved the supreme glory of "martyr" among his people. For Augustine of Hippo and the Catholics,

Supplementary notes 899 on the contrary, it represented the most tangible and scandalous proof of schismatic guilt: 1) due to its dark ability when it came to covering up the malice of its actions; 2) for his commitment to the temporal powers—Gildon and the Circumcelions above all—rebellious to the constituted power; 3) for his unworthy moral conduct, completely contrary to the purity and sanctity that the D. claimed for himself; 4) for his ecclesiological behavior, destructive of the theological system of the Schism by continuously disqualifying it from his anti-Maximianist repression and from his conduct as an undesirable minister.

His image, therefore, is less that of a historical figure than that of the exponent of Donatist ambiguity and discredit, the prototype of the ruthless persecutor and the powerful character, practically with the supremacy of command in the party (PAC 1.8005). Perhaps he was not a true revolutionary, as some maintain (TENGSTRÓM, 74-78), but his grandiose violence and his despotic and authoritarian manners spurred the social revolutionary elements within the Donatist Church itself (C. Cr. IV 25,32). His all-embracing power is symbolized by the majestic cathedral and the annexed buildings built for the glory of his name on a dominant hill of present-day Timgad (CourTOIS, 72s)—BibL.: E. [39] The Catholic Church and its admission of the Donatist ministers.—The Hippo council of 393 still seemed not to be concerned by the proselytizing campaign for readmission to the unity. What worried him was the vocational crisis: not all ways of procuring clergy were well regarded, not even that of monastic life, since Honorius had to promulgate a law authorizing it in case of need (CTh XVI 2,32; Breuiar. Hipp. 11 37: Manst 3,924; A. C. DE VEEr, 769). It was then that admitting converted Donatists to the clergy began to be seen as an opportune solution. The difficulty was that the previous councils had prohibited it: "... praecedentibus conciliis statutum est, ne quis donatistarum cum honore suo recipiatur a nobis" (Breuiar. Hipp. 11 37: Mansi 3,924). Nor was it a question of opposing a recent decision, of probable overseas origin, a prudence that would explain, at least in part, the slowness of the project (Cod. Can. Eccl. Afric., can. J6s: MansI 3,763; CRESPIN, 57, n.3). Hippo, therefore, maintained the prohibition, but proposed to introduce two derogations:... exceptis his, quos aut non rebaptizasse constiterit, aut qui cum suis plebibus ad communionem catholicam transire uoluerint» (Brewiar. Hipp. TI 37: Mans13,924). But the thing did not go beyond the project. He did not want to give the matter the force of law without first consulting the overseas Churches (Ib., 924; A. C. DE VEER, 770; CONGAR, 7375). Was it consulted? Did they respond?
One thing is certain: that the project subsisted as such in 401. The council of Carthage, meeting in June of that year, found the same problems and advocated the same solutions. But in September

A letter from Pope Anastasius is read. Tillemont refuses to believe that it was the response given to the consultation made in June (Mémoires, 348). It was certainly not what the Africans expected. In view of which, and after thanking the Pope for his paternal request, the African synods agreed to write again to the other Churches, Rome specifically - Tillemont estimates that this was the only time it was really done -, on this occasion not to ask for enlightenment or obtain approval, but in order to inform the "apostolic see of a decision already taken. The previous overseas rule may remain in force, yes, but the synod considers that every Catholic bishop is authorized to introduce exceptions—that is, to receive Donatist clerics who maintain their clerical dignity—whenever this seems useful to the cause of unity and peace (CCEA, Can. 65 .66.68: Mans1I 3,770-774; TILLEMONT, 348).

The strategic change of the episcopate is evident: above the shortage of clerics - vocational crisis - there is ending the scandal of division - ecclesial unity -. It was time to undertake new initiatives; The council should not remain in promises and words; It was necessary to take advantage of the argument of the internal fragmentation of primianists, maximianists, etc. (compl. no. 27-31). The Council of Carthage, meeting on August 25, 403, going one step further, laid the foundations for a future Catholic-Donatist meeting: each bishop must prepare this event assisted by the magistrates of his locality and put in conversation with his schismatic colleague. The Catholic initiative, however, collides with the anti-Catholic hardening of the Donatists. These are the dark circumcelionic times that the Carthaginian council of June 16, 404 must face, making moderation prevail (CRESPIN, 64-73; compl. n. 14). But the Donatists - Primianus among them -, at first so reluctant and opposed to the project, began to soften as soon as the emperor Honorius promulgated his edict of union on February 12, 405 (compl. no. 43). From 405 onwards, events progressively shifted towards the celebration of the Conference, which finally took place in Carthage during the first days of June 411 (compl. nos. 51 and 54).

There was no small amount that the Catholic side promised before and during that meeting, in which their rivals continued to be stubborn, although the fruits of so much Catholic effort would not take long to arrive (compl. n. 15,52,57 and 58). The massive entry of Donatists into the Catholic Church, with a good part of its clergy, required new measures to be taken in the African dioceses. A provincial council meeting in Byzacena—Telepte or Zella—on February 24, 418 approved the canons of the letter sent to the Africans by Pope Siricius after the council of Rome was held on January 6, 386 (Mater, 66s; MANS1, 3,669-71; 4,379-81). The Can. 8 ordered the reconciliation of Novatians and Montenses (Donatists of Rome) by the laying on of hands. It had, therefore, to do with the reception of Donatists. A no small difficulty had to be overcome: clerics subjected to penitential discipline normally lost their clerical status (CRESPIN, 49-51). The Catholics had promised to welcome the Donatist clerics, respecting their rank (G. c. Em. 9; Epp. 128,2-3; 142; Serm. 358,4). Aware of the difficulty, the Donatists did not fail to present the objection: their clerics had to be spared penance, or the ceremony of laying on of hands, or else not admit them to the clergy (Ep. 185,44). Probably, given the thorny situation, some Catholic bishop decided to omit the ceremony of laying on of hands, which would explain the conciliar decision of 418.

[401 The Augustinian theology of sacramental character.—The term character has in Augustinian literature a semantic richness similar to sacramentum (CoNGAR, 737; COUTURIER, l6lss). Character (sfragís) is a word already present in Saint Paul (2 Cor 1,21s; Eph 1,3) and the Apostolic Fathers (eight times in Hermas, especially for baptism), and among its meanings are those of tattoo, mark, military seal or belonging to the emperor (CONGAR, 738, citing works by Gr. Dix, Dólger and Quasten). Sfragís also designates the mark of recognition and belonging of animals, callednota, or also signum, and the branding iron, called karaktér, or Rautérion. Therefore, Saint Augustine innovates nothing when he talks about the signum or the character or when he invokes the military analogy: soldiers used to be marked on the flesh with an indelible number, printed with red-hot iron; It was, therefore, an example applicable to theology; And if that were not enough, the Pauline vocabulary full of military images even allowed it.

The aforementioned word, then, allows the Saint to expose in a plastic way what happens to truly baptized Christians and what happens to truly ordained ministers. Even so, it is far from having the connotations of later theological language. It does not simply evoke, for example, the permanence of baptism or ordination, a permanence that would result from the consecratio effected by said sacraments; nor does it designate the spiritual imprint that indelibly marks the soul of the baptized or ordained. It indicates, rather, the external form of the sacramental rite, which allows one to be recognized or not as a Christian, depending on whether the sacrament has been administered (better still, conferred or not) with the Christian formula, that is, the invocation of the Trinity. Hiáring has taken care of this, confirming his thesis with august texts.
902 Additional notes

tinians in which character is equivalent to nomen inuocatum (Ad Caes. eccl. 2; C. Cr. 1 35; HARING, 83). Sometimes Augustine uses interchangeably, to mean the same thing, the two expressions: sigmari nomine and signari charactere: «Pasce, bone serue, oues dominicas, habentes dominicum characterem..., ablutas Baptismo eius, signatas nomine eius» (Ser. 295,5: PL 38,1350); «... cum omnes Christiani dicuntur, et qui bene uiuunt, et qui male uiuunt, omnes charactere signantur, omnes ad unum altare accessunt, omnes eodem baptismo abluuntur» (In Ps. 30 TI 3: CC 38, p.214).

The word will later denote a theological reality. In Saint Augustine, on the contrary, it remains closely linked to the images for which it is used, that is, the military character, which allows the emperor to recognize his soldiers (C. Ep. Parm. 11 29; C. litt, Per. 11 247; C. Cr. 1 35; IV 6; Ad Caes. eccl. 2.4; C. Gaud. 1 13; Epp. 88,9; 185,43; or the mark of the flock, by which the master can recognize or find his sheep (De b. VI 1; Epp. 98,5; 105,1; 173,3; 185,23; C. Cr. 1 35; Sermt. 295,5; CRESPIN, 265-67; HaárING: Scholastik 30, p.481-512, with details; NEUNHEUSER: BAC IV/2, p.51). Although Augustine uses character more often, he also uses signum (De b. IV 16; Ad Caes. eccl. 4; Ep. 87,9); signaculum (Serm. 260A=Serm. Denis 8,2); note (From b. 15); and titulus (In Ps. 21 11 31; Concar, 739; CrespIN, 2675). The term character receives rather occasional use in anti-Donatist writings, which does not mean that it is objectively basic when it comes to understanding their baptismal doctrine. In the opinion of Saint Augustine, its essence lies in a consecratio, and a "cult" conmsecreatio. With character, "the neophyte forever receives the form of a member of Christ, is objectively incorporated into the body of Christ and obtains the capacity, the hope and the right to receive divine grace and eternal happiness" (HOFMANN, 3585; NEUNHEUSER: BAC 1V/2, p.52).

Saint Augustine draws two conclusions above all from the word: 1.*, permanence: whether the sheep or the soldier is lost, they remain the sign that they are not lost, hence when the sheep is recovered, or when the soldier returns to the ranks, there is no need to highlight the character; Well, something similar happens with baptism and ordination (De b. 15; C. Cr. IV 6; Ad Caes. eccl. 2; Ep. 185,23); 2.*, the origin: a deserter or a civilian may have already been marked, and the person marked will not cease to belong to the owner of the seal. It matters little to the master who recovers the sheep carrying his character whether the iron was put on it by himself or by a servant; Well, the same thing happens with baptism and order (C. Ep. Parm. 11 29; C. Cr. 135; De b. VI 1; Ep. 98,5; 105-1; CrEsPIN, 268).

The analogy, then, allows Saint Augustine to clarify the situation of the schismatics: separated from the Church, they preserve the mark of Christ, so that when they return it is not necessary for them to be rebaptized. And as for ministers ordained in the Church or in the Schism, they bear the seal that consecrates them to the service of Christ if the name of Christ has been invoked. They can, therefore, confer true sacraments. And even though his ministry does not serve spiritual health because it is exercised outside the Church, it is no less effective in the strictly sacramental realities, which constitute the proper field of the ministry (CRESPIN, 2435). Augustinian theological technique and decisive piece, this one of character, for the elaboration of the sacramental theory that the Bishop of Hippo carried out in the anti-Donatist campaign (CoNnGar, 739).—BiBL.: Y. [411 Pope Miltiades and the Council of Rome of 313.—Milciades (or Melquiades), natione Afer, according to the Liberian Catalog, was probably of Roman origin. Pope from 311 (or 310: Studer) to 314, he put an end to the schism of Heraclius, opposed to Eusebius, who was accused, as was his predecessor Marcellus, of too much severity. Around 313 Constantine sent him a letter in which he ordered him to preside in his name a kind of arbitration commission to put an end to the dispute that had arisen between Donatus and Caecilian. He, emperor, had already summoned on his part, and by virtue of his own authority, the bishops Reticio, of Autún; Materno, from Cologne, and Marín, from Arles, all three chosen in Gaul, in accordance with the Donatist plea of ​​April 15, 313, asking for judges from this country, to which the persecution had not reached, or where at least there was no record of traditors. The letter also announced the sending of the documents transmitted by the Carthaginian proconsul, Anulinus, and the appearance of Caecilian with ten representatives of each party (Eusebius, HE Anulinus also stressed the hostility of the Donatists against Caecilian, materialized in two documents that had been transmitted to him for action. They were, on the one hand, a libellus ecclesiae catholicae criminum Caeciliani traditus a parte Maiorini, sealed for the tranquility of their authors; on the other, a text, this one unsealed, that specialists usually identify with the demand (or Preces) of the party of Donatus at the command of Constantine that the ordination of Caecilian, precisely because it had been contested, be submitted to the arbitration of the Gallic bishops (Eusebius, HE X 5,18-20; PAC 1,81,666). The emperor appointed Miltiades udex datus of this cause, no doubt in view of the traditional prestige of the Roman Church (STuDER, 2250).

Miltiades summoned fifteen bishops from various Italian regions and managed to gather in Rome (Laterano), from October 2 to 4, 313, a council in which ten bishops from each party participated. It was not possible for Donato to sustain the accusations against Ceciliano. And not only that, but he himself was convicted of having rebaptized apostates and of having laid hands on renegades to ordain them as bishops, which violated disciplinary norms. Likewise, their intrigues and agitation were exposed to the people. He therefore turned from accuser to accused. Already absent from the second session, they waited in vain for him to present the evidence he had promised. Once this significant absence was confirmed, and after a double vote, the court declared Ceciliano innocent on October 4, in the last session, and Donato guilty, who was convicted (ConGar, 725; MatER, 265; InsTINSKY, 421; LaMIRANDE, 726).

Saint Augustine takes good care to point out the goodness and wisdom of Miltiades, who censured only Donatus, the author of all evil - he says - and declared himself, on the other hand, willing to send letters of communion even to the bishops ordained by Majorinus (Ep. 43,7,16). However

died on January 10, 314, it is likely that he knew nothing of the appeal filed by the Donatists at the end of 313 and before Constantine or of the investigation opened against Felix of Aptonga (ConGAr, 726; compl. n. 67). The emperor, in any case, seeing that the schismatics did not accept Miltiades' sentence, convened a synod himself, without major concerns about the Pope's collaboration (StuDER, 2250). It was apparently Parmenian who first launched malevolent insinuations against Hosius of Córdoba and Pope Miltiades (C. Ep. Parm. 13,4; 4,7,5,10; compl. n. 4). [42] The semi-Arian council of Serdica.—In the autumn of 343—+Made today by the majority—almost a hundred Western bishops arrived in Serdica, among them Hosius of Córdoba, leader of the group. Serdica—U pia Sardica, later capital of Dacia Ripensis—was part of Thrace, in the eastern Hilyric, and consequently belonged to the emperor Constantius TI. The council met to discuss problems of faith - not the Nicene creed -, regulate the situation of deposed bishops and establish ecclesiastical jurisdiction (BARNARD, 1-8.16; OPELT, 783s; SIMONETTI, 167, n.12). Grato of Carthage, an orthodox representative of an African Church decomposed by the Schism, was among the Westerners, joining them in search of help since the Easterners had tried with not entirely vain schemes to establish contact with the Donatists. Westerners mostly belonged to the Latin linguistic domain and considered themselves representatives of Athanasian orthodoxy (OpeLT, 784ss; FOLLIET, 19655; PINCHERLE, 169ss; SIMONETTI, 168, n.16; PAC 1,545, n.15).

The easterners, about seventy bishops of philo-Arian leanings, were kept waiting. Serdica, today Sofia, although it belonged to the dominions of Constantius II, was a stone's throw from the western lands of Constans, who, with the Western Orthodox, had convened the council. They came willing not to give in and not to let the meeting fail. Since the Westerners insisted that Athanasius, Marcellus and other Easterners deposed by anti-Arians in the East and then rehabilitated at the Council of Rome in 341 had to take part in the work, and the Easterners were roundly opposed, the council failed. The Easterners abandoned Serdica after writing a synodal (letter) excommunicating the most illustrious Westerners and confirming in substance the Antiochene formula of faith of 341. The Westerners then continued their work alone: they again rehabilitated Marcellus, Asclepa of Gaza and Athanasius, approved a series of canons (Hess), and gave their version of the events in another synodal (letter) condemning the leaders of the group that had abandoned (SIMONETTI, 1755; In., 3153).

In the writing sent to Saint Augustine, Cresconio included the heading of a synodal letter from Serdica where the name of Donatus of Carthage appeared, thereby attempting to demonstrate that the Eastern Churches had been in favor of the Donatists and had supported their separation from the traditors (C. Cr. 111 34,38; 71-83; IV 44,52). No

Additional notes 905 was the first time that this document was shown to Saint Augustine. Weeks after his episcopal ordination, and on his way to Cirta Constantina to confer another there in the company of Alypius, he had to stop at Thubursicu Numidarum, today Khamissa, in Algeria, to debate in public with the Donatists of the place, who, well united with their bishop Fortunio, seemed moderate and more willing to dialogue than their coreligionists of Hippo (Ep. 44; Monceaux, IV 275-279; PAC 1,500-503; J.-L. Marer=PerLEr, 208; When Augustine asked him to justify the Donatist break with the rest of the Christian world, oblivious to the African quarrels, Fortunio invoked the acquiescence of the transmarine Church to the Macarian persecution. Insisting that, in that case, he explain at least the attitude of the Schism during the years before Macarius, Fortunio pulled out a volume of letters addressed to the Africans, Donatus especially, by the orientals of the council of Serdica of 343 (Ep. 44,6). Augustine then wanted to find out if this Donatus was the one from Carthage, but since Alypius warned him in those measures of the Arian nature of the document, Fortunio refused to hand over the volume for further examination, and did not even allow the document to be marked with his hand to prevent it from being replaced (Ep. 44,6; PAC 1,501s; A. C. DE VEEr, 8055).

What St. Augustine was intrigued by in the document alleged by Cresconius—the synod of the Philo-Arians of Serdica, no doubt—was not so much that the Arians had tried to win over the Donatists, which seemed plausible to him, but rather that he found in the subscription transmitted by Cresconius the explicit mention of Carthage after the name of Donatus, a detail that did not exist in the text that he himself had consulted (C. Ep. Parm. TIT 34,38). The question now is to know if said synodal letter, as it appears in the Parisian Collectanea anti-Ariana (CSEL 65, p.48-78) is the only one that gives us the complete minutes of the council of the Eusebians of Serdica. Because taking into account Augustine's observations about the minutes and the text that has come down to us, problems of authenticity are detected. The beginning and the end must be attributed—according to A. C. de Veer—to a copyist. Regarding the signature, there are conflicting hypotheses: Feder stated at the time that it would have undergone various touch-ups. Pincherle, in 1925, that it was authentic, but that, after having broken with the Arians, the Donatists judged the document unfavorable and tried to make it disappear or hide it, until someone suppressed the mention of the episcopal sees in the subscription. For Zeiller and Achelis, the corrections are Donatist, without a doubt, and would consist not so much in the deletion of the names of the sees as in the subsequent addition of said names. Zeiller even dares to date these touches, attributing them to the final months of the 19th century. 1v. Brisson has raised serious objections to Zeiller's thesis (214ff). It is worth asking—continues A. C. de Veer—if Augustine could have had the full text of the synodal letter in his hands, since to the Donatists who presumed to have been recognized by Serdica, he usually answers nothing other than: Serdicense concilium arianorum Fuit. A careful reading of the document would have informed him of the celebration of another orthodox council in Serdica, compared to the council of the Philo-Arians (SIMONETTI, 167-177). Faced with the impossibility of going any further, A. [43] The edict of February 12, 405.—On February 12, 405, Honorius, through the general of the Vandals and his minister Stilicho, promulgated the famous edict of union: Edictum de unitate, or lex de unitate, or also lex unitatis (CTh XVI 6,4; MoNcEAux, IV 259; Brisson, 265). It ordered: 1. The reestablishment of unity. 2. The equation of Schism with heresy. 3. Rigorously apply the preceding antiheretical laws to D. 4.? Prohibit inheritances or donations. 5. Do not rebaptize in any way, under penalty of arrest and confiscation of property. 6.” Release slaves who are forcibly rebaptized or taken into the shelter of a Catholic Church. 7. Award the Donatist basilicas to Catholics. 8.2 Confiscate the houses and meeting places of D. 9.” Exile for clerics and bishops who persisted in the Schism. 10. Threaten with serious sanctions those who break or cause such laws to be breached, including governors (CTh XVI 6,44; Cod. Can. Eccl. Afric., Can. 94 ; 99; 117; 119; S. Ac., Epp. 88,5,10; 93,5,16-19; 185,7,26-29; C. Cr. 111 43,47).

The edict is part of the context of the previous legislation and responds in some way to the Circumcelionian-Donatist hardening (compl. n. 37.12.13). Substantially it is a reproduction of the Constantinian provisions of 317 and Constantus in 347, but with the not at all irrelevant addition of homologating for all punitive effects the Schism with heresy: «... Ideoque intercidendam specialiter eam sectam noua constitutione censuimus quae, ne haeresis uocaretur, appellationem schismatis praeferebat. In tantum enim sceleris progressi dicuntur hi quos Donatistas uocant ut baptisma sacrosanctum mysteriis recalcatis fearitate noxia iterarint et homines semel, ut traditum est, munere diuinitatis ablutos contagione profanae repetitionis infecerint. Ita contigit ut haeresis ex schismate nasceretur» (CTh XVI 6,4: ed. MommsSen, p.881; CRESPIN, 73).

With the aforementioned approval, the edict put an end to a relative imperial clemency. The edict was confirmed on March 5 of the same year: edictum quod de unitate per Afros regions clementia nostra dixerit (CTh XVI 11,2). The Bishop of Hippo specifies that this edict, compared to the previous legislation, aims not to rectify the error of the Donatists, but rather to eliminate the D. itself from the roots (Epp. 185. 7.28). This time the terms used could not help but remind the schismatics of the damned dates of Constantus's edict of unity in 347 and the infamous repression of Paul and Macarius.

[44] Donatus the Great.—Original of Casae Nigrae, a Numidian city a hundred kilometers south of Thebesa, Donatist bishop from 315 to 355, inspirer, eponym of the party, head and guide of the Church of the Martyrs in North Africa, Donatus was born around 270. When the schism officially occurred with the election of Majorinus, he was already bishop of Casae Nigrae, and as such He participated in the Council of Carthage in 312. He succeeded Majorinus, who died on a date impossible to specify - perhaps in the middle of 312 - and as a rival of Caecilian he went to the Council of Rome in 313, where he was condemned (PAC 1,6665; compl. n. 41). Although in the succession of Mensurio, which ends up falling on Ceciliano, he is already seen as coordinator of the opposition, it is only after the death of Ceciliano's main rival and Lucilla's chaplain, the aforementioned Mayorino, that he assumes the leadership of the party (Gesta apud Zenopbilum=0OPTATO, app. I: CSEL 26, p.185). His identification, in no way his great personality, may be discussed. He served as a true primate thanks to his dominant genius, his powerful oratory and his organizational skills. Hence the adjective Great (FREND, 153s, 1655; CONGAR, 14).

Two Donatos? Just one? There are many African people with this name (Mar, 293-96). The question of identifying or distinguishing Donatus of Casae Nigrae and Donatus of Carthage or Donatus the Great has been raised many times (ConGAR, 14s; LAMIRANDE, 727; GRASMÚCK, 41, n.155; ALEXANDER, 540ss; PAC 1, 2925). What makes the underlying problem insoluble is that tradition is contradictory. From the outset, the documents from the 1st century apparently imply the unity of character, while those from the fifth century present variants. But the thing is not that simple. Augustine himself, for example, believes at first that it is only one, but then seems to rectify it (Ep. 185,10,47; C. Chr. 11 1,2; 2,3: he distinguishes without ruling on the matter; De bhaer. 69,2: he points out that many attribute the origin of the word Donatist to the successor of Majorinus rather than to Donatus "arrived from Numidia"). Contrary to those who had been maintaining that Saint Augustine admits in Brew. 111 18.36 for the first time, as a hypothesis, the splitting of the pro-

908 Complementary notes fought by the Donatists in the Conference of 411 (Retract. 1 20 [21]; De haer, 69; Breu. 111 12,24; 17,31; PAC 1,292), A. C. de Veer assures that he does so before in Contra Cresconium, although without opposing any difficulty to the distinction, which would indicate that the thing by then was no longer new for him, favorable long ago due to identification, as Optato. It is in any case, in C. Cr. II 1,2; 2,3, where we have the first Augustinian testimony of the splitting of the character, apparently an invention of the Donatists to benefit their cause (A. C. DE VEer, 758; Marer, 296). Augustine believed for a time that Donatus's personal schism predated the Schism of 312, and that he, Donatus, had been the cause of all the evil (Ep. 43,5,16; LAMIRANDE, 727). The Casae Nigrae thing would have only been a split introduced by the Donatists, who were interested in it, and therefore suspicious. Nowhere is it clearly stated that Donatus had been bishop of this Numidian locality. It would be enough to recognize it as originating from her (ConGar, 14s; BARDY, 1175). Augustine certainly did not seem to attach much importance to the matter. He was more interested, of course, in not linking the cause of the Church with that of Ceciliano, nor that of Donato with the D. (compl. no. 65).

It is very likely that as a result of his conviction in Rome, Donatus returned to Africa, where protests against the Roman decision that he sought to instigate spread (PAC 1,296, n.41). His name appears in the conciliar documents of Arles, whose sentence he appealed. Although no secure document allows us to know precisely his activity between 316 and 321, it is clear that he spared no effort to consolidate his cause in North Africa (Opraro, 1 25; III 1; PAC 1,298; DPAC 1 1029). His prestige was enormous. Like Saint Cyprian before, he too now united the priestly and prophetic functions. People swore "by their white hair" (In Ps. 10,5; In lo. 13,17; Oprato, UI 1). Known as Donatus of Carthage (OpTATO, IU 3), and also, at the end of his days, as "the man who had purified the Church of Carthage from error" (C. Cr. 111 52,62).

In 336, he managed to remove the prefect of Africa, Gregory, and bring together the Carthaginian council of the two hundred and seventy bishops in which he was flexible with the Mauritanians, authorizing exceptions to the rebaptizing rule, which represented for Optatus, Augustine and Tyconius himself an irrefutable anti-Donatist argument (compl. no. 30). The Eusebian synodal of Serdica also includes his name, which forces us to wonder if in his lost De Trinitate, or in De Spiritu sancto, he offered an orthodox Trinitarian doctrine voluntarily disfigured by some disciples, or perhaps partially heterodox, but, in certain points, practically ignored by his own - possibilities advanced by Augustine (De haer. 69,2) - or even, as Saint Jerome writes, a "convergent" doctrine with the Arian dogma» (De uir. ill. 93; cf. S. Ac., C. Cr. III 34,38; IV 44,52; Ep. 44,3,6; compl. n. 42). Of more weight than these hypotheses are the accusations of Tyconius attributing baptismal theses that are not very Donatist when he supported the conciliar decision of 336 (PAC 1,300).

With Caecilian now out of the scene, Donatus requests from Constans, in 346, that he be recognized as the sole bishop of Carthage (OpTaATo, III 1). The emperor decides to act and sends Paul and Macarius to inspect the situation. Once in Carthage, it does not take them long to understand what is happening and they support the rival of the cause, Gratus. The sullen and harsh response that the leader gives to the commissioners when they come to him: Quid est imperatori cum ecclesia? (Oprato, III 3), was the trigger for the terrible repression

[46] Segundo of Tigisi and Silvanus of Cirta.—Bishop of Tigisi, current Ain el Bordj, in Algeria, Segundo presides as primate of Numidia over the improperly called "council of Cirta" and officially the first Donatist council, which convened in Carthage (311/312) seventy Numidian bishops to thwart the election and ordination of Caecilian as successor of Mensurio, recently deceased (compl. no. 1). In the correspondence that Mensurius exchanged with him following the persecution of Diocletian, he denied to Segundo that he had been a traditor on May 19, 303; «Christianus sum et episcopus, non traditor» (Brew, 111 13,25; C. Gaud. 1 37,47). In the context of this phrase he also alleged that what had been handed over had not been Scripture, but rather other books, which seemed to more than one person like a half-confession of guilt. Segundo responded by telling him what had happened in Numidia, a sign that communion still reigned between them (compl. no. 71).

His readiness to respond to the call of Caecilian's Carthaginian adversaries responds to the fact that he considers the time of that correspondence with Mensurius past and, therefore, the possible difficulties and suspicions that its memory could arouse. And this is how S. de T. finally supports with its authority and the presence of Numidian bishops a series of acts concerning the condemnation of Caecilian. So he not only pardoned convicted traditors in Cirta after not

Additional Notes 911 not only managed to prove his own innocence, but he, precisely, had an absentee—Cecilianus—convicted for an unproven accusation, and consequently elected another in his position, thereby officially giving rise to the Donatist split, as Saint Augustine often states (C. Gaud. 1 37,47; C. Ep. Parm. 13,5; Epp. 43,2-9; 53,2,4). The Donatists themselves used to consider the ordination of Mayorinus conferred by S. de T. as the official moment, so to speak, of the birth of the Schism (Gesta apud Zenophilum: CSEL 26, p.185.189; Dr BERARDINO, 3141).

Silvanus was only subdeacon of Cirta on May 19, 303, when Munatius Felix, flamen perpetuus, curator colony Cirtensium, broke into the house where Christians met with Bishop Paul to execute Diocletian's edict that ordered the requisitioning of the property of the Church and the Scriptures. Between 304/305 (Lancel prefers the spring of 307), S. is elected bishop to succeed Paul, an election that, according to references made some years later by eyewitnesses, was eventful and tumultuous (PAC 1,1078). Indeed, in the year 320 Domitius Zenophilus, governor of Numidia, presided over an investigation in Tamugadi into Silvanus of Cirta, whom his deacon Nundinario accused of having handed over the Holy Books and some Church property during the investigation of 303. The occasion was unbeatable for the Catholics to accuse their adversaries the Donatists of being the traditors and not the Catholics. To confuse Silvanus and his main witness, the grammarian Victor, former reader of the Church of Cirta (PAC 1,1152), the verbal process stenographed on May 19, 303 by order of Munacio Félix (PAC 1,408) was read, a long and precise text, in which the confiscated objects are inventoried in detail, which is why Monceaux went so far as to write that the community of Cirta, as of Diocletian is concerned, it is better known to us than any other community in the Christian world (MoNcEaUx, TIL 95; LerELLEY, Il 391s).

And this is also why on December 8, 320, said records were adduced as evidence in the summary opened by Zenófilo, in turn titled Gesta apud Zenopbilum. The same did not happen in the trial of Félix de Aptonga, since it was impossible to find the documents in the archive. It is true that the archivist (tabularius) of Aptonga had already died (Acta purgationis Felicis: CSEL 26, p.197s). And also that in an important city like Cirta Constantina the archive service worked better than in a small one like Aptonga (LkPELLEY, 11 391-93; compl. n. 67). The Gesta apud Zenophilum consularem were filed with other documents used by Catholics to prove their case. This is what is called the dossier of Donatism (OrTaro, app. CSEL 26, p.185-197; cf. its analysis in MONCEAUX, III 93-96; IV 229-33; LereLtey, 11 391).—BiBL.: A. [48] The Patriarchs and the four categories of baptized according to Saint Augustine.—Saint Augustine resorts to the allegorical interpretation of the union of the Patriarchs with their wives and their servants in De b. 1 10.14 and 1 15.23. To the Donatist dilemma "utrum generet filios baptismus Christi in parte Donati an non generet" (De b. 1 10,13: CSEL 51, p.158) Augustine responds by specifying that there is only one Church, the only one, called Catholic. It does not engender separation from it, but rather what of it is preserved in separation. And they do not belong to it, in short, neither those who are separated by schisms nor those who, "corporally mixed in their unity, are separated by a detestable way", because it is charity that makes one belong fully and fruitfully to the Church (compl. n. 47). She is the one who, now in her womb, now in that of her slaves, engenders children: "ergo ipsa generat et per uterum suum et per uteros ancillarum ex eisdem sacramentis tamquam ex uiri sui semine" (De b. 1 10,14, p.160; 1 15,23).

The path to this interpretation had been opened by Saint Paul in Gal 4:22-31, when he discovered in Hagar and her son the symbols of the Old Testament (Old Covenant), and in Isaac and Sarah, those of the New (KeEppLE and LAMIRANDE; SIMONETTI, Profilo storico, 18.70.75). Augustine, then, discovers in the history of the Patriarchs an illustration of his doctrine (A.-M. La BONNARDIERE, 28855), since it is always Christ, the only spouse of the Church, who generates Christians through baptism. Now: this mystery acts either for the legitimate wife (the Catholic), or for her slaves, or dissident communities (De b. 1 10,14). And there is more: among the children conceived in the first or second way, some recognize the authentic Church and live by grace (good Catholics and dissidents who convert); and others, on the contrary, persist within the schism or live reprobates in the Catholic Church. Saint Augustine distinguishes, thus, four categories of baptized:

1* Those baptized by the Catholic Church and faithful to their faith. They have as symbols Isaac and Jacob, authentic believers, born to Sara and Rebekah, legitimate wives. 2.* Those baptized by dissidents, but converted to Catholicism, and whose symbols are the children of Jacob conceived by the servants Leah and Rachel (for example, Asher). In De b. 1 10,14 Augustine does not yet clearly distinguish this second category from the first (cf. on Leah and Rachel, Serm. 137,6; BorGomeE0, 78ff). 3. Those baptized by the Catholic Church, but unfaithful to divine law.

Symbol? Esau, born of Rebekah, Isaac's legitimate wife: "There are evil ones in the Church who belong to Esau, for they are children of Rebekah, children of the Mother Church, born from her womb, hirsute, persevering in their carnal sins, but born from her womb" (Ser. 4,31: BAC 53/VIL, p.78; cf. on Esau, symbol of the carnal man, SIMONETTI, Sulla esegetic technique, 198ff; BOrRGOMEO, 283). 4.* Those baptized in the schism and persevering in it. Your symbol? Ishmael, born to Hagar, Abraham's servant (PonTET, 351).

If the servants can have children, it is because the same wife, the Catholic, acts in them. Saint Augustine believes he sees this corroborated by the fact that the slaves did not join the Patriarchs without the will of their legitimate wives (Gen 16,2; 30,3.9). Sara, in fact, conceived Ishmael, but Hagar consented: "Sara quidem sed per Hagar" (De b. 1 16,25, p.169; 1 15,23). As time went by, Augustine

In this way, sinful Catholic ministers are also symbolized by the servants. The Bishop of Hippo, finally, returns to this allegorical interpretation in Ad Caes. eccl. 5 (Bavaun, 588).—BrBL.: G. [491 Saint Cyprian and rebaptism.—Regarding the rebaptismal question, Saint Augustine came to believe that after Agrippin the entire African Church had returned to the universal tradition. Did the Church perish, he asks, for not rebaptizing the heretics under Cyprian? (From b. 11 2,3; 11 6,8; 7,11). There are four points in his response, especially interesting 1." and 4." It comes to saying in the 1.%: We remain secure in that Church whose universality practices today what it already practiced before Agrippin. And in 4.: By stating that they imitate Cyprian, the Donatists do not know how to answer about the baptism of the Maximianists. Furthermore, Saint Cyprian - he adds - did not rebaptize apostates who returned to the Church, nor was his practice new, since the thing had already come from Agrippinus (111 12,17). On the other hand, if this custom had continued from Agrippinus to Cyprian, what reason would Cyprian have had to continue calling synods on the matter?

The truth is that he summoned them to reaffirm the rebaptizing practice. Here Augustine seems to resist wanting to understand, even proposing an exegesis that is notoriously strange to the thought of Saint Cyprian, who would have wanted to tell Jubayan - according to Augustine - that the dissidents rebaptized in the time of Agrippinus were neither disturbed nor was any threat of excommunication launched against them (S. Cip., Ep. 73,3). The Augustinian strangeness surrounding said Cyprian text never ceases to surprise, since the African rebaptismal practice was maintained without interruption from Agrippinus to Saint Cyprian (SAXER, 106; MAIER, 253). Thirty years is not such a great chronological distance that Cyprian was wrong when he wrote: "from then until today, so many thousands of heretics in our provinces who have converted to the Church have not disdained or put an obstacle in their way; rather, according to reason and with good will, they embraced receiving the grace of the bath of life and the baptism of salvation” (Ep. 73,3: BA 241, p.675).

It is likely that, given the influence of Rome, some Mauritanian bishops questioned the legitimacy of this rebaptism, which would explain Jubaiano's concerns. But Augustine, in De b. 111 12, 17, does not take this Roman influence into account. If the African bishops

Complementary notes 915 controversy about this custom was because the Pope had based his doctrine on tradition (n. compl. 7.10). The Bishop of Hippo forgets this capital fact when imagining that such bishops, before Cyprian intervened, were not in the habit of rebaptizing heretics, and that to justify the new attitude, arrived by Cyprian, they resorted to the demands of the truth recognized by reason. Augustine also declares that the Cyprianist attitude in the councils proves that the custom of rebaptizing converted dissidents had been abandoned in Africa, a very weak explanation indeed, since the threats of Pope Stephen constituted more than sufficient reasons for the holy bishop of Carthage to convene synods in order to strengthen and consolidate his position against Rome (LANGA, 7528).

It may be that the holy memory of the martyred bishop inclined Saint Augustine to be lenient with him to the point of resisting admitting the reality of the facts. The Augustinian crossroads in De baptismo, as far as the authority of Saint Cyprian is concerned, consisted in having to adopt a difficult and to a certain extent contradictory strategy as he had no choice but to move between refutation and apology. Certainly, the tranquility with which he analyzes, discusses and develops when evoking the theme of ecclesial unity in Saint Cyprian becomes evasive, compromising and ultimately condemning in the matter of rebaptization, which is precisely the basis of support for the sacramental theology of the Donatists (BrISSON, passim; BAVAUD, 5975).—BIBL.: G.
