[50] "Tu es Petrus" (Peter, symbol of unity) in Saint Cyprian and Saint Augustine.—Saint Cyprian evokes in his Ep. 73 Tu is Petrus to prove that the baptism of dissidents does not forgive sins (Ep. 73,7,1: CSEL 3/2, p.783). The same thing happens in De unit. Eccl. 4 (CSEL 3/1, p.212): Peter was the first to receive the episcopacy because in it Christ wanted to symbolize the unity of ecclesiastical power. But the apostles all later received the same power as Peter. His successors, equal in dignity, the bishops form, according to the thought of Christ, a single body animated by the Holy Spirit. Any bishop who breaks communion with the Catholic Church therefore loses the power to forgive sins (MoncELLI, 104-201; Bavaun, 605). The Christian must remain in it, because there is only one Church, the one built on Peter. The Lord says to Saint Peter: "I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church..." (Mt 16,18; K. Anam). And while it is true that he grants all the apostles equal power after his resurrection, it is also true, however, that to manifest unity he established a cathedra, and with his authority he ordered that the origin of this unity began with one (De unit. Eccl. 4.5; QuAsTEN, 645). From the aforementioned De unit. Eccl. 4 there are two editions. The general opinion holds

The oldest is the one in which he expresses himself in favor of the primacy of Rome. As for the other, there are already conflicting opinions, although there is a tendency to assume that it would be a recomposition of Cyprian himself at the time of the baptismal controversy, when confronting Stephen (SAXER, 679; compl. n. 7 and 49).
We have abundant bibliography about the patristic and Augustinian exegesis of Tu es Petrus (Loos; SiEBEN; ConGar; La Bon-
916 Additional notes

NARDIERE). The Augustinian reveals that the same regula fidet is heard, according to the Bishop of Hippo, in the Petri Sees, "over which the primacy of the apostolic chair was always in force" (Ep. 43,7). The Saint goes to this chair either to recognize "with greater certainty and healthy usefulness" to the true Church (Ep. 53,2), or to authoritatively resolve doctrinal questions (Serm. 131,10: causa finita est; YRAPE, 57-75; Io.: BAC 422, p.533). Clearly dependent on Optatus of Milevi, Augustine uses in the Psalmus an exegesis summarized in the maxim Petrus a Petra, according to which Petra designates Christ and Petrus the Christian people or the Church considered in its unity.

Starting in 400, Augustine begins to develop a theology that makes Peter the type of unity present in the saints through charity, and whose ecclesiological subject of power is the keys (cf. texts in CONGAR, 717). Confronting the Donatists, who insisted with Saint Cyprian that the bishops were the subject of the power of the keys, Saint Augustine reiterates that the bishops and priests are only ministers, and that the subject is the same unity of the Church built on the stone, that is, truly Christian. He has no problem in adopting the Cyprianist idea of ​​Tu es Petrus (Peter, symbol of unity), but with a meaning that is not directly hierarchical, as was the case in San Cipriano, because the Donatist controversy leads him to place in his ecclesiology very close to the dissident bishop and the sinning bishop: both of them outside the Dove.

The novelty of the Augustinian exegesis of Tu es Petrus lies in the fact that Peter ceases to be the symbol of the episcopate, in the style of Cyprian, to become a type of the true believer, who, in the image of Peter, professes the divinity of Jesus. The stone on which the Church is built is no longer, according to this interpretation, the person of Peter, but Christ: «If Christ is the stone, Peter is the Christian people. Stone is the main name; That is why Peter comes from a stone, not a stone from Peter, just as Christ does not come from a Christian, but the Christian is called that way because of Christ" (Serrz. 76,1; BAC 441/X, p.392; Serm. 76,2. On the interpretations Stone = Peter and Stone = Christ - which in Saint Augustine are neither successive nor exclusive -, cf. P. DÉ Lurs, 884). He advocates against the Donatists, in short, that the power of the keys is not, as was the case in Cyprian, the community of bishops, but that of the saints, so that God forgives sins through the prayers of the Dove (BAvaun, 606.600).—BIBL.: K. [51] Imperial edict convening the Carthage Conference of 411.—On October 14, 410, the emperor Honorius sent a long document from Ravenna to the tribune and notary of Africa, Flavius Marcellinus (cf. Inter imperii: CTh XVI 11,3; Manst 4,535; J.-L. Mater,

Additional notes 917 278, n.3). First by the mandates, whose text has been lost; then by a praeceptio of Honorius, dated in Ravenna on October 14, 410 and specified by imperiale praeceptum circumstantiated by the same date, Marcellinus received an exceptional delegation of power that made him a lunatic principis iud(ex) with the task of convening in Carthage a conference of Catholic and Donatist bishops destined to "confuse the heresy at the end of the debates" (Gesta 14-5; S. AG., Breu. 11; Such a document appears in the minutes under different names: lex, constitutio, exdictum, principalis sanctio, imperiale praeceptum, rescriptum (=rescriptum imperatoris: Breu. 11), pragmaticum rescriptum. Even that of oraculum (Gesta 1 146; 1II 140; LanceL, 23.26.30). The literary piece constitutes one of the oldest known testimonies of this type of legal documentation, and bears the signature of Honorio with a few words of friendly greeting to Marcellin: "Okay, Marceline, carissime nobis", a novel factor mainly due to adding them at the end (Gesta 14; TII 29; LanceL 26, n.2; LAMIRANDE, 32, n.7).

This imperiale praeceptum opened a long exordium on the religious concerns of the emperor, his policy with the Donatists and, to top it off, a stern appeal to the law of August 25, 410. Next, the object itself: it had seemed good to the emperor, having listened to the Catholic suggestion, to call with his authority a contradictory conference between Catholics and Donatists within a period of four months, after which, and also after the three summons had passed, each With an interval of twenty days, the limit time for the contumacious attitude, the Donatists would be condemned by default. They wanted to see in this measure the first hint of imperial partiality. Lancel affirms that the mere mention of the Donatists is clumsy from a psychological point of view. From the legal point of view, however, it seems that the imperial chancellery wanted to refer rather to the procedure of litis denuntiatio (LANCEL, 28,678).

The emperor delegated his powers to Marcellinus, assuring him of his trust. At the end of his mission, he had to enforce the provisions that were decreed against the D. (Gesta 14; FrEND, 274; MonCEAUX, IV 392; CreEsPIN, 80). Lancel believes that we are not dealing with conservative measures, since the subsection "novella subreptione submota" must be understood with a sense of the future, that is, of the definitive condemnation of the Schism that Honorius already seems to take for granted, and which he anticipates. And although it is true that Marcellinus behaved during the first months in a liberal manner and little in accordance with the spirit of this document (note that he ordered the basilicas to be returned to the Donatists in exchange for them going to Carthage: Gesta III, principle; LANCEL, 28, n.2; compl. n. 54) this would not have been possible if the aforementioned phrase meant, as has been claimed, that Honorius wanted all the provisions to be fully respected until the day of the Conference. Regarding Marcelino, he left it beyond doubt that for the performance of his mission he could have access to African administrative services, as well as the obligation to notify any hint of infraction in this regard and, of course, the final result of his mission.

The text is clearly biased. It is denounced by phrases such as "the vain error and the sterile schism" and words such as superstitio and surreptio, or the understanding settled in advance of "the entire truth of the Catholic religion" (Gesta 14); or, finally, the anti-donatist phrase "ut... habitis disputationibus, superstitionem ratio manifesta confutet" (Gesta 14), which
918 Additional notes

Marcellinus adopted it in his edict of January 19, 411 (Gesta 15; TI 45.86.90-94; LanceL, 29). It is possible that Marcellin regretted having to divulge in advance a text as partial as it was cynical (Gesta 14-5; LancEL, 30). In any case, he did it, and the Donatists were soon able to learn what was coming to them. Regarding partiality—“brutal partiality,” Lancel describes—Monceaux, Crespin, Lancel and Lamirande agree. Lancel, furthermore, considers it impossible that Marcellin kept the document secret in view of such partiality (LanceL, 30; LAMIRANDE: BA 32, p.33; MONCEAUX, IV 393; CrespIN, 81).—BrbL.: S. LanckL, Actes de la Conférence de Carthage in 411: SCh 194/1, 25-31; J.-L. Marer=PERLER, Les voyages...278. Cf. the bibl. of the n. compl. 16.

[52] The question of the "lapsus temporis."—On May 18, 411, the Donatist episcopate ostentatiously entered Carthage, no doubt to give an impression of strength in the face of the debates that were to come. They immediately drew up a record of the date, an unmistakable sign that they were determined to make use of even the lapsus temporis or the famous praescriptio de tempore: "Congregantur ex uniuersa Africa tot episcopi, ingrediuntur Carthaginem cum tanta speciosi agminis pompa, ut tam magnae ciuitatis oculos in se intentionemque convertant" (4d Donat. p. coll. 25,43: CSEL 53, p.144;

The Conference had to be opened within a period of four months from October 14, 410. This was what was established in the imperial edict (Gesta 14). But the edict of convocation was not made public by Marcellinus until January 19, 411 (Gesta 15; Breu. 12.8). On the other hand, it must be taken into account that if the delay period expired on June 1, it was that day when the debates really began (Gesta 15). The case would not have had greater importance if it had gone unnoticed or silenced at the Conference. But it wasn't like that. The Donatists used the famous lapsus temporis again and again as a compelling legal argument. Was there negligence on Marcelino? Were there other causes? It will have to be assumed either that Marcellinus obtained another delaying period from the emperor, or that the imperial rescript must be interpreted counting the four months from the imperial notification. And yet, another difficulty persists: calculating the four-month moratorium from January 19, 411—a reason given by the Donatists (Breu. 18.9.11; 11 2; TIT 5,6)—its term would have to end on May 19 and not June 1 (Brew. 11 3). Perhaps Marcellin calculated the legal period not from the day the edict was signed, but from the date of its promulgation (February 1). Because he believes himself authorized—and he makes it known—to extend the planned period by two months (Brew. 18; MONCcEAUX, IV 394s; LAMIRANDE, 34).

The issue of lapsus temporis consisted of enforcing the prescription of the working time for the legally valid celebration of the Conference, a prescription originated by a lapse of working time: once the Catholics had not arrived in Carthage to intervene in the Conference on the date on which they had done so, that is, May 18, the Donatists tried by all means to appeal to the right of prescription, demonstrating that the deadline had expired, and as it turned out that the Catholics had not appeared within the time useful, had provoked the legal figure of lapsus temporis. Once this was demonstrated, it would also be clear that the Catholics had lost the process beforehand (LAMIRANDE, 33; LaAncEL, 74-83). Regarding the legal cursus temporum of four months (KipPp, 224-26,239), it presents a

Additional notes 919 analogue in the rescript of Honorius that Steinwenter has been able to highlight based on CTh 11 4.5 (STEINWENTER, 131).—BIBL.: Tn. Kipr, Die Litisdenuntiation als Prozesseinleitungsform in rómischen Civilprozess, 1887; E. LAMIRANDE: BA 32, p.33-35; S. LANCEL, Actes de la Conférence...: SCh 194/1, 74-83; P. Monceaux, IV 3905; A. STEINWENTER, Line kirchliche Quelle des nachklassischen Zivilprozesses. Acta Congressus Iuridici Internationalis, vol. 11 (Rome 1935) p.125-144,

[53] The "gesta municipalia".—In the convocation edict with which he began to put into practice the mission that Honorius had entrusted to him, Marcellin ordered the municipal magistrates vested with authority to officially notify the bishops of the convocation in the form of a verbal process, and to then send him a detailed list of the responses (compl. n. 54, 51 and 21). Marcellin left without force, as of the date of the edict, all the repressive laws previously issued against the D., so that his envoys began to travel the African routes within an atmosphere of truce. These officials came either from the central services or from the African offices, and they made up the personnel placed especially at the service of Marcellin for the better development of his mission. As for the formulas used and their sending to the provinces, it must have preceded the promulgation of the edict somewhat, perhaps so that the documents were notified simultaneously in the main African towns and in Carthage (LANCEL, 33).

The task seemed enormous to be carried out in the not excessive four-month moratorium. The number of municipal records (gesta municipalia) and reports (relationes) that were sent to Carthage thanks to the diligence of the postal services duly assisted by itinerant officials at the disposal of the imperial commissioner can be estimated at several hundred - about eight hundred, if we look at the same records (LANCEL, 33,118s) -. Of such documents—which have not reached us—we only know indirectly what is known as Primiani professio, that is, Primianus' response to the magistrates, to which both Augustine and Possidius allude (Brew. 11 3; Posinius, VA 16; Gesta TI 206; II 50). It is strange that Marcellin did not use these reports either in his edict of the Conference regulations, or for the reading of the signatures of both parties during the first session. The strangeness is greater if one takes into account that such reports, if he had used them, would have allowed him to settle a good number of disputes that arose in the course of the debates. They would have provided him, for example, with interesting details about the real strength of each party; data to clarify the confusion of two possible Ausuaga or Auzaga and similar (Gesta 1 177-180; Mater, 107; PAC 1,921, n.1; LaNcEL, 34, n.1). According to Alypius, one hundred and twenty Catholic bishops were absent due to illness, age or other reasons; and for similar reasons, a greater number of Donatists. Marcelino limited himself to Jevantar minutes. The aforementioned documents, however, provided him with the means to investigate such allegations. It is seen, therefore, that he ignored the problem of number. Or that it did not fit into his instructions (Gesta 1 166.217; Breu. 1 14).—BiBL.: S. LANCEL: SCh 194/1, p.31-34. Cf. the bibl. of the n. compl. 21.

[54] Marcellinus' edict of convocation.—On January 19, 411, undoubtedly hours after having arrived in African lands, Marcellinus had an edict posted in Carthage and spread throughout Africa in which he announced that the emperor Honorius, eager to reestablish the
920 Additional notes

unity of faith, and having heard the opinion of the Catholic episcopal delegation in Ravenna, he had arranged to convene the joint Conference demanded by both parties. After establishing June 1 as the opening date in Carthage, Marcellin ordered curatores, magistrates, curials, procurators and notables (seniores locorum) to notify the bishops of the imperial resolution and to promptly take the appropriate steps in order to send him the answers given in the summaries as soon as possible (Gesta 1 15; 1 27: pointing out that the fourth month had expired on May 19; Breuw. 12; PAC 1,672; It also ordered that the basilicas and property confiscated on February 12, 405 be returned to the Donatist bishops, once the Conference procedure was accepted by them (compl. no. 43). The system of mobilization of the municipal authorities with the verbal process and its subsequent and prompt referral to the commissioner had already been provided for in the forma conuentionis donatistarum of 403, although then only at the initiative of the Catholics and without the call having the same imperative character as now (Cod. Can. Eccl. Afr. c.92: Manst 3,791-794).

Given his personality, and perhaps out of courtesy, without discarding prudence either, Marcellin proposed to the schismatic bishops to elect a judge (iudex) of similar or superior rank to their own to sit with him in the audience (Gesta 15; LAMIRANDE, 48s; LANCEL, 32). It is unlikely that Marcellin would make such concessions - including the suspension of all anti-Donatist measures in force until then - which implied close collaboration with the proconsul and vicar of Africa, without the at least tacit agreement of the emperor (LANCEL, 32, n.4). Note that Marcellin goes so far as to guarantee the Donatists the possibility of filing lawsuits if they are disturbed during the preparations for the Conference; and even promises them immunity from any ongoing legal action.

Contrast this edict, without a doubt, with that of Honorius. Marcellin not only silences anything that could horrify the schismatics, but he even tries to win them over with substantial concessions. The suspension of the edict of February 12, 405 and the spirit of this same document are factors that, in Monceaux's opinion (IV 397), favor the good image of Judge Marcellinus: his clairvoyance, his loyalty, his moderation and his political disposition, excellent skills, in a word, that reveal how unfair the Donatists were to him by giving him a tragic end (LAMIRANDE, 49; compl. n. 16). In fact, Primianus had no other option than to obey and go to the Conference, but not before sending his colleagues a circular (tractoria) pressuring them to also go to Carthage (Gesta 11 50: Primiani professio; 111 206; Brew. 11 3). This is an interesting document from Primianus, which we only know from Augustine (Ad Donat. p. coll. 24,41), but to which the minutes of the Conference themselves allude when they mention a letter of apology from an elderly schismatic prelate, undoubtedly in response to this Primianist circular (Gesta 1 133; LAMIRANDE, 34s). Finally, Marcellin ordered that the place of the debates be the secretarium of the baths of Gargilius (compl. n. 55).—BIBL.: E. LAMIRANDE: BA 32, p.48-51; S. LANCEL, Actes de la Conférence...: SCh 194/1, p.31-34; A. Manbouze: PAC 1,671-688.

[551 The "secretarium" of the "Gargilius" baths.—It is understandable that Marcellin decided to hold the Catholic-Donatist Conference in Carthage, the African primal seat of both parties, whose demographic density was then around one hundred thousand inhabitants, the most

Additional notes 921 great African (LamIrANDE, 35; LerELLEY, 11ff; compl. n. 54). Not so much, of course, the chosen enclosure, the secretarium of the «Gargilius» thermal baths, as recorded in the minutes; «in secretary thermarum Gargilianarum» (Gesta 11.2.10); and in Saint Augustine: «In loco ergo collationis, hoc est in thermis Gargilianis, quia ipse postea locus placuerat» (Breu. 1 14: CSEL 53, p.47; Ad Donat. p. coll. 25,43; 35,58). We do not know what the originally intended location could have been, given that the Augustinian post leads us to conclude that at first another location was thought of. The exact location of the Gargilian hot springs has not yet been located either. Some specialists lean with Saint Augustine towards the center of the city: a middle city (Ad Donat. p. coll. 25,43, p.144), and towards a spacious, fresh and clear place, certainly very different from what the complaints of the Donatist bishops suggest, who spread the idea that they had been confined in a narrow enclosure, like a prison (Ad Donat. p. coll. 35,58). It couldn't have been so small when it housed more than five hundred bishops, in addition to the officium (compl. n. 56). In front of the Donatists, and within the same room, the Catholics took their seats. Neither of them left there until the end of the session (Gesta 1 97.217). It was planned to place chairs for the fourteen bishops—lawyers and advisors—of each party, but the crowd of attendees prevented them from being used (Gesta TI 3; LAMIRANDE, 35; LANCEL, 52).

The term secretarium then had multiple meanings, for example, the judicial one (SEEcK, 979s; HansLIk, 1655). In Carthage, the proconsul's praetorium had a secretarium (Passio Montani V1 13, 18), and in a secretarium Saint Cyprian was interrogated (Acta proconsularia Cypriani, 1; LAncEL, 52, n.3). Also the conciliar, by which was meant various enclosures and especially annexes to the basilicas large enough to hold a council inside. Many of Aurelius were celebrated in the secretarium, either of the Basilica Restituta (years 397, 399, 401, 408, 419: Mans 3,915,752,770,810,823), or of the Basilica Fausti (years 418, 419, 421: Mans13,810,699; 4,447; LanceL, 52, n.4; Maler=PERLER, 417 ss). The mention of a secretariuim in the Gargilian baths, then, should not be surprising. It is known that judges could set up their court in very different places, and it is not surprising that "Gargilius" was one of those prepared for such a circumstance. Appropriately enabled on occasions like this, these premises consisted of two different rooms: the dais or audience room for the hearing of the case (tribunalia), and the notary's premises, who were assisted by ecclesiastical notaries and bishops commissioned to follow the process. It was not necessary for the scrimia to be adjacent to the tribunalia, but close (LANCcEL, 342-347). In short, the tribunalia were the bench on which the judge sat, surrounded by his clerks. In that of "Gargilius" it was where Marcellinus, on the night of June 8 to 9 of the year 411, and after the parties had retired, wrote the sentence: "... et utriusque exeuntibus sententiam scripsit" (Breu. TI 25,43: CSEL 53, p.92).—BrBL.: R. HANsLIK, Secretarium und tribunal in den Acta Martyrum Scillitanorum: Mélanges Chr. Mohrmann (Utrecht-Anvers 1963) p.165-168; E. LAMIRANDE: BA 32, p.35; S. [561 The "officium" of the Conference of Carthage.—On the morning of June 1, 411, Marcellin entered the audience hall surrounded by a fairly large officium, unchanged during the second session and completed on June 8 to a total of twenty-three, including scribes and secretaries. For the registration of processes, the imperial commissioner used to have his officium, that is, the work office or team of the aforementioned scribae and exceptionres (LePELLEY, bibl. infra; compl. n. 21). The members of the Conference of Carthage were: Nampio, clerk of the legate's office; Rufinianus, clerk of the curator of Carthage; Hilario and Pretextato, secretaries (exceptors) of the proconsul's office; Fabio, secretary of the vicar, and Rómulo, secretary of the legate. These six bureaucrats were assisted by two notaries (motarii) from each party: Jenaro and Vidal for the Catholics; Victor and Cresconio for the Donatists. The stenography was ensured, therefore, with four secretaries of the official services and four ecclesiastical notaries, of whom the Conference document does not seem to have given the complete list (LancEL, 345.390s).

The members of Marcellin's officium kept during the Conference not the hierarchical order of their personal dignity, but that of the authorities they represented (Gesta 11; 11 1; TI 1; Lancer, 342-346): first the three protectors domestici as officers of the general staff of the imperial authority (STEIN, 123.240; FRANK, 88. 178; Jones, 548.637-639); then, two agents in rebus (Gesta 11; LanceL, 54; LePELLEY, 11 1455). Provisionally separated from each other from the central services (deputati), they had been placed - probably from the autumn of the year 410 - under the direct responsibility of the imperial commissioner. During the months prior to the Conference they were in charge of controlling the edicts of the emperor and Marcellinus and of carrying out numerous municipal minutes (compl. no. 53). Their silence in the debates would be due, according to Lancel, to the fact that they attended as senior officials of order. The intervention of agents in rebus in religious matters is frequently attested from the 4th century onwards: they served as messengers between the imperial court and the bishops and attended councils as spokespersons for the emperor (FRANK, 1155; LANCEL, 55, n.2). On the other hand, the attendance of protectors domestici at an ecclesiastical meeting like this one of the Conference does not seem to have had a precedent within their usual missions (FRANK, 90-96; Jones, 637; LanCEL, 56).

Five officials of the prefect of the praetorium followed in rank: three of the equestrian order (ducenarii), an honorific title still in the 1st century, and two apparitores, that is, illiterate officials, or ushers, or simple executors of justice (LanceL, 56-57; LerELLEY, 11 1285; STEIN, 57; CHASTAGNOL, 377.382). And behind, two apparitores representing the count of Africa, this time qualified as illustris (Gesta 11; STEIN, 27, n.2). And the proconsul (spectabilis) had detached from his office, to put at the disposal of Marcellinus, in addition to two notaries, five officials, namely: two subordinates (adimtores cornicularii) of two important chiefs of office - cel cornicularius was the second person in the proconsular chancery - and three subordinates of the chief himself. [571 The objective of the Catholics at the Carthage Conference of 411.—At first glance it seems clear: "ut superstitionem manifesta ratio confutaret" (Breu, 11: CSEL 53, p.39). Analyzed closely, however, problems of interpretation emerge. Expanding on Lancel's judgments about the imperial edict of convocation, and against the common sentiment of specialists, Courtois allows himself to doubt Augustinian honesty and moderation in the debates (136, n.2; compl. n. 51). Also in accordance with the "partialité naive ou cynique" of the imperial rescript, Monceaux, on the contrary, is indignant against those who claim that the Conference was rigged by the Catholics, and it seems unserious to suppose that three hundred Catholic bishops came to Carthage to perform the comedy, whereas for an overseas Catholic, just as for the civil authority and even the Church itself, "peu importait au fond que le Donatisme fút victorieux ou vaincu» (Breu. TIT 5.6; MonceaAux, IV 715.393). The question is not so simple for Lamirande (BA 38, p.36).

Can a "brutal partiality" really be admitted in the convocation edict? (LANCEL, 29s). For now, Lancel disagrees with previous specialists when he considers it untenable for Marcellin to keep Honorius' edict secret until the day of the opening. But if he made it public beforehand, why didn't the Donatists raise this argument during the debates, knowing as they did the good dispositions of Marcellin, and they were so willing, moreover, to take advantage of the slightest favorable loophole, such as the lapsus temporis? (mn. compl. 54 and 52). Courtois addresses such an important matter "sans vouloir aborder ici une question quí sort du cadre de this étude" (136, n.2).

The objective of the Catholics at the Conference was, of course, to clarify the truth. They were sure of their cause, which is not a bad thing. Augustine, in particular, not only says that the Conference had set out to confuse error (Brew. 11; III 2). He also states that it was celebrated to achieve peace and unity: "ut pax atque unitas ieront" (Brey. 17, p.42); «ut nobis conferentibus ueritas appareret et dissensio quae nos diuidit de medio tolleretur» (Ad Donat. p. coll. 11: CSEL 53, p.97). It is difficult to interpret the events and environment of that time with our categories. That Catholics took a favorable ruling for granted, true. It didn't even occur to them to doubt, too. They were sure of victory, so that what they intended
924 Additional notes

It was to commit the civil power to the cause so that, in this way, it would apply more rigorously, it is possible, but above all more effectively the measures taken in order to reestablish unity, as surely as possible. But this does not mean, in the least, that they intended anything less than to represent a comedy. A good starting point, perhaps indispensable, seem to me to be the Augustinian facets of the debater and the pastor (W1rLLIs, 169; MaNDouzE, 333; LAMIRANDE, 37).

In short, it was about good for the Church and the health of the brothers. The holding of a "contradictory" Conference could not but be beneficial. With it, the truth would emerge clarified and strengthened. Augustine himself became convinced of this when he noticed the limited results achieved with particular and isolated debates. The same thing had to be done, but with a dialectical hand in hand between the two episcopates reunited. The Catholics were so sure of themselves that they went to Carthage almost, as it were, mortgaging the pastoral position. One may agree or disagree regarding the means used to enclose the two episcopates in the baths of "Gargilius", but it must also be recognized that Donatist obstinacy and excesses overwhelmed Honorius's patience (compl. no. 13). With the 411 Conference, Catholics sought less punishment than reconciliation; less to condemn than to clarify the truth. Nor had the Donatists refused to go to the emperor in situations advantageous to them. After all, neither for one nor for the other was the emperor's last word, although it was a confirmatur or valuable endorsement in the context of the time. And more than elucidating the truth, which was absolutely clear to them, what the Catholics intended was to convince of it those who, in their opinion, were undoubtedly in error (Brisson, 2s).—BrBL.: P. [58] The argument of number at the Carthage Conference.—What was the cause that pushed Primianus to the Carthage Conference of 411 is not known exactly. Maybe several. We do know, however, the news of his circular letter (tractoria), in which he told his followers that "those who did not come would leave the best of their cause compromised", in clear allusion to the argument of the number (Ad Donat. p. coll. 24,41; Brew. 11 2). This is where Petiliano's insistence on the first day of sessions points out: «... id primum peto de nobilitate tua ut superfluum non sit de numero utriusque partis ferre debene iudicium celsitudinem tuam (Gesta 1 70); «Omnis enim intentio nostra, uir nobilis, sicut meminisse dignaris, de numero saepissime causata est, atque in eodem uchementissime haeret» (Gesta 1 165; cf. 1 61, final).

The Donatist episcopate was probably weighed down by the conviction that, if they did not attend, they would lose everything without having measured themselves against the Catholics, even though they formed such a large number. Marcellin's tempting promises would also have their incentive, regardless of the fact that some were later unfulfilled, which gives rise to more than one specialist to negatively judge Catholic behavior at said Conference (LANCEL, 35, n.3; compl. n. 57). Nor would it fail to contribute to seeing the Maximianists excluded from the debate, a decision made only in a second edict, that is, on December 20.

Complementary notes 925 May (Gesta 1 10; compl. n. 60). There are those who are inclined to believe that Marcellin would have made known by word of mouth or by any other means - not an edict, of course, since there is no record of his existence - the inappropriateness of the Maximianist presence. Some texts allow us to conjecture that they would have addressed a libellus of appeal not precisely to Marcellin, but to the Catholics themselves, who, in turn, would have advised the judge to dismiss the matter (C. lul. o. ¿. HI 5). Finally, the pompous entry of the Donatists into Carthage (compl. no. 52) could have been due to the argument of number.

Saint Augustine ironically refers to the vanity of the Donatists wanting to claim numerical superiority (Ad Donat. p. coll. 24,41). Of course. For truth, as for law, it is not the number that counts, but the arguments. But the D. was a schism of growing strength from its origins, to the point of disturbing the civil authorities and the Catholic Church itself, whose bishops, after recognizing in their synodal letter that they were a minority only in consular Numidia, did not fail to warn through the mouth of Fortunaciano de Sica that if the debate had depended on this reason they would have been able to demonstrate that they were the majority in Africa (Gesta 1 18.168; PAC 1,482-485). For the rest, the pressing reasons and dry discussions of Fortunatian and Alypius about the Donatist list as well as about the absence of bishops and vacant sees, and the concern of the latter, once the discount had been made, to assert through the commissioner a supplementary list of Catholic bishops, most of them actually absent, clearly shows the importance that in the circles of Aurelius and Augustine was given to the fact of not appearing, in order of accounts, inferior in number. Well proven, on the Donatist side, is the determined will to assert mass, number, as a sign of superiority. Petiliano especially let it shine through when he accused the Catholics of having multiplied the dioceses without valid reason and only for the sake of numbers (Gesta 1 65.117; LanceL, 109).—BiBL.: S. LanceL, Actes de la Conférence...: SCh 194/L, p.34-38; cf. also c.Il: La représentation des deux Églises á la Conférence de 411, p.107-190.

[60] The second edict of Marcellin.—Informed of the arrival of the parties, Marcellin prepared to cover the final stretch of the preparations for the Conference (n. compl. 51 and 54). Dated, therefore, probably after May 18, and certainly before May 25, since the Donatists responded that same May 25, 411, he published a second edict to set the opening date and the regulations to be followed in the debates (Gesta 1 10.14; PAC 1,672; LANcEL, 338).

With this long and detailed document, revealing the good administrative work of his chancellery, Marcellin: 1) Protested in the brief preamble of his unworthiness to handle the case, at the same time underlining the importance of the debate and its preparation (Gesta 1 10,3). 2) He then dictated the procedure that should be followed; adopting an incidental phrase from Honorius – “ut electis etiam sacerdotibus quos pars utraque delegerit” (Gesta 14) – he made it known that each party had to designate seven spokespersons before the opening day. It seems that the Catholics had suggested this initiative to Honorius, and now, with Marcellin, they continued with it, understanding that it was the best. Regarding the figure, Lancel believes that it could have been due to practical reasons (Gesta 1 10; LanceL, 38, n.4; 95). 3) These spokespersons could have seven advisors with whom they can communicate in places close to or adjacent to the room, certainly not in the room and during the debates. 4) It established that the opening date would be June 1 and the place would be the "Gargilius" baths, whose session premises could only be entered by delegate bishops with their respective advisors. Marcellin also insisted that both clergy and laity remain on the sidelines in order to ensure tranquility in the debates (Gesta 1 10). 5) It was necessary for the delegates or representatives to ratify before

Additional notes 927 of the opening the credentials of its spokespersons. 6) As proof of impartiality, and given that the majority of the public and the bishops were going to be left outside the session room, Marcellin promised to publish in full and without delay the verbal process of the debates, whose stenographic message would always be authenticated with the signature of the spokespersons, in order to specify responsibilities and avoid useless responses (Gesta 1 10; Lancet, 350). 7) Detailed exposition of the provisions in order to ensure, as far as possible, taking notes, drawing up minutes and publishing, in short, the content of the processes (LANCEL, 342-353). 8) It excluded the Maximianists from the debates, since they were condemned by the D. 9) It reminded the parties of the obligation to express before the opening day and through a document signed by the respective primates their agreement or disagreement with the clauses of the edict (Gesta 1 10).—BrBL.: S. LancEL, Actes de la Conférence...: SCh 194/1 (Paris 1972); A. Manbouze: PAC 1,672s.

[61] Catholic proposals of May 25, 411.—In a letter of May 25, the Catholics gave their open and generous consent to the second edict of Marcellin, at the same time advancing to the Donatists two new and fundamental proposals: one, of a tactical nature, which consisted of inviting the opposing party to abandon its obstinate refusal to meet with the Catholics and put an end to the delaying maneuvers (Gesta 1 16; S.A., Ep. 128,1; The Catholics returned to it with a second letter and above all with the Mandatum (Gesta 1 18; Lancet, 41, n.3; compl. n. 15); another, rather ecclesiological, by virtue of which the Catholics pointed out that for them there would be neither winners nor losers, since it was not about winning, but about convincing and reconciling. Hence his proposal was double in this case: a) if the Donatists won the cause, the Catholics would then resign in favor of those who had made the truth known and prevail (Gesta 1 16; Brew. 15; Ep. 128,2); b) Otherwise, the Catholics would welcome the Donatists who had returned to Catholicism, sharing with them on an equal basis—since they were not going to lose either sacramental powers or dignity—the tasks and responsibilities of the ministry (Gesta 1 16; Ep. 128,2; LAMIRANDE, 285-308).

We know from Saint Augustine some particulars of section a): at first the plenary assembly of three hundred Catholic bishops, apparently by a commission formed for this purpose that probably studied the case in the secretariat of the Restituta basilica, supported what was nothing less than a mortgaging of his permanence in the pastoral ministry. There were only two exceptions: an elderly prelate who rejected the agreement and another who remained silent. Both, however, ended up joining the common opinion, thus making it unanimous (G. c. Em. 16; MoncEaAux, IV 404; LanceL, 42, n.1; compl. n. 59). Regarding section bh), it is necessary to point out that the text presents a solution of alternation between both bishops of the place, with variable periodicity and rotation, it is true, but in which it is seen that the existence of a Donatist basilica and another Catholic one in the same city is already a material element that can greatly facilitate things. There are indications that this solution could have been inspired by the case of the Donatist Prímulo, bishop of Vaga, in the Proconsular, today Beja, in Tunisia. Primulus: and Ampelio sat next to each other at the Conference, although it is true that it is unknown what forms of coexistence existed between the two and whether it continued (Gesta 1 215.176; PAC 1,67.916). the same

Regardless of the pastoral and legal complications that the aforementioned hypothesis posed, it is necessary to recognize that the Catholic document reflected great skill, proven experience - such a project was not new (Ep. 128,3) - and above all great ecumenical stature, because it meant going ahead of the brother to open the door to an honorable exit. [62] Preparation of the minutes at the Carthage Conference of 411. The textual composition of these minutes constitutes one of the most interesting arguments that the student of religious history of Antiquity can face, since it allows us to know the most common methods, at the beginning of the 20th century. v, in the work of the imperial chancery and the ecclesiastical scrinia. They are mostly a mosaic of loose pieces of diverse origin, added by order of Marcellin to the summary of the Conference itself. Lancel and Lamirande offer their list, which, for the study of the now lost part of the minutes, relies, like Monceaux, on the indications of the Brewiculus (LanceL, 238-242; LAMIRANDE, 69-76; MONCEAUX, IV 503s). To ensure the editorial integrity of the debates, a large team of secretaries, archivists and stenographers was mobilized and timely measures were taken to put the issue of authenticity beyond suspicion (Breu. 14; Ep. 141,2; STEINWENTER, 136ss; LANCEL, 390s; compl. n. 56). To the list of documents fully written and read during the debates it is necessary to add other pieces not small in number. The dossier, however, suffers from important gaps in two thirds of the total of the third session (LANCEL, 366; LAMIRANDE, 73-76; MONCEAUX, 1V 487-490). Duchesne once studied the issue of dating, which can be consulted in Optato's appendix, and even more exhaustively in Von Soden.

The most voluminous part contains: 1) the interventions of the two parties (prosecutions); 2) the judge's interlocutory sentences (inmterlocuciones); 3) the formulas of presentation and recognition of the bishops when reading the signatures; 4) the annotation of certain details regarding the material organization and some incidents that occurred during the session. These are texts scrupulously stenographed, recorded and edited according to techniques that have been used by some scholars.

Additional notes 929 pecialists in recent decades (TENGSTRÓM, who is closely followed by LanceL, 342-53, and STEINWENTER, 136-39). The task of the officium of the Carthage Conference was heavy (compl. n. 56) and the responsibility of the exceptionr in charge of coordinating the records and reviewing the clean transcription was particularly great. Each team worked for about six hours before its members were relieved and, flanked by the archivists (custodes chartarum), began the operation of clearing up the work. Cleaning up the stenography was another no less delicate task. Before leaving the room, the archivists of both parties, in the presence of the judge and closely watched by the closest scrinia, stamped the respective seal on the codices (or tabulae).

Cleaning up the stenography meant: 1) confronting the parallels of the different writings; 2) eliminate possible discrepancies; 3) supervise the transcription (descriptio) with features that are legible and understandable to all (obvious apexes: Gesta 1 10). It was an operation ordered by Marcellin, it was slow, cumbersome in every way and it served to explain some reactions of the schismatics in the second session and even the postponement of the Conference itself (Gesta 1 10; II 23-25.28.35. 48.55, interventions especially by Emeritus and Petiliano; cf. TENGSTRÓM, 19; LANCEL, 348s). It took the notaries and notaries entire nights to clean up the processes of the first two sessions in several copies. Only on June 6 in the morning did both parties acknowledge receipt of the copies, and that thing turned out faster than expected, since Hilario, the main person responsible for this task, had promised to deliver them by June 8 (LancEL, 349, n.2; PAC 1,560).

This clean copy in several copies (editio) was the last phase of a process in which the following steps had to be taken: 1.", stenograph on sheets of parchment gathered in a thick volume bound in cloth; 2.", authenticate the judge and the spokespersons their interventions and those of their interlocutors (Gesta 1 10; 115; III 195, passim); 3.2, make purely formal corrections (emendationes) that the writing may sometimes require (TENGSTRÓM, 20-25; LANCEL, 350, n.2); 42, at the dictation of the notaries, finally, the notaries retranscribe what had been corrected (scheda subscripta atque emendata) to submit it to the seals of the judge and the eight archivist bishops, thus being ready, and authorized, the original minutes, to be kept in the archives probably of the proconsul of Africa (TENGSTRÓM, 27-30; LANCEL, 351, n.1). Lancel states in his excellent study that three fixations were necessary: ​​1.*, of the codices; 2.*, of the scheda or state of the descriptio; and 3.*, of the summary recomposed and ready for filing. And this is not all. There is still the information that could eventually be requested during the debates, which is why those in charge, in cases like this, had to obtain the data requested either by one party or by both parties, either by the judge or by the judge's officium; even by the public, since Marcellin had so arranged it in the famous document number 12, which, according to Monceaux, appeared at the head of the minutes of the first two days of the Conference. [63] Refusal of the Donatists on the second day of the Conference.

On June 3, 411, the Catholic and Donatist episcopates met again in "Gargilius" (Brem. 11 1-3; LamiranDe, 65.71.121-127; LawCEL, 82-84; Ip,, t.II). It was the second session of the Conference, which Augustine summarizes in the Brewiculus in this order: 1) the judge asks the parties to sit down; Catholics accept and Donatists refuse; the judge then comments that, in that case, “he will also fulfill his mission standing” (Brem. 11 1); 2) reading of the demand filed by the Donatists the day before and in which they demanded that "they be shown the mandate of the Catholics, with whose careful examination they could attend and be instructed on the appointed day"; 3) compliance of Catholics with the requirement of signatures (compl. n. 60); 4) Donatist disagreement: "they said they felt moved, since this was not the custom," and then asked to be shown the written minutes, which caused an uproar; 5) stubbornness of the schismatics in their attitude: they claimed to be unaware of the stenographic writing and demanded that, before continuing, a copy of the minutes be presented to them, to which the judge had to agree by ordering that the codices kept under seal be brought and what their own secretaries had written be read; 6) new Donatist complaints, this time because the secretaries had not managed to collect the entire previous report; 7) reply from the Catholics: what was initially demanded was that the Donatists be shown the mandate of the Catholics, which had been fulfilled; 8) new Donatist entanglement: without anything to object, the schismatics then raised the prescription of the day: «uoluerunt iterum praescriptionem diei refri. care» (Breu. 11 3: CSEL 53, p.49; m. compl. 52). Despite the complete response to all of the above, they insisted on requesting a delay, which the judge ended up granting, and of no less than six days (Brem. I 3, final).

Short session, then, and purely formal, not even described as such by the speakers of the 8th, since his expressions such as praeterito iudicio (Gesta YI 49), recenti negotio (TI 78), priore iudicio (111 88) do not refer precisely to this second session, but to the first. A session, moreover, that ended up disenchanting Marcellin and the Catholics: first, not wanting to sit down for the debate; then, do not access the authentication clause of your interventions until you have in front of you what was written on the first day (Gesta TI 20.23.25; Brew. 11 1-3). That was a dialogue of the deaf; something that was not standing (LANCEL, 83, n.1; KASER, 389.486). Without any obligation, Marcellin gave in and the Donatists grew, until they resorted to the fact that the judge's promise to make the verbal process pass cleanly had not been fulfilled: "notas non uidimus" (Gesta TI 43; 32.44.45.59; Breu. 11 3; LanceL, 3485.83). Nor was it to censure the scribes, who were very busy with so many stenograms to get ready, because it was no longer just the material difficulty of the task, but the short period of time to complete it (n. compl. 62).

It was a shrewd intervention by Augustine of Hippo that helped the judge get out of the impasse by granting the stubbornly requested postponement (Gesta 11 56.61; Breu. TÍ 3). It was preferable this way rather than overloading the minutes with verbiage. At least that is what Augustine says in this significant text of the Breuiculus: «quod cum uidissent catholici ad

In Carthage, indeed, the issue of clarifying who presented themselves as plaintiffs and who as defendants was much discussed. [65] Cause of the Church and cause of Caecilian.—Cecilian is a central figure in the Catholic-Donatist controversy. Chosen to succeed Mensurius in the Carthaginian see, he was strongly opposed by the most radical and dissatisfied, who preferred Mayorinus in his place, who soon disappeared and was replaced by Donatus (compl. no. 44). Accused before the emperor, he was declared innocent at the councils of Rome (313) and Arles (314) and was recognized as legitimate bishop of Carthage. His episcopal ordination was declared invalid by the aforementioned opposition elements as he had received the imposition at the hands of Félix de Aptonga, a traditor according to them (compl. no. 67). Having prevented food from being brought to the imprisoned Christians during the persecution of 303 and prohibiting certain forms of worship of the martyrs were the two biggest charges leveled against him (Breu. 111 13,25). Although he was acquitted as many times as his case was brought to court, the Munca schismatics never agreed to recognize him as the bishop of Carthage, so that, after the disappearance of Mayorinus, his rival would be the great Donatus for the rest of his years. Present at the council of Nicaea (325), he disappeared from the ecclesiastical scene shortly after (FrEND, 6375). Wishing to reserve the term Catholic for the party that emerged victorious, the Donatists attempted to describe Catholics as Caecilianists at least once at the Conference of 411, but Augustine of Hippo and his colleagues rejected any paternity of this type: the interpellation of Petilianus and Adeodatos is followed by a heated debate directly led by Augustine (Gesta 111 30.34.123.227-237; S. Ac., C. Cr. IV 45,54;

The idea of cecilianistas was linked in the minds of the schismatics to the desire to relate the cause of the Catholics with the cause of Caecilian (Breu. 11 4,5). For those in the party, the best way to justify their schism was to prove that they had been right in separating themselves from the sinners. Their thesis was, therefore, ecclesiological and sacramental: the first, demonstrating that they were the Church of the pure and should not be contaminated, hence the separation; the second, demonstrating that Caecilian's ordination had been null and void and that both he and his followers, due to their crimes or sins, had been left outside the Church. The Catholics' reply consisted of demonstrating that the value of the sacraments

The historical evidence had declared him innocent, but even if that were not the case, even if it were proven that he had been guilty, his cause could in no way prejudge or condition the cause of the Catholic Church: "causa causae non praeiudicat, nec persona personae" (Capitula gest. 11 272: PL 11,1251), a formula that the Emeritus himself had the imprudence of - it supposed the very denial of the D.— to launch in the middle of the Conference of 411, and that Augustine's brilliant dialectic caught him on the fly (LAMIRANDE, 694).

[66] The ordination of bishops in Africa.—At the end of the conciliar sessions, and already back in their seats, the bishops of Byzacena, on August 28, 397 —the first session had been on the 13th— forty proconsular, Mumid and Mauritanian prelates approved the Breuiarium of Hippo, with the following package of disciplinary measures: prohibition of rebaptizing, reordering, transferring to bishops and create new dioceses; necessary presence of three bishops for any episcopal ordination; announcement of the date of Easter by the primate of Carthage; providences against the usurpations of bishops over the rights of others, with the exception of the primate of Carthage, by custom authorized to support the churches that request it, the ordinations of candidates to the episcopate and the clergy in all African dioceses (CCL 149,143; MAIER, 37-39; MUNIER, 6045).

At the proposal of Aurelius of Carthage, annoyed at having to mobilize twelve neighboring bishops almost every Sunday, the question was raised again and it was agreed to renew what was established in Nicaea, that is, that for episcopal ordination the presence of three bishops was necessary. The fact that twelve were proposed in Africa suggests some tradition in this regard, probably forgotten or abandoned. Upon opening his schism within the party, Maximian was ordained by twelve bishops (C. Cr. 111 52,58; IV 4,4-5; compl. n. 31). The central Donatists

During the Conference of 411 Augustine clarifies that having the bishop of Carthage ordained by the primate of Numidia is a custom of the Donatists, and that among Catholics this function is performed by the bishops of the neighboring sees (Brew. 111 16,29), a moderately satisfactory answer according to Congar, since one of the consecrators of Cecilian - Felix of Aptonga - was from the Byzacena (Concar, 12, n.2; LAMIRANDE, 730). [67] Felix of Aptonmga.—Already bishop of Aptonga at the time of the persecution of Diocletian, Felix is usually known as episcopus Aptugnitanus, Abtungensis, Aptungitanus, Aptugnensis, Aptungensis, Aptucensis, Autumnitanus and also Autumnitanorum. The first council of the Schism, that of the seventy African bishops gathered in Carthage in the year 312, declared F. the source of all evil (fons omnium malorum), dismissed Caecilian and elected Majorinus. False accusation and unjust condemnation, however, of this council declaring F. a traditor, since the proconsul Aelianus, after meticulous investigations, proclaimed on February 15, 314 the innocence of F. while revealing, on the contrary, the clumsy slanders of the Donatists (CoNGArR, 714)..

The conciliar ruling of 312 served as a pretext for the Donatists not to abide by the Council of Rome of 313, which declared Cecilian's ordination valid; In his opinion, the judges of the Roman council had neglected to examine the accusations made against the consecrators of Caecilian, and for this reason they decided to appeal said sentence. Constantine then instructed his vicar of Africa, Aelius Paulinus, to reopen the case. Aptonga was the setting for the consultations, concluded in Carthage on February 15, 314, with the proconsul of Africa, Aelianus, presiding over the closing (PAC 1,44,838). The Council of Arles in the same year 314, finally, decided to put an end to the misunderstanding by declaring valid the ordination conferred by any traditor bishop (Can. 13). The dossier of the trial - Acta, or Gesta purgationis Felicis - has been largely preserved in the Gesta purgationis Caeciliani et Felícis, whose authenticity is attested to by Optatus, Augustine and the Gesta collationis. [68] Accusations against Saint Augustine at the Conference of Carthage.—Dated somewhat before May/June 395, the Catholic bishop and primate of Numidia, Megalius of Calama, wrote angrily to the still priest Augustine. We know nothing about the complaints that Megalio presented in said letter—now lost—against the young presbyter of Hippo; only that he opposed his episcopal consecration. Later required in a synodical assembly to prove the veracity of such charges, Megalius completely condemned them, judging them a slanderous accusation, and not content with having asked for forgiveness, he himself presided over the episcopal ordination of Augustine, thus becoming coadjutor or auxiliary of the bishop of Hippo, Valerius. Megalius died around August 28, 397. His personality, however, continued to be used after his death by the Donatists, who at the Carthage Conference of 411, for example, had no shame in manipulating his attitude when Augustine's episcopal ordination, highlighting the first part, the negative, and omitting, on the other hand, the second, the positive (Gesta 111 238-247: SCh 224, p.1176-1186; PAC 1,742).

The thing happened following an intervention by Augustine regarding the discussions raised by the title of father, applicable to bishops. Petilianus then abruptly asked Hippo: "Quis te ordinauit ut episcopus esses?" (Gesta III 238; cf. 2435). Petilian undoubtedly remembered the personal attacks launched ten years ago in his Epistula ad Augustinum (C. litt. Pet. YI 16,19, final) and he undoubtedly took advantage of the opportunity to repeat them provided by a topic raised precisely by Catholic bishops, Alypius among them, and which was off the program. Marcellinus then asked the Bishop of Hippo to respond to this charge, which the Saint immediately did, clarifying the superfluous nature of such a question, since neither Caecilian's cause, nor his own, nor anyone else's could condition or endanger that of the Church (compl. no. 65). However, he added a profession of faith to his response, which would be difficult to explain if it had not been in the spirit of the accusations (Gesta III 238-247). Once the paragraph was clarified, the discussion returned to Cecilian, and there was no more of the case of Augustine (LAMIRANDE, 711).

What accusations these were we do not know. Losses of youth perhaps? It does not seem that they worried the man of Hippo too much, who, moreover, had already responded to Petilianus about them (C. lit£, Pet. 1 10,11). His Manichaean past perhaps? This is already more plausible if we look at the aforementioned formula of faith, since Petiliano and Cresconius himself had hinted at this point on another occasion. Frend has studied the role of Manichaeism in the Donatist controversy and considers it considerable (859ff). Augustine himself admits in De un. b. 16,29 that the new bishop of Constantine, Fortunatus, like his predecessor, Profuturus, had been Manichaeans like him. Perhaps Petiliano intended, in this case, to cast doubt on the sincerity of Augustine's conversion, which he replies with the testimony of his numerous anti-Manichean works. In any case, it gives the impression that the Petillianist attack could have been of a general nature, that is, directed against Catholics in general, without ruling out, of course, Augustine himself, whose Manichaeism would have prevented him from meeting the Donatists during his youth (LAMIRANDE, 7115).
Additional notes 937

And what can we say about Megalio's refusal to ordain the priest Augustine as bishop? Petiliano had in mind, since not reading the famous letter of Megalio, which circulated among the Donatists (C. Cr. TII 80,92), but at least exploiting its content as much as possible. It would not be unreasonable to suppose that, among other reservations expressed in the famous letter—that of a love curse, for example (C. litt. Pet. TII 16,19)—were that of Augustine's Manichaean past (LAMIRANDE, 712s; LANCEL, 282).

Nor can it be ruled out that Petiliano intended to air the alleged irregular nature of the episcopal ordination of the Bishop of Hippo. Augustine consented to be consecrated after not a little hesitation, not to say that he yielded compulsus atque coactus (Posipio, VA 8), and after being convinced that no irregularity was committed with his ordination. But the truth is that canon 8 of Nicaea prohibited it (MansI 3,672). Ignorant of this prohibition, moreover, persuaded that his case had precedents, he ended up giving in (Epp. 223,4; 31,4; Manbouzk, 140s). When he later learned of the aforementioned canon, "he said and wrote that they should not have consecrated it," and that for his part "he did not want to be done to others what he regretted having been done to him" (Posipio, VA 8; BAC 10/1%, p.314s). For this reason, when the time came to proceed with the designation of a successor a few years before his death, he did not have him consecrated bishop while he was alive, in order to avoid any irregularity (Ep. 213=Acta ecclesiastica of September 26, 426). He managed to reestablish in the episcopal synods the norm by virtue of which the ordaining bishops had to notify the ordained and ordained of the statutes referring to the priesthood (Posinio, VA 8; CAPÁNAGA, n.7-9 (BAC 10) p.367s; LaMIRANDE, 713). Finally, the accusation of a certain type of Manichean monasticism in African lands could have had to do with Petiliano's grievances. The truth is that the serenity of Saint Augustine prevailed, convincing the Donatists that by this path of personal grievances they were not going to get anywhere (Quinor, 15ff; LANCEL, 282).—BrBL.: W. [69] Epistolary correspondence between Mensurius and Second of Tigisi.—Saint Augustine repeatedly mentions the epistolary correspondence exchanged between Mensurius and Second of Tigisi following the persecution of Diocletian and around the time of the "council of Cirta" (Breu. 111 17,32; Ad Donat. p. coll. 14,18; C. Gaud. 1 37,47; The Donatists used this correspondence to incriminate Mensurius at the Conference of 411 (Breu. 111 13,25; Gesta III 333-341: SCh 195, p.510-12). And Catholics, in the same circumstance, to reject such an accusation and at the same time demonstrate the reality of the "council of Cirta" or "council of Numidia" (Breu. TI 17,32; compl. n. 1).
In this correspondence, Mensurio is, on the one hand, formally free of the accusation of traditio, to the extent that the books delivered to the

938 Additional notes authorities in 303 were, rather, heretical books; and on the other, to a certain extent, suspected of commitment to power, to the extent that the proconsul, noticing that the bishop was concealing the "authentic Scriptures, closed his eyes (C. litt. Pet. YI 92,202; Brem. 1 13,35). This, added to the fact of expressing himself against those who, taking advantage of the persecution, posed as "confessors", as well as putting on guard the Christians faced with the provoked search for martyrdom, will be ample reason for, after 304, the martyrs of Abitina, through the famous manifesto, to accuse him, and the deacon Cecilian his collaborator, of the crime of traditio (Passio ss. Datiui, Saturnini presb. et aliorum, 20; mn. compl. 71).

If, on the one hand, the aforementioned correspondence leads us to suppose that Mensurius was cornered by Segundo - those of Numidia were more radical than those of Carthage -, to the point of forcing him to justify himself for the annoying matter, it reveals, on the other hand, that the communion between both regions and both prelates had not yet been broken and, therefore, that it is not necessary to take the definitive break beyond 312, when the party council deposed Caecilian (PAC 1,748; LAMIRANDE, 728). In light of this fact, the statements of Optatus and Saint Cyprian are apparently contradictory (MONCEAUxX, - 1V 9,321). It is true that the correspondence reveals a tone of suspicion and rivalry between the two bishops. Segundo leans – logically – towards the radicalism of the zealous Numidians. It has even been assumed that Second and the Numidians had entrusted Donatus with the mission of opposing Mensurius (Monceaux, V 100-109). But it must also be said, in honor of the truth, that the two parties remained united as long as Mensurius lived (De un. b. 16,29). In fact, the title of this last Catholic bishop of Carthage, before the breakdown of unity, is Carthaginiensis ecclesiae episcopus unitatis tempore (Gesta 1II 333: SCh 195; p.510; PAC 1,748, n.1). Anyway, in this era, yes; The tendencies that would eventually lead to schismatic consummation began to harden (LAMIRANDE, 727s).—BIBL.: E. LAMIRANDE, 31. [70] The Donatist basilicas and the Conference of Carthage.—The basilicas confiscated by Honorius in 405 and restored by Marcellinus to the Donatists in 411 were confiscated again after the Conference (compl. n.: 43 and 54). Marcellin himself made it known that the measure of benevolence had been his, not the emperor's, and that, therefore, "ita ut ecclesias quas eis humanitate mea absque imperiali praecepto constat indultas catholicis tradere sine ulla dilatione festinent" (PL 11,1419). The number of these basilicas is high and their identification is a difficult task: the ruins of Christian buildings still visible in Algeria and Tunisia number in the hundreds, and most of the time the archaeologist has a hard time distinguishing a Catholic building from a Donatist one. The advances made in this field are reflected in the good studies by J.-L. Mater and O. PerLEr, Cl. LEPELLEY, G. LaprYrE-A. PELLEGRINO and Ch. PicarD (compl. no. 59).

In the time of Father Monceaux there was much darkness. The only thing that was practically certain was the Donatist origin of the basilica of Ala Miliaria, currently Benian, about 40 km from Mascara, built before the Vandal invasion, between 434 and 439, in honor of the martyr Robba, victim.

Additional notes 939 scam of Catholics (MONCEAUX, IV 139; LAMIRANDE, 689). The inscriptions from the provincial period found in this building range between 422 and 446 (LereLLEY, 11 5205, citing works by Gsell). Add also that of Vegesela of Numidia, today Ksar el Kelb, in Tunisia, on the route from Teveste to Mascula, where archaeological discoveries have brought to light inscriptions, among which it is worth highlighting one related to the martyr Marculus, caned in this place, it seems, before dying in Nova Petra, rushing into the abyss either by order of the imperial commissioner Macarius, as the Donatists said, or by his own accord. suicidal will, as the Catholics replied. Saint Augustine confesses not knowing anything certain about the death of Marculo (C.. Cr. TIL 49,54; In Jo. 11,15; CaAYREL, 114ff; CourcELLE, 166ff; PAC 1,6965; Monceaux, V 69-82). The Donatist basilica of Hippo has not yet been found; After the Second World War, Erwan Marec discovered a Christian basilica, with important outbuildings, probably the Basilica Pacis of Saint Augustine (Marrc, 219ff; MARROU, 147ff; LEPELLEY, II 114).

In Cirta Constantina, where the Donatists managed to gather a council around 414 (C. Gaud. 1 37,47), the vicar of Africa, Claudius Avician, built in the time of Julian the Apostate a basilica with the name of the emperor Constantius (basilica Constantiana), a square building with four large arched openings, with a portico and tetrapylar, some of whose elements still survive with engraved inscriptions. on two of the reverse sides of the tetrapyle (LepELLEY, 11 385). In Thamugadi, now Timgad, the terrible Optatus Gildonian built a large church - <63 meters long - with important rooms, in whose episcopal house there was an inscription in memory of the famous schismatic bishop, which is still preserved. The Donatists of Timgad resisted fanatically after the Conference, to such an extent that in the year 422 the Donatist bishop Gaudentius threatened to burn himself and his faithful inside the basilica rather than hand it over to the traditors. The tribune Dulquicio, in charge of liquidating the resistance of the Schism in Timgad, the last stronghold of the D., hesitated whether to use force. Gaudencio, in the end, did not carry out his threat, but it is not known how that ended. It is significant that the great building built at that time in the town was the great cathedral of Optato, with its dependencies naturally, specifically a whole group of buildings forming a rectangle measuring 165 by 115 meters, with a surface area larger than that of the forum and its annexes. The complex was improperly called the monastery of the West. It is in the house, with a peristyle next to the church, towards the West, where an inscription has been found on the mosaic, in which it is read that the building was built "willingly by the bishop of God, Optato": Haec, lubente / priest Dei Op/tato, perfecte (LereLLEY, 11 474, n.112; 445, n.10; 4735; FrenD, 1018).— BimL.: P. [71] Mensurius and Caecilian.—Mensurius Carthaginian, bishop at least from the time of the persecution of 303 until his death in 311/312, appears in the minutes of the Conference of 411 as the last Catholic bishop of Carthage before the breakdown of unity: Carthaginiensis ecclesiae episcopus unitatis tempore (Gesta 111 333; SCh 195, p.510; S. Ac., From a. b., 16,29). In accordance with his moderate attitude, he decided to curb the martyrdom's impulses during the persecution, sometimes translated into spontaneous denunciations, which brought him hostility and, ultimately, the accusation of traditor in Numidian circles, suspicious of the growing authority of the bishop of Carthage. Mensurio was explained in correspondence with Segundo de Tigisi (compl. no. 69). For the Donatists, however, he would have given in during the persecution, and hence his importance in the debates of 411 (Mater, 364).

In 311 he was summoned to Rome by the emperor Maxentius to explain why he had refused to hand over the deacon Felix to the authorities: following the African massacres committed by Maxentius after his triumph over Alexander, Mensurius had hidden the deacon Felix, author of a harsh pamphlet against the tyrant (PAC 1,413). Before leaving for Rome, Mensurius entrusted the treasures of the Church to the seniors of Carthage, taking however the precaution of hiding his inventory in the hands of an elderly woman, whom he commissioned to deliver it, when the Christians recovered peace, to his eventual successor, in case he did not return. In fact, after the dispute in Rome, he was authorized to return, but he died on the way, at the end of 311 or beginning of 312 (Opratus, 1 17). His relationship with Theonas, bishop of Alexandria, is not impossible, nor even improbable (NALDINI, 2758). It is, however, true that his succession was the spark of the definitive rupture, and that at the Conference of 411 he will be, with Cecilian, accused by the Donatists. Petiliano's phrase is eloquent: «sed et Carthaginis Mensurius et Caecilianus ex ipsis sacrilegis flammis ut fauillae uel cineres remanserunt. turis enim conscientia omnes implicuit, qui Mensurio consentistis» (C. litt. Pet. 11 92,202: CSEL 52, p.125).

Caecilian is the first Carthaginian Catholic bishop after the schismatic division. Around the year 300, when he was still archdeacon of Carthage, he dared to confront the influential and ambitious Spanish lady Lucilla, because she, before receiving communion, had kissed the bones of an unrecognized martyr (mecdum uindicatus), which attracted the resentment of an entire group led by this woman (Opraro, 1 16; S. Ac., C. Ep. Parm. 13,5; Ep. 43,6,17.9,25). During the persecution, he urged compliance with Mensurio's instructions, which is why the martyrs of Abitina, through the famous manifesto, condemned him after 304 as a cruel man who had brutally prevented bringing food to the "confessors" detained in prison (Passio ss. Datini, Saturnini presb. et aliorum, 20; S. AG.,

Breu. IT 14,26). It is true that in this document he is not yet accused of being a traditor, but it is no less true that in an African text from the 5th century, he is associated with Mensurius (Liber Genealogus, 626). He was also a witness, in his diaconal times, of the schism that the Numidian Donatus caused to Cassis Nigris in Carthage, a schism that, according to Augustine, is found in the origins of the pars Donati directed against the Catholic Church (Breu. 111 12,24; compl. nm. 44).
With Mensurius dead, Caecilian is unanimously elected to succeed him (Opraro, 1 18); but as soon as it is ordered by Felix

Additional notes 941 of Aptonga, he is opposed by Botro and Celestius, ambitious for the position, who are incited by Lucilla and the prevaricating semiores of the Carthaginian presbytery, in whose possession was the treasure that Mensurius had left when he went to Rome, and that Caecilian claims for the Church. Desiring that the ordination be annulled, his adversaries appeal to the primate of Numidia, Second of Tigisi (compl. nos. 67 and 46). Second, then, he meets and presides in Carthage itself over the first Donatist "council" of the seventy Numidian bishops, and in the absence of Caecilian, he ordains Majorinus, his former collaborator, who, in this way, becomes the first Donatist bishop of Carthage (PAC 1,666 s.). Caecilian, furthermore, is accused before the Emperor Constantine through the proconsul, who transmits on April 15, 313, on the one hand, the libellus ecclesiae catholicae criminum Caeciliani traditus a parte Maiorini, now lost, and which Augustine mentions (Ep. 88,2; 93,4,13; Breu. TII 7,8), and on the other, the document generally identified with the demand for the "bishops of the party of Donatus" elevated to Constantine, or also "Preces", so that the matter of Caecilian could be submitted to the arbitration of the Gallic bishops (OpTaTO, 1 22; S. AG., Epp. 4324; 532.5; 76.2).

Cecilian was declared innocent in all the civil and ecclesiastical trials his case was studied: Rome, Arles, Milan (PAC 1,169-173). We barely have any news of his activity in Carthage, but it is known that in the years 316-321 he occupied the headquarters, and that Donatus - Mayorinus now dead - and those of the party evoked him with the enigmatic adjective Eudinepisus (Sermo de passione Donati, 2: PL 8,753B). It is problematic to affirm or deny his presence in Nicaea (325). On the other hand, it can be assured that in 343 he had already died, since that year it is Gratus who appears as bishop of Carthage. Along with the propaganda and reverence of the Donatists—and admiration of the Catholics—for Donatus, contrasts the little or no mention that Catholics make of Caecilian, limited, however, to defending his memory. Perhaps the lines of conduct of both Churches are involved in this: the Donatists, passionate about the prominence of the chief and leader and always proud of numbers; Catholics, on the other hand, are tenacious defenders of a theology in which it is necessary to always distinguish the cause of the Church from the cause of men. Faithful to this happy distinction, Augustine of Hippo rejected at the Conference of Carthage the appellation of caecilianists that the schismatics wanted to impose on the Catholics (n. compl. 65).—BrIBL.: W. [72] "Exsufflare Christum-exsufflare sacramenta"—The term. exsufflare, or exufflare (expel by blowing), precisely opposed to insufflare (introduce by blowing; infuse), appears with some frequency in Augustinian writings, especially anti-Donatist, with a sense mainly of baptismal exorcism, of an action liberating from sin and contrary to the devil (De pec. orig. TI 40,45; C. lul. VI 5,11). Referring indifferently to the image of the emperor, or to God, it is usually a derogatory meaning. With this rather insulting meaning it is usually applied to the devil, madness, and darkness (C. Iul. o. ¡. YI 199; TV 120). And with this insulting and contemptuous meaning it often appears in Saint Augustine when he wants to signify a sacramental action of the donors.

tists contrary to Christ and the sacraments, the baptismal above all (exsufflare Christum-exsufflare sacramenta): «quodsi haec et uestra sententia est, non in nobis detestemur et exsufflemus uel dei sacramenta quae nouimus uel ipsam fidem» (C. litt. Pet. YI 77,172: CSEL 52, p.107); «quomodo uindicandum est a regibus, quod Christi sacramenta exsufflantur, si prophetae membra, quia in periculum missa sunt, sic uindicati meruerunt?» (lb. 11 92,212, p.137s; 1I 92,211; 77,172; Quinor, 762). Saint Augustine blames the Donatists for exsufflare Cbristum when they rebaptize, that is, for despising the sacrament of God and trying to reduce it to nothing with their mania for rebaptization.

If baptism is always and in itself holy and, consequently, remains in the person who has received it, attempting to repeat it is equivalent to belittling the very action of God and considering it null. Hence the strong meaning of this term exsufflare, which comes to mean, I insist, the exorcism through which the demon is expelled from the catechumen: "ut paganus impius exsufflatur" (C. litt. Pet. 1 12,13, p.12). Well, that is what the Donatists do with Christ when they rebaptize: "sacramentum nominis Christi quod in eis sanctum est, exsufflatis" (C. litt. Pet. 11 81,180, p.112; 1 17,18; Ep. 52,3: "innocentes rebaptizantur et Christus in innocentibus exsufflatur"; Epp. 43, 8,21; 105,7; 108,3; In lo. ep. 2,3: «... exsufílare Christum»: PL 35, 1991; cf. De b. IV 15,22; Ad Caesa. eccl. 5; Adu. Fulg. 22; In lo. 11,14; In Ps. 145,16).

It is impious, therefore, and sacrilegious, baptismum exsufflare, and that happens every time the Donatists rebaptize: "aut quomodo non spernunt dominum, qui baptismum eius in eis, quorum causam non audierunt et de quibus iudicare nullo moda potuerunt, incredibili temeritate impietatis exsufflant et sibi audent arrogare quod dei est» (C. Ep. Parm. 11 19,38; CSEL 51, p.94); «et non patcitur ne ipse Christus in tot gentium milibus exuffletur» (15. YI 4,22, p.127; UI 6,29). A second baptism is, in itself, a null act that cannot erase the first, and in the intention of the person who confers or receives it consciously, a rejection of the alliance established with God in the first celebration occurs. For this very reason, the Catholic Church flatly condemns rebaptization, and in the Donatist who returns to it, it will try to straighten and heal the perfidia desertoris, but at the same time recognizing the characterem imperatoris (C. litt. Pet. TI 108,247; n. compl. 40 and 39). It will be well to remember, in conclusion, that the term exsufflare has frequently been used in debates about the sacramental validity or of heretical or simoniac ordinations, sometimes with the strong sense of annulling, that is, of considering or declaring them null (SALTET, 2255; CONGAR, 478, n.1; Quinor, 762).—BIBL,: C£. exsufflare voice, in A.
